News.title: Flight chaos caused by software defect in space of a millisecond, report says
News.content:
An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect" affecting the system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said.

The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.

The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred.

The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of its chief executive Martin Rolfe.

There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances.

In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety.

The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours.

The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place.

Martin Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption.

"It's our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong," he said.

"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."

Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports.

"It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway.

This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years.

In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers.

There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations.

Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences."

He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed".

Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience."

News.title: MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case
News.content:
He said "MI5 accepts without reservation" the findings of a damning report which concluded that it gave evidence based on "lies" about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the neo-Nazi informant.

The security service claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from a woman who was abused by him.

But what MI5 said was untrue. The security service had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.

A panel of three senior judges - England and Wales' most senior judge, Lady Chief Justice Baroness Sue Carr, President of the King's Bench Division Dame Victoria Sharp and Mr Justice Chamberlain - is considering what action to take over the false evidence.

In particular, it will decide whether to initiate contempt of court proceedings against certain MI5 officers or MI5 itself. Any such move would be unprecedented.

The report, by then-deputy investigatory powers commissioner Sir John Goldring, found that one senior MI5 spy - known as Officer 2 - lied repeatedly, while another - Officer 3 - misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.

He also found there were "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.

Otty said MI5 "fully accepts and acknowledges the gravity of the issues raised" in the report, published in July, and they must never happen again.

He added that MI5 had committed to a major programme of reform under the leadership of director general Sir Ken McCallum.

Otty argued against contempt proceedings being brought, saying it would not be in the public interest given Sir John's detailed investigation, MI5's apologies, and its commitment to a programme of reform.

He said Officer 2 had resigned from the service and that Officer 3 had been suspended and was facing disciplinary proceedings, which could lead to his dismissal.

Lawyers for both officers also argued against launching contempt proceedings.

Matthew Butt KC, for Officer 2, said said the officer accepted that his conduct had fallen "below the standard expected of him", for which he apologised and expressed regret.

But he said he denied acting dishonestly or having interfered with the administration of justice, and did not accept the report's findings.

Aaron Watkins apologised on behalf of Officer 3 and accepted his conduct "undoubtably" contributed to the courts and parties involved being misled, but denied it had been the result of dishonesty.

He said the evidence presented by Sir John fell short of the threshold for contempt of court, and said such proceedings would not be in the public interest because there had already been a thorough investigation.

Meanwhile, lawyers for the BBC said the corporation considered the threshold had been met and said there was a "very clear public interest" in doing so.

Jude Bunting KC said providing false evidence was "a particularly serious affront to the administration of justice" and noted that while MI5 now offered a sincere apology to the court, its response when the lies were first exposed was "not consistent with transparency or responsibility".

News.title: Women told breasts removed needlessly as NHS trust finds more than 300 suffered harm
News.content:
Dozens of affected women and their families contacted us after we reported concerns about serious failings at the trust's breast cancer unit. These included:

A high number of mastectomies compared with other NHS trusts

Operations that were carried out "too quickly"

Outsourcing of some treatment to private clinics run by the trust's breast cancer clinical lead - an arrangement that one independent expert said created "a clear conflict of interest

Patients described the shock they had felt on being told a mastectomy (the removal of all or part of a breast) could have been avoided, as well as the psychological and physical pain that many still live with.

We also met former patients who have come together to support each other and call for a public inquiry.

CDDFT is now carrying out an internal review of breast cancer cases between January 2023 and February 2025, alongside the cases of 640 former patients who contacted a dedicated helpline.

Of 514 cases reviewed by the trust so far, 315 patients have been found to have suffered harm, including 77 who were significantly harmed. One patient is known to have died.

It says that cases have also been identified where cancer diagnoses were missed or delayed. Some of these patients subsequently saw their cancer spread.

Russell has told BBC's Today programme that the trust will meet in the coming week to decide whether to extend the scope of the review, and look at up to 10,000 cases dating back as far as 2015.

He says the trust has been taking advice from patients' groups, clinical experts and legal representatives, and it will have to take "a really balanced view". Any decision, he adds, will be made public.

The National Crime Agency says it is now working with Durham Police to investigate allegations by former patients and determine if any criminal offences have taken place.

News.title: British rapper Sway dies aged 44
News.content:
But in 2010, DaSafo was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma.

"It felt like I had been dropped in the middle of the sea with no lifejacket," he later recalled.

"I didn't have time to think about how I was going to get to the other side, I just had to deal with it."

After receiving chemotherapy and radiotherapy, he went into remission, releasing his biggest hits Still Speedin' (which sampled Black Box's Ride On Time) and Level Up (featuring a verse from Kano) in 2012.

He enjoyed further critical and commercial success with albums including Deliverance, and Verses from the Vault; and collaborated with artists like Mark Ronson, Ed Sheeran, Akon and Childish Gambino.

Through his record label Dcypha, he also signed and developed artists including Tiggs Da Author and KSI.

All three appeared on the 2013 single No Sleep, and KSI went on to become a hugely successful YouTuber, with a sideline in music.

DaSafo also dabbled with an acting career, appearing in two episodes of the crime drama Top Boy and the 2012 film The Grind.

At the time of his death, he was working on new music. His final Instagram post, shared last week, external, celebrated his 44th birthday.

He is survived by two sons, Jalil and Ammar-Joseph, and twin daughters, Queen-Inaya and Queen-Imara. At the time of his death, he was raising them as a single parent in Ghana, his friend Kash Ahmad told BBC News.

"It was an honour and a pleasure to have known and worked with him, and my thoughts and prayers are with his family," he added.

Other tributes came from the Mitchell Brothers, who wrote: "We were privileged to have worked with you", and praised Sway's "true penmanship level and delivery".

News.title: Sisters of 'Putney pusher' suspect say DNA will clear his name
News.content:
The results of a DNA test will clear the name of Nicholas Brandram, the suspect in the "Putney pusher" case, his sisters have told the BBC.

The banker was arrested in June, nine years after a woman was pushed in front of a moving bus by a jogger on Putney Bridge in May 2017. He gave a DNA sample to police two months ago but never received the results, his sisters said.

Brandram was found dead in his west London home on Tuesday. His family have insisted he was innocent and said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the Met investigation.

The Met said it recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause, but did not respond to this specific claim.

News.title: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
News.content:
If the UK suddenly found itself at war, would you know what to do? Do you know what would be expected of you?

The government wants us all to start preparing for severe disruption to our lives. It wants us to stockpile canned food and drinking water, strengthen our civic resilience, and plan for the possibility of war.

Work has begun on the government's so-called "war book", which hasn't been updated in decades.

The UK's most senior soldier has sounded the alarm. The Chief of the Defence Staff Sir Richard Knighton this week said the threat from Russia meant Britain was living through the "most dangerous" period of his 35-year career in the armed forces.

But what is the threat? In 1940 the danger of a German invasion of the UK was very real. But the chances of Russian tanks rolling up Whitehall are surely negligible.

"It's not the tanks you need to worry about," says historian Margaret MacMillan, author of War: How Conflict Shaped Us.

"It's the cutting of cables on the ocean floor. It's the hacking into systems on which so many things depend. The possibility for asymmetric war, for cyber war, is growing by leaps and bounds."

But are we ready? After 80 years without war on our own soil, are we, as a society, psychologically prepared for it? Are we ready to approve large increases in defence spending, and for the sacrifices that that might entail in other areas of our national life? Or does the threat seem too far-fetched to be real?

News.title: 'Insufficient funds' to pay Brewdog creditors and unpaid wages after takeover deal
News.content:
Several creditors of collapsed Scottish beer giant Brewdog are not expected to receive anything from the administration process.

A report from administrators AlixPartners said there were "insufficient funds" for payouts from Brewdog's retail arm - including Â£2.4m owed to HMRC for unpaid VAT.

Brewdog had also owed Â£489,000 for wages and holiday pay, which will not be paid through the administration process. Staff have instead received compensation from the UK government's Insolvency Service.

The Aberdeenshire-based brewer had more than Â£500m of debts when it was sold in March to US drinks firm Tilray in a Â£33m rescue deal.

News.title: British woman rescued in Malawi shootout that left four suspected kidnappers dead
News.content:
A British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi nearly a week ago has been rescued in a police operation that left four suspected kidnappers dead and a senior police chief wounded.

Nusrat Osman, 47, was freed on Thursday during an operation on the outskirts of the southern city of Blantyre, police said.

Officers exchanged gunfire with the suspected kidnappers, who police said were armed with an AK-47 rifle and a pistol.

"The criminals got shot and were rushed to the hospital where they succumbed to the injuries," the Malawi Police Service said in a statement.

Deputy Inspector General of Police Noel Kayira, who was involved in the operation, also sustained gunshot injuries and is being treated in hospital. The police statement said he was in a stable condition.

Osman was reunited with her family following the rescue and was also taken to hospital for treatment, and for physical and mental health assessments, local media reported.

Police inspector general Richard Luhanga said she was "still traumatised", and told AFP news agency that they will interview her when she is "settled properly".

"The motive is still not known but the investigations are ongoing," he added.

Osman's younger brother, Shobi Jiwa, praised the Malawian police for securing her release, telling the UK's Sun newspaper that the family was deeply grateful for the force's efforts in investigating the kidnapping.

He also paid tribute to Kayira, the police chief who was shot during the rescue operation, describing him as the family's "hero" for putting his own life at risk to save her.

Police have not identified the four suspected kidnappers who were killed and have not provided further details about how officers located the group.

Osman was abducted by four unidentified men in Blantyre's Mount Pleasant neighbourhood on 11 September.

Police said she had been driving home when the men blocked her vehicle, forced her into another car and drove away.

Her disappearance prompted a major search operation, with authorities offering a reward of 30 million Malawian kwacha ($17,000; Â£12,500) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest and conviction of those responsible.

Osman, who is from Leicester in the UK, has lived in Malawi for several years and works for an auditing firm. She is married and has two young children.

The UK Foreign Office earlier told the BBC that it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities.

The case had puzzled investigators because police said there had been no known ransom demand or communication from the kidnappers following her disappearance.

Her family had made emotional public appeals for her safe return, describing the disappearance as deeply distressing and urging anyone with information to contact police.

The kidnapping also caused concern among Malawi's business community and British nationals living in the southern African country, where abductions of foreign nationals are relatively uncommon.

Police have not disclosed whether they believe other people were involved.

They said investigations were continuing to establish the full circumstances surrounding the kidnapping and the subsequent rescue operation.

Authorities have urged the public to remain calm while the investigation continues.

News.title: British Steel plan lacks credibility, MPs say
News.content:
The government has no credible plan for the future of British Steel, MPs have claimed.

A report by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) said the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST) had not set out how British Steel, which runs its main plant in Scunthorpe and has operations in Teeside, would become profitable.

MPs warned steel tariffs could drive firms out of business or to move abroad.

A spokesperson for DBIST said it welcomed the report and would review the recommendations, adding securing the long-term future of the UK steel sector "was in the national interest".

A 26-page report, external, published on Friday, said the government was unable to provide clear estimates of how much the overall nationalisation could cost.

It had projected costs to reach Â£642m by 30 June this year, but the government later said it had only been Â£555m.

In April last year, the government passed an emergency bill to take control of British Steel amid reports the then-owner Jingye was planning to switch off two blast furnaces in Scunthorpe.

The Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Bill became law in July, taking the company into public ownership.

The government then published its steel strategy in March this year, which included an ambition for 50% of steel used in the UK to be made in Britain.

The strategy confirmed electric arc furnaces as the future of British steelmaking, replacing traditional blast furnaces, which resulted in job losses at steelworks including Port Talbot.

It also highlighted concerns that British Steel's 4,052 workers face uncertainty and the steel strategy is still vague about when the 50% target would be achieved.

The report said: "Without a credible long-term plan, uncertainty and costs for workers, industry and taxpayers will continue to increase."

News.title: Teenager jailed for life over ambush murder
News.content:
A teenager who travelled more than 150 miles from Leeds to London to stab a man has been jailed for at least 25 years for his murder.

Sulaiman Tajzai, 18, ambushed shop worker Farmanullah Sherzad outside the 26-year-old's home in Westminster on 27 March, stabbing him at least 10 times.

Sentencing him at the Old Bailey to a life term, Judge Angela Rafferty KC said he had held a grudge against Sherzad "based on a false suggestion of misconduct" and had been "effectively stalking him down like prey".

Describing the attack as "exceptionally violent", she told Tajzai: "It is not said on your behalf, nor could it be, that you had any justifiable or excusable grievance against this man."

News.title: Football club apologises for United 93 shirt advert
News.content:
A football club has apologised after it published images of a new clothing line with "United 93" printed on the back - the call sign of one of the aircraft hijacked on 9/11.

The clothing was supposed to make reference to Oxford United's founding year of 1893.

However, it said it had been released "without understanding of the historical context and associations".

United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing all 44 people on board after being hijacked on 11 September 2001. A docudrama film titled United 93 was made about the tragedy and released in 2006.

Oxford United was founded in 1893 as an amateur club called Headington and now plays in League One - the third tier of the English football pyramid.

In a statement, the club said its Campus Clothing range had been withdrawn and it "sincerely apologised" for the error.

"It should not have reached the point of sale and we take full responsibility for not undertaking proper due diligence," it said.

"We have removed the collection with immediate effect and are reviewing our approval processes to ensure nothing like this happens again."

The 9/11 attacks saw 19 Al Qaeda members hijack four commercial passenger planes in the US.

Two of them were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City, resulting in them both collapsing.

Another plane struck the Pentagon, near Washington DC, while the fourth plane - United 93 - crashed in rural Pennsylvania. It was believed to be destined for the US Capitol Building, also in Washington DC.

The attacks killed 2,977 people and injured tens of thousands more.

News.title: Woman detained indefinitely for stabbing two boys
News.content:
A woman who stabbed two 10-year-old boys has been detained indefinitely in a psychiatric hospital.

Armed police found the injured boys after forcing their way into a flat in Friskney in November 2022 following a stand-off lasting several hours.

Ann Marie McEvoy, 45, of Church Walk, Colchester, was tasered and arrested. In July, she pleaded guilty to two counts of attempted murder.

On Friday, she was sentenced to a hospital order under the Mental Health Act at Lincoln Crown Court.

The boys were treated in hospital for non life-threatening injuries.

McEvoy was seen holding a large knife prior to her arrest, the court heard.

Dr Tim Rogers, a consultant forensic psychiatrist, told the latest hearing the offences would not have happened had McEvoy been mentally well.

McEvoy suffered from schizoaffective disorder, the expert said, adding it was clear she needed treatment, potentially for the remainder of her life.

Judge Simon Hirst said he was satisfied the best way to protect the public was to impose a hospital order.

Doctors and the Secretary of State will decide if and when she can be released.

Addressing McEvoy, Hirst said: "Your need for treatment is likely to be significantly longer than a prison sentence.

"It is necessary to protect the public and it is not possible to say for how long that will be."

McEvoy was previously deemed unfit to stand trial and was made the subject of a hospital order in September 2024 after a jury found she was responsible for stabbing the boys.

The Crown Prosecution Service chose to resume criminal proceedings against McEvoy in March this year after her condition improved in hospital. She was deemed fit enough to enter her pleas.

Mark Knowles, defending, said McEvoy had entered guilty pleas because she not want to subject the boys to the ordeal of a trial.

Impact statements from both boys were read out in court.

One of them described how he suffered a punctured lung and was rushed to hospital for surgery on his neck.

The other boy said he had only just started feeling better.

Hirst also made a restraining order which prevents McEvoy contacting the children.

Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.

News.title: We have a duty to 'progress' Good Friday Agreement, taoiseach tells PM
News.content:
Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin has told Prime Minister Andy Burnham their governments have a duty to "mind and progress" the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.

Burnham said the relationship between the UK and Ireland matters "on every single level" as they met at Number 10 North for talks on Friday.

The pair were expected to discuss a further strengthening of ties including boosting trade, security and working with the European Union.

The prime minister said they were "working together" to uphold the principles of the peace deal for Northern Ireland.

Speaking ahead of their talks, Burnham said it "feels very fitting" to welcome Martin as the first international visitor to Number 10 North in Manchester.

"The relationship between the UK and Ireland matters so much on every single level," he said.

Burnham added that as "co-custodians of the Good Friday Agreement, we are working together to uphold its principles as we approach the 30th anniversary".

The Good Friday Agreement, also known as the Belfast Agreement, was a political deal designed to bring an end to 30 years of violent conflict in Northern Ireland, known as the Troubles.

The taoiseach expressed his sympathies with Burnham following the recent death of his father.

Following the meeting, Martin said the two leaders had gotten off to "a very good start".

"We have a prime minister who is instinctively very friendly towards us," he said.

News.title: Badenoch says she is instructing lawyers to challenge government after Tory-run council's 94% tax hike
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to potentially challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record council tax rise in one of her party's flagship local authorities.

She told BBC Newsnight the proposed 94% hike in Wandsworth, a south-west London borough run by the Tories, was "outrageous" but that "they're not doing it because they want to".

Badenoch said the Conservative Party had "instructed lawyers" to see if an Â£84m-a-year government funding cut, which Wandsworth Council has blamed for the increase, can be blocked.

The government said it was "fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest".

Wandsworth has long had one of the lowest council tax rates in the country, with an average Band D property currently paying just over Â£1,000, compared to above Â£2,000 in an increasing number of London boroughs.

But this would nearly double with the planned Â£958 rise.

There has been heavy criticism since the move was announced in a council meeting on Tuesday. A final decision is to be made early next year.

Changes to the funding formula for councils announced last year will see money redistributed from some council areas to others. Wandsworth Council said it stood to lose Â£84m annually in funding by the end of the next three years.

Commenting for the first time on the row, Badenoch accused ministers of seemingly "taking money from areas that don't vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour".

"I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth Council is having to put up council tax.

"But they're not doing it because they want to. It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding.

"So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative Party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision."

News.title: Teen who piloted Channel boat with 165 migrants jailed
News.content:
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, from South Sudan, admitted endangering others during a sea crossing on 23 July.

Prosecutors at Canterbury Crown Court said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat.

At the time, the so-called "mega dinghy" set a record for the largest number of migrants brought over on a small boat in recent years. That figure has since been surpassed with 230 people on board a vessel in August.

At Canterbury Crown Court on Friday, Judge Sarah Counsell said the offence was so serious "only an immediate custodial sentence can be justified".

She warned Atak that as a foreign national he was liable in principle to automatic deportation once he completed his sentence.

James Harrison, prosecuting, told the court the boat Atak was piloting was 12.8ft (3.9m) wide and 46.9ft (14.3m) long, a similar length to a standard bus.

The boat had travelled between Calais and the UK and was deflating when it was picked up by border force vessels.

News.title: Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail nine years after being detained in India
News.content:
A Scottish Sikh activist who has been locked up in India for almost nine years without conviction has been granted bail.

Jagtar Singh Johal, from Dumbarton, was arrested and detained in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.

The Indian authorities have accused him of having a role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures.

His family said they were still waiting for the details of what will happen next but are "relieved" by the Indian court's decision.

Court documents show Johal was granted bail at Delhi High Court.

As part of his bail conditions, he has to surrender his passport and is barred from speaking to the media about the case.

He must pay a personal bond of 500,000 rupees (Â£3,907) and is only allowed to access one phone.

The 39-year-old was acquitted last year in a case in which he was accused of financially supporting terror group the Khalistan Liberation Force (KLF), which has carried out attacks in the Punjab region.

But he still faces federal charges lodged by the Indian authorities.

Duncan Sheik, the Tony Award-winning composer of the hit Broadway musical Spring Awakening, had died at 56.

The New York Times was first to report the news. Sheik died Thursday night of organ failure at a hospital in Manhattan, his mother told the outlet.

Sheik’s family put out a statement earlier this week on Instagram that the composer was “receiving medical care” and was in “critical but stable condition.” Further details weren’t made available.

In a follow up post announcing his death, his family wrote: “The world has a lost a singular talent, and deeply influential voice in music and theater. From his Grammy-nominated hit ‘Barely Breathing’ to his groundbreaking, Tony and Grammy Award-winning work on Spring Awakening, Duncan’s artistry touched many and leaves an indelible mark on the cultural landscape.

“Duncan was a father, husband, son, brother, and friend. He will be remembered for his sensitivity, wit, intelligence, and depth of spirit he brought to those who knew and loved him.

“We are deeply grateful for the outpouring of love from his fans, friends, collaborators, and the artistic community. His musical legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.”

At the time of his death, Sheik was working on the new musical Memoirs of Amorous Gentlemen, which is slated to begin preview performances September 25 at Off-Broadway’s new venue, The Night Egg at the Culture Club.

A revival of Spring Awakening, which won Sheik two Tonys for Best Original Score and Best Orchestrations, is also slated to open Off-Broadway in the coming months.

Before he became beloved for his theatrical contributions, Sheik released several albums, including his 1996 self-titled debut.

Actor Stephanie Cole, best known for her roles on the TV shows Coronation Street, Tenko, and Doc Martin, has died at the age of 84.

Her agent John Grant confirmed the news on Friday in a statement issued on behalf of that family.

Cole had died that morning, after “living with Alzheimer’s disease for some years”, he said.

“Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television.

“She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama. She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities.

“During this incredibly difficult time, the family kindly requests privacy.”

Cole was born in Warwickshire in 1941 and trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School.

She played Dr Bea Mason in the 1980s TV series Tenko, a drama about a group of British women living in Singapore during the Second World War and their subsequent confinement in a Japanese prisoner of war camp.

She appeared in the ITV comedy-drama Doc Martin as Jean Norton from 2004-2009 and in Coronation Street as Sylvia Goodwin, the mother of Roy Cropper, from 2011-2013.

She was also known for her roles in Open All Hours and Waiting For God, for which she received the 1992 Best TV Comedy Actress award at the British Comedy Awards (now called the National Comedy Awards).

In 2005, she was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for her services to drama, the elderly and mental health charities.

Venezuela is nearing a deal to move $4 billion (£2.9 billion) in gold from the Bank of England to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York after a years-long legal tussle, it has been reported.

Led by acting president Delcy Rodriguez, the government and the opposition reached a rare consensus in August - to work together to recover 31 tonnes of precious metal locked away in London’s underground vaults.

Under the terms of the agreement, the Interim President would gain legal control over the bullion, but would not be unable to sell it immediately, the Financial Times reported.

“The gold is going to the US but Delcy won’t have direct access to it,” said an opposition figure reportedly involved in the ongoing negotiations . “It will be supervised and restricted.”

open image in gallery Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez has been involved in the deal ( Reuters )

The reserve could be deployed as collateral for government borrowings, including for reconstruction after the twin earthquakes devastated the South American country at the end of June, killing more than 6,000 people.

The World Bank previously estimated that the damage of what has been described as the biggest natural disaster in decades amounts to $19.6 billion (£14.4 billion).

If finalised, the deal would bring an end to a major dispute, which has lasted almost eight years, after Britain refused to recognise Nicolas Maduro as the legitimate president of Venezuela, claiming the 2018 elections were rigged.

In practice, the move blocked the Venezuelan government’s access to the gold.

open image in gallery Venezuela suffered widespread damage when it was hit by earthquakes earlier this year ( AFP/Getty )

The bullion has since been the ‌subject of a prolonged legal dispute in ⁠UK courts, and has not been released despite Maduro's capture by the US ⁠in January.

The UK Foreign Office said the government is not a party in the legal case to determine who should have control of the reserve.

“The matter is being considered through independent legal processes and is not a decision that HMG can direct or influence,” a spokesperson said. “UK Courts and the Bank of England are independent of HMG.

“The UK maintains its longstanding position of support for a democratic transition of power in Venezuela which reflects the will of the Venezuelan people.”

open image in gallery People walk past the Bank of England building in London ( Reuters )

Reports of the deal come as Donald Trump is making plans for a first-ever meeting with Rodriguez, as early as next week, sources familiar with the discussions told Axios.

It is unclear if the deal will be discussed, if the meeting between the two leaders takes place.

“Iran is tough, but Venezuela is without a doubt the president's top success and Delcy is a key to that," a Trump adviser cited by Axios said. “Unless something goes really wrong, the president wants to make time.”

The Independent has contacted the Bank of England for a statement.

Singer-songwriter Blackbear has settled a lawsuit brought by a social media influencer who accused him of manipulating her after first meeting her online when she was 17 and later encouraging her to use drugs.

The woman, identified only as Jane Doe, sued the 35-year-old musician, whose real name is Matthew Tyler Musto, in Los Angeles Superior Court.

Her attorneys notified Judge Jeffery D. McFarland on Wednesday that the case had been resolved and said they would seek its dismissal within 60 days. The settlement terms were not disclosed.

open image in gallery Blackbear attends the 2022 MTV VMAs at Prudential Center in New Jersey ( Getty )

Doe alleged that Musto took advantage of her youth and vulnerability for his own benefit and subjected her to controlling and verbally abusive behavior.

According to the lawsuit, she first met Musto online in 2012 while she was 17 and living in Texas.

Musto, who was already established in the music industry, allegedly recognized her youth, vulnerability and admiration for him and began communicating with her through social media.

The lawsuit alleged the "Hot Girl Bummer" singer later manipulated Doe's romantic relationships and exploited her emotional attachment to him for his own personal gain and publicity.

open image in gallery blackbear performs onstage during 2018 Coachella Valley Music And Arts Festival Weekend ( Getty )

Doe also alleged Musto provided her with excessive amounts of drugs and alcohol when she was 19 and 20, sometimes leaving her incapacitated, disoriented and unable to remember what had happened.

Musto's attorneys disputed her claims.

They previously described the pair's relationship as "tumultuous and emotionally fraught" and said they separated in summer 2025. His lawyers alleged the breakup became so difficult that Musto forced Doe to leave his home and later sought a restraining order against her.

The settlement comes months after McFarland dismissed several of Doe's claims after an anti-SLAPP motion filed by Musto.

The judge threw out allegations involving non-consensual distribution of intimate images, civil exploitation, invasion of privacy, defamation and public disclosure of private facts.

However, McFarland allowed other allegations, including civil theft and civil harassment and stalking, to proceed.

The judge said those allegations involved conduct including the alleged theft of Doe's possessions, encouraging her to use controlled substances, unwanted communications, monitoring and psychological manipulation.

Musto's attorneys had filed notice that they intended to appeal the decision allowing the remaining claims to move forward before the settlement was announced.

Doe's attorneys had argued that Musto's anti-SLAPP motion was "frivolous" and intended to harass their client and delay the proceedings.

The lawsuit, filed last November, also alleged that Doe remained in regular contact with Musto while he received treatment following diabetic shock in December 2024 and stayed sober in solidarity with him.

During that period, she alleged, Musto played songs he claimed he had written for and about her.

Within the halls of the Pentagon, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s wife has been given an unflattering nickname, according to a new report.

Jennifer Hegseth, who previously worked as her husband’s producer at Fox News, has become a prominent presence at the Pentagon and is viewed by some as one of his closest advisers.

Unnamed sources told The Daily Mail that she has a hand in managing the defense secretary’s activities and public image. “Now there’s a woman with an extremely tight leash on the man she married,” one source told the outlet. “She’s like his parole officer and PR agent all at once,” another source previously said.

Her degree of influence, the sources suggested, has prompted a derisive comparison among some staffers.

They have reportedly dubbed her “Yoko Ono” after John Lennon’s widow, who was often portrayed by critics as a controlling influence on the late Beatles superstar. A narrative has also persisted for decades that she was the reason the band broke up.

open image in gallery Some Pentagon staffers have reportedly used an unflattering nickname for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's wife ( AFP via Getty Images )

When reached by the outlet, a Pentagon spokesperson described her as a “vital asset and a true force multiplier for our mission.”

The spokesperson added: “The Department of War not only welcomes her current leadership but actively plans to involve her even more deeply in the future. She is simply that valuable to our community and our nation.”

The Independent has contacted the Pentagon for comment.

Jennifer Hegseth, 49, is reportedly the defense secretary’s “most influential adviser,” attending high-level meetings, conducting interviews with prospective staffers and readying her husband for appearances.

She reportedly supported her husband’s combative posture toward the press, working with him to keep reporters out of the Pentagon, a Trump administration official previously told The New York Times.

Jennifer Hegseth, the defense secretary’s third wife, also attended a sensitive meeting last year between her husband and British defense officials, who were made “uneasy” by her presence. Also last year, she was included in a now-infamous Signal group chat last year in which her husband shared plans for a U.S. attack on Yemen.

open image in gallery Jennifer Hegseth attends Lindsey Graham’s funeral service in July alongside her husband, Todd Blanche, Scott Bessent and other Trump administration officials ( Getty Images )

In August, the Trump administration announced Jennifer Hegseth was taking on more responsibilities, naming her the chair of the newly created Presidential Military Spouse Commission.

Democrats have described her degree of access and influence as highly unusual.

The defense secretary, who has played a leading role in the ongoing Iran war and has enacted sweeping changes at the Pentagon, has also been given a few nicknames of his own.

Behind his back, some staffers are said to call him “Colonel Vodka” and “Whiskey Pete,” references to accusations that he had drinking problems — claims the Trump administration has dubbed “completely unfounded,” the Mail reported.

Some staffers have also dubbed Pete Hegseth “No Tab Pete” — a nod to his “lack of elite combat insignia,” per the outlet. The defense secretary, who served in the Army National Guard, previously deployed to Afghanistan and Iraq.

A Pentagon spokesperson characterized these claims as “fake news.”

News.title: Woman convicted of negligent homicide in Super Bowl reporter’s death in New Orleans
News.content:

A woman was convicted of negligent homicide Thursday in the death of a Telemundo television reporter who had been visiting New Orleans to cover the Super Bowl.

Danette Colbert, 49, was also convicted of racketeering, as was her accomplice, 35-year-old Rickey White, according to the Jefferson Parish district attorney's office. Racketeering carries up to a 50-year sentence in Louisiana.

The two had spent years carrying out a criminal enterprise that drew in victims in the city’s historic French Quarter with the promise of sex, then used drugs to knock them out and drain their bank accounts using stolen cards and phones, prosecutors said.

Colbert was the last person seen leaving the room of Adan Manzano, a 27-year-old reporter and anchor for Telemundo based in Kansas City, Missouri, who was found dead in his hotel room Feb. 5 in the New Orleans suburb of Kenner days before the Super Bowl last year.

open image in gallery Police quickly zeroed in on Danette Colbert, who was seen leaving Adan Manzano’s room before he was found dead ( Kenner Police Department )

An autopsy revealed that Manzano died lying face down on a pillow, unable to breathe after ingesting a combination of alcohol and the depressant Xanax.

Prosecutors had sought to convict both Colbert and White on the charge of manslaughter, which carries up to a 40-year sentence. White was found not guilty.

Colbert's negligent homicide conviction carries a maximum sentence of 10 years, Jefferson Parish Assistant District Attorney Jenny Voss told reporters. She said the jury had carefully weighed all the evidence and she respected its decision.

“We are pleased with the verdict — we knew this was a difficult case going in," she told reporters. “Justice was served."

Manzano’s family was unable to attend the trial, Voss added.

Colbert, whose arrest record included allegations of drugging men and theft, later used Manzano's credit card at a New Orleans gas station and other stores in the area.

open image in gallery Manzano’s death came a year after his wife died in a car accident. The couple left behind a toddler daughter ( Instagram/Adan Manzano )

In court documents, prosecutors described Colbert as acting under the guise of a “prostitute or ‘party girl’” while White served as her “pimp,” who provided security and helped find and rob victims.

Another man who assisted Colbert and White with their criminal ring, Christian Anderson, 35, testified against them in exchange for reducing his charges to simple robbery and access device fraud, according to Purpura. Court records show he pleaded guilty to both charges and received a six-year prison sentence.

Anderson “is relieved to be able to put this behind him,” said his attorney, Bradley Phillips. Anderson has been cooperating with law enforcement since his arrest and "has clearly demonstrated remorse for his past behavior."

In court documents, prosecutors revealed extensive text messages dating back years among Colbert, White and Anderson, discussing using drugs to incapacitate and rob victims.

Colbert and White are scheduled to be sentenced in late September, according to the Jefferson Parish district attorney's office.

Manzano’s death came a year after his wife died in a car accident. The couple left behind a toddler daughter.

News.title: That’s So Raven star found with stolen firearm sentenced to federal prison
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

An actor who starred in the hit 2000’s Disney sitcom That’s So Raven has been sentenced to 30 months behind bars at a federal jail for a firearm charge.

​Bobb’e J. Thompson, a 30-year-old actor from Kansas City who also appeared in NBC’s 30 Rock and the movie Role Models, was caught driving at 104 mph in a 70 mph zone by law enforcement back in September 2025.

​According to federal prosecutors, officers conducting a traffic stop in Cerro Gordo County, Iowa noticed Thompson and a passenger swap seats, and the smell of marijuana from the vehicle.

​During their search of the car, authorities discovered several bags containing marijuana as well as a fully loaded .40 caliber handgun - complete with a 15-round magazine and a round in the chamber.

open image in gallery Bobb'e J. Thompson has been jailed after being found in his vehicle with firearm that had been reported as stolen ( Getty )

​The firearm had been reported as stolen from a vehicle in Kansas City, prosecutors state. Thompson entered a guilty plea to the charge of possession of a firearm by a felon in April.

He was sentenced to 30 months behind bars at a federal prison by U.S. District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand in Sioux City on September 16. Under the federal system, there is no offer of parole. Thompson will also serve a 3-year term of supervised release after he leaves prison.

​The actor was known for playing neighborhood trickster Stanley in Disney’s That’s So Raven, as well as appearing on Tina Fey’s 30 Rock as Tracy Jr, the son of Tracy Morgan’s character.

​Thompson has appeared in several major film productions, including 2008’s Role Models, for which he was nominated for the Best Breakthrough Performance award at the MTV Movie Awards. He also appeared in the 2007 Christmas classic Fred Claus.

open image in gallery Thompson previously starred on several hit shows, including That's So Raven and 30 Rock ( Getty )

​Prosecutors say that Thompson was convicted of battery with serious bodily injury back in 2020, as well as assault with force. In 2022, he was convicted of prohibited possession of a firearm.

​The actor opened up about his previous convictions on the Eating While Broke podcast in 2024.

​“I caught a gun case," Thompson said on the podcast. "And then before that, I caught a case. I got in a fistfight and broke the boy (sic) jaw. And because of the jaw being broken, it was a great bodily injury, and it became a felony."

​The star is currently being held by the U.S. Marshals Service and will be transported to a federal prison.

Miley Cyrus revealed her final conversation with godmother Dolly Parton, saying the country music icon’s advice helped her understand how to maintain a larger-than-life public persona without losing sight of who she was away from the stage.

“I’m just trying to keep myself together, but the time that we talked, which was the last time we would talk, it was actually me telling her about this record, because even though we are so different, that is what made us so perfect for each other,” Cyrus told Apple Music presenter Zane Lowe, talking about her 10th and latest studio album Bass Persuades.

The “Flowers” singer explained that Parton had long been “the first person” she sent a vinyl record to whenever she had one printed. “And this time around I was going to send her a vinyl because I always do,” she said.

Parton died on 25 August in Nashville at the age of 80 after a brief battle with cancer.

Cyrus paid tribute to her godmother the following day, saying the “feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share”.

“Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour and between our hearts,” she wrote at the time. “What I know is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong. I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis.”

open image in gallery Miley Cyrus said godmother Dolly Parton had long been ‘the first person’ she sent a vinyl record to whenever she had one printed ( AFP/Getty )

Speaking to Lowe, Cyrus recalled how Parton’s advice helped her make sense of her own relationship with performance, especially during her years as Hannah Montana on the Disney Channel.

“She’s known for the fake, the hair, the makeup, and the show of it,” said Cyrus. “But there’s a part of her that I think is what everyone gravitates towards – how real she is and how authentic she is.

“There was a time in my life – we hit on it with Hannah – so much of my life was about persona. And I think a way that I could look at that as you can have a persona and still be who you are is because I’d Dolly.”

open image in gallery Dolly Parton died on 25 August in Nashville at the age of 80 after a brief battle with cancer ( AFP/Getty )

The “Wrecking Ball” singer likened her public persona to doing drag “because the way that I present myself is just someone that is so different from the person that feeds the tortoise every morning”.

“But again, that person’s inside of me. I just kind of have her off,” she said.

Cyrus talked about her tendency to cry on stage, bringing up her performance of “End of the World” on David Letterman’s My Next Guest Needs No Introduction in 2024 which she said was about “the world ending and me never seeing my mom again”.

“I start crying and she watched me on Letterman and was like, ‘What are you crying about?’” Cyrus said.

open image in gallery Miley Cyrus also talked about performing ‘I Will Always Love You’ with Dolly Parton in 2022 ( Getty )

Lowe said Parton was likely trying to tell her goddaughter to “be professional”. Cyrus agreed, saying “that’s pretty much what she said”.

“She was like, ‘Music is escapism. Let them cry. You need to get through it.’ And I was like, ‘I know, but this is who I am.’ And she loved me for it.”

Cyrus also talked about performing “I Will Always Love You” with Parton during the NBC special Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party in 2022, saying the “Jolene” singer “knew at that time that the reason I was crying is the reason that I cry now”.

“So many of my really stabilising peers that I have in my life [come from] generations before me,” she said. “And they’ve laid down, brick by brick, the road that I travel now. And they aren’t always going to be here for me to call them and say, ‘What do I do now?,’ which I always did with Dolly.”

“And she was always right. It’s like how your mom’s always right, and when you are a kid, you are like, ‘What does she know?’ And then as you get older, you’re like, ‘How? Where did this come from? You’re just a normal person. Why do you know everything?’ Dolly was just always right about stuff.”

Parton was a recurring presence in Cyrus’s career, appearing as Aunt Dolly in three episodes of Hannah Montana before they collaborated musically on “Rainbowland” and performed “Jolene” together at the 2019 Grammy Awards.

They also reunited in the recording studio for a reimagined rendition of Cyrus’s 2013 song “Wrecking Ball” for Parton’s 2023 album Rockstar, where the lyric “I will always want you” was changed to “I will always love you”.

News.title: Tuchel: Ninety-nine per cent of England fans do not discuss Argentina tactical mistakes
News.content:
Thomas Tuchel has claimed that “99.9 per cent” of England fans do not talk to him about tactical mistakes made in the World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.

The England manager has since admitted he was stuck in a defensive mindset during the match in Atlanta, but said on Friday – when he named his first squad since the summer – that supporters focus on other aspects of the tournament during interactions with him.

England also won against Mexico at the iconic Azteca Stadium and finished third in the World Cup after a 6-4 win over France in the ‘bronze final’.

“I’ll tell you something like 99.9 per cent of the fans don’t speak about substitutions, tactical twists and tactical things,” Tuchel said. “They speak about where they have watched the Mexico game. They speak about the second half and the energy of the Croatia match. They speak about how nerve-racking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated. This is the feedback that I get, and it’s 99.9 per cent.

“This is what we created, and this is how it should be. This is what a World Cup is for, to connect with the people and to give them experiences that they will not forget. And this is the feedback that I get; it makes me proud. Even if it’s just in a cab or in the coffee place or the supermarket, you share these little moments and you understand that it actually meant something and that what the players built was transmitted.”

News.title: Fiji declares national crisis as HIV epidemic escalates
News.content:
“The rollout has been slow and frustrating, and Fiji will pay for it in terms of lives lost,” said Prof Lisa Maher, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute in Sydney who is supporting Fiji’s response. “This is the only thing that will turn the epidemic around and stop people dying, and stop onward transmission of HIV to the general population.”

But the emergency declaration should provide political cover to introduce the needle and syringe programme, with a Cabinet subcommittee now created to remove barriers to action.

“The government is signalling that it is prepared to act in this particularly important and controversial area,” said Prof Maher. “It’s not coincidental that the draft bill [to legalise the distribution of needles and syringes for certain groups] now looks likely to go before parliament, after being blocked for 10 months… So it’s not just symbolic.”

Dr Jason Mitchell, head of Fiji’s HIV taskforce, added: “Since the government announced [the crisis], it has followed with some very rapid actions in progressing the needle and syringe programme. So that is being fast tracked through the necessary channels, and the government is determined to get that out in the next couple of weeks.

“We’ve gotten to the point where we really needed to take some really strong action,” he told The Telegraph. “This is the government realising that there have been challenges, and they need to step it up.”

It is hoped that the declaration will also turbocharge other elements of the response – for instance the scale-up of the post-exposure prophylaxis (Prep) scheme, which was introduced in May – as the virus gains a foothold in the broader population.

Although there has been a major focus on testing, treatment and education, UNAIDS still estimates that only 39 per cent of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in 2025 knew their positive status. Just 22 per cent were accessing antiretroviral treatment, and 117 people died in 2025, compared to 25 in 2021.

News.title: Floyd Samba’s Man City debut double has father Chris dancing
News.content:
There was very much a Samba beat to this Manchester City victory – and it almost had a famous father in the crowd up dancing.

This was a night when Brazilian Allan Elias scored his first goal on an enterprising first appearance for City.

But it was another debutant who stole the show as the Carabao Cup holders sailed past Norwich City to set up a fourth-round meeting with Brighton.

Floyd Samba scored two fine goals and had a hand in another on a dream debut that had his beaming dad up off his seat and thrusting his arms in the air as if ready to party.

If the Samba surname feels familiar, that is because Floyd’s father Christopher played more than 200 games for Blackburn Rovers, Queens Park Rangers and Aston Villa.

In fact, it was very much a family affair as Floyd’s brothers Tyrone and Emerson, who are also in City’s academy and hoping one day to tread a similar path, joined in the jubilant celebrations alongside their mother, a visibly emotional Theresa.

News.title: Banton shows his worth as England cruise to series victory against Sri Lanka
News.content:
A patchy Test team and a one-day international side learning on the job should not obscure the fact that under Harry Brook, England have built a formidable T20 outfit.

Missing a slew of first-choice players, they dispatched Sri Lanka with a game to spare and an emphatic show of their depth in the format, with Sonny Baker and Tom Banton – two men still finding their feet in the side – to the fore. England have now won 20 of the 23 completed T20s since Brook took over last year, and six matches in a row this summer. It is easily their best format and, as Liam Dawson said, they have “match-winners throughout” and plenty of “freak” performers.

In this six-wicket win, Baker’s one for 15 limited England’s target to a paltry 146, which Banton, a natural opener who is being recommissioned in the middle order, helped knock off with 47 balls remaining. “Tonight was a special performance, very clinical,” said Brook.

News.title: Interest rate increase ‘likely’, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Andrew Bailey has said that interest rates are likely to rise if the Middle East war rages on, warning inflation is now on course to hit 4pc.

The Bank of England opted to hold borrowing costs at 3.75pc on Thursday, the sixth time in a row it has left them unchanged.

However, the Governor said a “material” increase in energy prices since July would push up inflation to twice the Bank’s 2pc target.

He warned the outlook for inflation “continues to be on the upside” and criticised the “seeming loss of urgency to find solutions” to the war in Iran.

Oil prices are back above $100 a barrel and analysts expect average gas and electricity bills to rise above £2,000 this winter as the conflict continues.

Mr Bailey said: “So far, higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK.

“But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2pc target.”

Investors expect the Bank to raise interest rates as soon as November, which has pushed average mortgage rates to their highest level in three years.

The average five-year fixed mortgage deal has risen to 5.87pc, according to Moneyfacts, which is the highest level since November 2023 and up from 4.95pc before the Iran war.

Thursday’s rate hold leaves the Bank out of step with central banks around the world after the US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank voted to raise borrowing costs this month.

However, economists said there had been a change in tone from policymakers over the threat posed by energy prices and whether this would feed into the wider economy.

The Bank of England predicted that inflation would hit 4pc early next year, just as most workers are negotiating pay rises.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said: “It seems as though a majority of the MPC is on the cusp of wanting to tighten policy.”

In a warning on the impending pain facing households, Mr Bailey told the Chancellor that energy bills would rise by 24pc early next year under the Ofgem price cap.

This will push up annual average bills by £413 to £2,136, which the Governor blamed on the war in the Middle East.

The Governor is required to write a formal letter to the Chancellor every time inflation is more than a percentage point above its 2pc target.

Official data showed inflation rose to 3.1pc in August.

Mr Bailey said: “The energy price shock has been the most important factor driving recent short-term movements in inflation.”

Despite expectations of higher rates, the FTSE 100 rose on Thursday at its steepest pace since July, climbing more than 1pc, as the Bank of England eased the pressure on the UK bond market.

Policymakers also confirmed a Telegraph report that the Bank will stop selling the long-dated bonds it amassed during the financial crisis and lockdown.

The Bank will continue actively selling £20bn of government bonds per year until the rest of the stockpile is wound down to zero in 2034.

The announcement triggered a sharp fall in the cost of borrowing for the Treasury, with the yield on 30-year UK gilts falling at the fastest pace since May.

News.title: Next-generation antivenom fights India’s deadliest snakes
News.content:
The process to make antivenom has barely changed in a century: snakes are milked, their venom is injected into horses, and their antibodies are harvested to form the basis of the product. The resulting treatments are difficult to administer, can trigger severe side effects, and the quality varies from batch to batch.

“The big four snakes contribute to 70 per cent of poisonous bites [in India]… so 30 per cent of poisonous snakes are not covered, even to begin with,” said Dr Yogesh Jain, a public health physician in Chhattisgarh state and a member of The Global Snakebite Taskforce.

“But there are huge quality and efficacy issues even against these 70 per cent of bites. We’re relying on a 100-year-old technique of getting antivenoms, and at least 50,000 people are dying every year,” he told The Telegraph.

“There’s a real need for new technology. We don’t have a safe and appropriate antivenom for the largest majority of people in rural India.”

Now, scientists are hopeful that they have developed a potential alternative.

In the latest study, published last week, researchers showed that an experimental antivenom cocktail with five components protected mice against lethal doses of antivenom in Indian cobras, even when delayed by up to 20 minutes – a scenario that mimics the real-world lag between a bite and treatment.

“If you go 10 years back, people didn’t think you could make sufficiently simple products with new, modern biotechnology that could cover all these different snake venoms,” said Prof Andreas Laustsen-Kiel, head of the Section of Biologics Engineering at the Technical University of Denmark and co-author of the paper.

“People simply believed it was too complex, too expensive to manufacture, and so on… But the data we are gathering is convincing enough to say this is something that could make a huge dent in the lost lives and limbs snakebite causes every year.”

The antivenom itself was based on lab-made nanobodies – antibodies derived from a group of animals including camels, llamas and some species of shark. Scientists believe their structure means they could be a more potent, more precise, more temperature-stable alternative to man-made monoclonal antibodies – and cheaper to manufacture.

“The latest study builds on an earlier discovery of nanobodies that can protect across a broad spectrum of African snakes,” said Prof Nicholas Casewell, director of the Centre for Snakebite Research and Interventions at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, who has previously collaborated with Prof Laustsen-Kiel.

“In this paper they have iterated and demonstrated that a narrow number of nanobodies can protect against Indian cobras and king cobras. This demonstration brings the nanobody technology closer to market,” he added.

But that is likely still years away, depending on how much funding the researchers can attract. The next steps – a larger animal study, scaling up manufacture, and launching human trials – are expensive.

“If money was no issue, we could probably be testing in humans in 1.5 to three years from now,” said Prof Laustsen-Kiel. “But since money is a big issue, it is more likely that human trials won’t be able to start until 2.5 to four years from now.

“But I really think that this [study shows] there’s no doubt that biotech can deliver better antivenoms. The question is whether people are willing to fund it,” he said.

News.title: Manchester United hounded off pitch by own fans
News.content:
The joke goes that Michael Carrick has already bettered Ruben Amorim’s efforts by reaching the third round of the League Cup, but Manchester United will need to find a way past free-flowing Brighton if they are to go any further.

United were eliminated in the second round by League Two Grimsby Town last season, but start the competition a stage later because they are one of nine Premier League clubs playing in European competition.

Brighton knocked United out of the FA Cup in the third round, with Danny Welbeck scoring at Old Trafford, meaning the club played just 40 matches in 2025-26.

Carrick will want to make a better fist of the cup competitions, but he could really use a win of any kind after taking just four points from United’s first four league games of the new season.

The no-show at Hull and derby defeat by City’s 10 men were especially dispiriting, and the relationship between the club and supporters is becoming increasingly strained.

There were no flags on the Stretford End for the game against City, as fans voiced their opposition to what they view as a heavy-handed ticketing policy. The club says the measures are to stop ticket-touting but critics believe many innocent season-ticket holders are being caught in the crossfire and having their tickets revoked.

Discontent is never too far away given the continued presence of the Glazer family, and confidence is fragile regarding the club’s sporting direction under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos.

The news that 15-year-old JJ Gabriel, possibly the country’s outstanding academy player in his year group, wants out (broken by Matt Law in a Telegraph Sport exclusive) nagged at some of those fears.



Gabriel could have been in contention for a place on the bench this evening, but that is now surely out of the question even if United say they have not given up hope of persuading him to stay.



Full team news on the way shortly.

Sports.title: Kylian Mbappe ditches Nike and links up with Roger Federer and Thierry Henry in lucrative new brand deal
Sports.content:
Next

KYLIAN MBAPPE has ditched Nike to become the face of On.

The Real Madrid star had been endorsed by Nike since the age of nine but has now severed the relationship to play a central role in On’s first foray into football.



The Swiss brand is only 17 years old and started off specialising in running trainers before branching out into tennis.

A landmark sponsorship deal with Roger Federer in 2019 played a key role in their booming growth.



But Mbappe is also a mammoth coup as they prepare to enter the football boots market.

The 27-year-old was convinced to make the shock switch by fellow Frenchman Thierry Henry, who has been working as On’s Director of Football since last year.

Details of the deal that brought Mbappe onboard are undisclosed but, like Federer, he has reportedly been given equity in the company.

It is understood that Mbappe’s latest Nike contract, which expired this summer, netted him £13million a year.

On’s boots will not hit the retail market until 2027 but Mbappe is expected to be seen playing in them within the next few weeks.

After competing with the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo and Erling Haaland for the spotlight at Nike, Mbappe will now be the undisputed poster boy for his new sponsors, who are set to give him crucial input over their boot designs.

“I want to bring my experience and perspective into what we create, push what’s possible through innovation, and always stay true to the joy of football.

“We have a shared dream, and this is only the beginning.”



On founder David Allemann added: “Football doesn’t need another sportswear brand to do more of the same. Football needs new ideas and a challenge to what is possible.

Nike bid Mbappe a classy farewell, writing: “Kylian’s journey with Nike began when he was nine years old.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick snaps back in heated exchange over lack of passion – but insists Man Utd situation ‘not a catastrophe’

MICHAEL CARRICK fought off accusations of showing a “lack of emotion” in a heated exchange when pressed by a Manchester United journalist.

United were dumped out of the Carabao Cup at the first hurdle in a historic night at Old Trafford, after picking up four points from four to languish 13th in the Premier League.



Carrick reacted strongly when asked if he “needs to show more emotion?”

He sternly told the reporter: “I need to show more emotion? In what way?”



To which the journalist responded: “Some of the fans might want to see it?”

But Carrick then quipped: “No, but I’m asking, how, what do you want me to show [it]?”



Before that, the United head coach insisted that United’s poor start to the season is “not a catastrophe or disaster”.

Carrick still has the backing of the United board and laughed off “ridiculous” notions that he should be stressed about his long-term future.

The 45-year-old, who has lost three of his opening six matches, said: “It’s not a catastrophe or a disaster. It’s not the end of the world.

“We’re not in a place where we’ve got an awful long run of horrific results.

“We’ve lost a couple of games recently, and we feel that we’ve started and been in all the games that we’ve played, if not being a better team at the start of a game.”

Sports.title: West Ham legend Julian Dicks reveals he was pelted with a BRICK at Millwall away – only for ref to crack a joke about it
Sports.content:

WEST HAM legend Julian Dicks has recalled the moment he was pelted with a BRICK at Millwall — only for the ref to crack a joke about it.

Ahead of tomorrow’s Dockers Derby at the Den, the former tough-guy defender known as The Terminator has lifted the lid on the terrifying environment he faced as a 19-year-old back in 1988.



He arrived at Upton Park from Birmingham but nothing had prepared him for the Bermondsey bear pit.

And Dicks told SunSport: “I was waiting for a corner to come over at Millwall and back then the full-backs had to be on the posts.



“Suddenly half a house brick hit me on the elbow so after defending the cross I pointed to it on the floor to the ref.

“He just said to me, ‘Good job it wasn’t a whole one.’ And that was it!”

That brutal introduction to the fixture set the tone for what remains one of English football’s most volatile rivalries.

Despite the hail of missiles from the terraces, John Lyall’s side managed to scrap their way to a famous 1-0 win thanks to a strike from Paul Ince.

But the drama was far from over when the final whistle blew.

Dicks added: “I remember going to clap our fans at the far end, and as we’re walking back there must have been about 25 police officers come on the pitch with batons and shields.

“We’re thinking, ‘Why?’ And all of a sudden, you know why, because you got pounded with coins and bricks and everything else.

“You saw a lot of violence on the terraces. Every game more or less, there was fighting.”

Even returning decades later he visited the New Den as an assistant coach to Slaven Bilic with West Brom there was no respite from the Lions hostility.

He recalled: “I’ve got off the coach and this woman shouted, ‘Hello Julian!’ in a really nice, lovely, friendly voice.

“I turned around and she went: ‘You’re a fing w***er!’ “I burst out laughing because you know what it’s all about. It was just a part of trying to put you off your game.



“With me, obviously they didn’t succeed, but with some players, it scared them, playing at the Old Den.”

Modern Premier League stars rely on strict nutritionists, ice baths, and endless sports science warm-ups.

Yet during his playing days, Dicks prepared for derby wars in a very different, old-school fashion.

He said: “Nowadays players are staying in an hotel overnight for away games — but back then we didn’t. We just turned up at the ground and we’d go on the coach.

“My routine was to listen to what the manager had to say, then I’d run a hot bath and have a Mars bar and a couple of cans of coke.

“And that was me done. I didn’t do any warm-up. I’d just go out about 10 minutes before kick-off with everybody else, and that was it. That’s what I did throughout my career.”

Authorities have moved derbies to early 12:30pm kick-offs in a bid to curb fan trouble outside the stadium.

However, Dicks scoffs at the idea that early starts stop supporters from drinking ahead of the match.

He insisted: “It doesn’t make any difference in my opinion, because you can go to Tesco or whatever and get your cans of beer.



“Back when I played, every game was a 3pm apart from West Ham-Millwall, which they brought in early.

“So it’s a bit of an eye-opener really, kicking off at 12, because you’re three hours in front of what you normally do.”

Dicks used to lock horns with Millwall’s legendary midfield enforcer Terry Hurlock.

The ex-Lion epitomised The Den spirit.

He said: “Terry was obviously very tough as a player, but he was better than what people give him credit for. I thought he was a good player.



“You knew he was a typical Millwall player — give 100%, run through brick walls for the fans, for the club, for his team-mates.

“He could mix it with the best of them, so I’m sure there was a few midfield players that didn’t like coming up against him.”

Ahead of the latest battle between the rivals, Dicks has laid down the law to the current West Ham squad on what it takes to survive in Bermondsey.

He insisted that while most modern derbies may feel more sanitised in comparison to his playing career, players must match the passion of the fans in the stands.

Dicks said: “I didn’t really know what Millwall-West Ham was all about until the supporters told me. They told me within the first week I was at West Ham.



“If there’s two games that you want to win, it’s against Tottenham and Millwall. Hopefully that gets over to the players because they are big games.

“I play for the supporters and I can put my hand on my heart and say that every game I give 100 per cent.

“I let the club down and the supporters down by getting sent off and things like that, but when I played I gave 100 per cent. And that’s all the supporters want from their players.
