World.title: Could trees developed with gene-editing technology protect Florida's citrus industry?
World.content:
Could trees developed with gene-editing technology protect Florida's citrus industry?

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Citrus growers in Florida are planting new trees that have been modified using gene-editing technology to ward against the lethal citrus greening disease.

Growers have tried everything from tents to sprays to protect citrus trees from the bacterial infection, which has killed off many of Florida's citrus trees and led to a massive decline in the amount of citrus the state produces. Now growers are waiting to see if the genetic modifications, which the Environmental Protection Agency approved earlier this year, will keep the trees alive.

Citrus greening arrived in Florida in 2005. The disease is spread by a tiny winged insect called an Asian citrus psyllid. It attacks the trees' immune system, so they can't fight the infection. Once infected, a tree produces bitter, discolored fruit and usually dies a few years later. There's no cure.

Sponsor Message

Ron English's family ran a citrus business in Valrico, Fla., for generations until greening wiped it out, forcing them to close in 2015.

"We had some of the best looking groves around, and all the time and effort that we had spent, you just see it diminish right before you," English said.

In the late 1990s, before citrus greening arrived in Florida, growers were shipping out around 300 million boxes of fruit each season, said Matt Joyner, CEO of Florida Citrus Mutual, a trade association that represents citrus growers. By comparison, they shipped a little more than 15 million boxes during this year's season, which ended in June, he said.

Soilcea, a Tampa-based company, used CRISPR gene-editing technology to design a rootstock that resists greening. Known as CarriCea T1, it keeps a tree's immune system working, allowing growers to rely less on insecticides.

Focusing on the rootstock to fight the bacteria is key, said Soilcea CEO Yianni Lagos. He explained that although the first sign that a tree is infected is yellowing leaves, "before you even have symptoms, half the root system is already dead."

Lagos is now waiting to see what happens when the rootstock is grafted onto trees and planted.

toggle caption Catherine Welch

In a SoilCea test field, the results so far are promising. Trees with the CarriCea T1 rootstock are taller and greener.

Sponsor Message

English cares for the dozens of trees in the test field that have the modified rootstock. They were planted last summer next to trees without it.

"That's the CarriCea rootstock — see how big the leaves have filled out," English said, pointing to a tree with the modification.

The smaller tree next to it does not have the CarriCea T1 rootstock. It's smaller with yellower leaves.

"See the discoloration, that's the disease already working through the tree," he said.

The real test for the CarriCea T1 tree will be the fruit, which takes years to show up — not only how it grows, but also how it tastes.

"The data suggests it's gonna work, but until you have a 10-year-old tree, you don't know how the tree is going to perform," Lagos said.

World.title: Republican 'cavalry' arrives with a Trump-backed $150 million ad blitz in key races
World.content:
Republican 'cavalry' arrives with a Trump-backed $150 million ad blitz in key races

toggle caption Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

For months, Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton was outspent on the air in Texas, first in a bruising primary, then as Democratic nominee James Talarico spent millions of dollars to introduce himself to voters.

That all changed this month with a massive money bomb from Republican super PACs and dark money groups, including President Trump's MAGA Inc. and Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Republicans.

All told, pro-Paxton ad reservations for the month of September add up to more than $94 million, enough to swamp the roughly $20 million supporting Talarico in the same timeframe. According to the tracking firm AdImpact, that GOP total for September seeking to boost the scandal-plagued Paxton is more than Democrats have spent the entire cycle on ads in Texas.

Sponsor Message

Last week at the Republican convention in Dallas, Paxton, the state's attorney general, made no secret of the fact that he needed backup.

"He is the most radical Democrat in Texas history, but he's also the most well funded," Paxton said about Talarico, in an address to convention-goers. "Which is why today I need your prayers, your votes and your support."

Talarico, a state representative, has been able to raise blockbuster sums for his campaign through viral television appearances and fundraising appeals. As of the most recent campaign finance deadline at the end of June, the Democrat had 12 times more cash on hand than Paxton. But that advantage is easily overwhelmed by super PACs and dark money groups that can raise unlimited funds and since Labor Day have swooped in to boost Republicans all over the country.

When it comes to ad spending, Republicans now have a significant advantage heading into the closing weeks of the 2026 midterms.

According to an NPR analysis of AdImpact data, Republican candidates and groups have pledged to spend more than $557 million to Democrats' $343 million in the nine most competitive Senate races this fall. Republican reservations outpace Democrats in all but one of those contests (Georgia). That advantage stretches further once House elections are factored in.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

"Look across the battleground Senate states, look at the House districts, the cavalry has come," said Scott Jennings, a longtime Republican strategist. "Now, the Republicans have enough money to make an actual argument, to draw a real contrast, to have a real debate. And in some of these districts, in some of these states, it's going to make a difference."

The cavalry has arrived in the form of more than $150 million in initial ad reservations in the last two weeks from MAGA Inc. and two new Trump-aligned groups: No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC.

What does it buy? TV ads, streaming ads, digital ads and a chance to bloody up Democratic candidates, in both Senate and House races.

"Some of these ads are going to be ugly and it's going to be a pretty negative campaign, but that's the nature of a midterm when you've got an environment like the one that the Republicans are facing," said Jennings, referencing headwinds the GOP faces this election. "And honestly I think the resources are going to allow them to win some of these races."

Much of the big spending is on defense

Aside from the volume of money flowing into these races, it's notable where these ad reservations signal Republicans need the most help. Alongside traditional swing contests that have been narrowly decided, there is serious cash going to bail out candidates in places that supported Trump by notable margins in 2024.

In the Senate, that includes races in Alaska, Texas, North Carolina and Ohio — where defeats could give Democrats a majority in the chamber. In the House, Trump-aligned PAC ad spending includes Texas' 15th Congressional District, which he won by nearly 18 points in 2024; Kentucky's 6th District, which he won by 15 points; and Alabama's 2nd, a seat he carried by 14.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

The political environment is brutal for Republicans. The president's party almost always suffers losses in the midterms, and this president is historically unpopular, getting into trade wars with allies and overseeing an unpopular war with Iran that has caused gas prices to spike in a year when voters say the issue they care about most is the cost of living.

But that hasn't slowed down Trump's ability to raise campaign cash.

"I think I have like close to $1 billion in the super PAC," Trump told reporters recently in the Oval Office. "And I'm allocating probably $400 or $500 million [to the midterms]. So I'll be spending."

Trump added that he and his allies were "going to spend a lot of money because we don't want to lose our country."

Democratic operative Jesse Ferguson says this cash deficit for Democrats was predictable.

"Democrats are the party out of power and Donald Trump is more transactional than any president in history," said Ferguson. "There's no scenario where [Republicans] weren't going to have a massive financial advantage."

The GOP ad advantage is a snapshot of where the parties are allocating their resources, and spending can and will change. According to AdImpact, virtually no ads have been booked by either party in Texas from October onward, while the Ohio Senate race has more than $116 million locked in for the rest of the election.

In these ad wars, it is worth noting that while outside Republican groups have more cash than Democrats, the dynamic is reversed for the campaigns. And candidates can get more bang for their buck with that money through cheaper ad rates than super PACs.

Ferguson says money can buy a lot, but it can't sell a product people don't want.

"Money can't change the weather, but it can be an umbrella for them going into this election," Ferguson said. "It can help insulate them, but it can't change the fundamentals of what voters are feeling."

Sponsor Message

Those fundamentals are why Republicans are dipping into their vast war chests in hopes of holding on to GOP-held Senate seats and dumping tens of millions of dollars into House districts where Republican lawmakers redrew the maps to make them safer and, in a better year, would not be competitive.

World.title: A DHS email raises new questions about the Trump administration's election plans
World.content:
A DHS email raises new questions about the Trump administration's election plans

toggle caption Stephen Maturen/Getty Images

An internal Department of Homeland Security email raises new questions about the agency's efforts to hunt for non-U.S. citizens who may be on state voter rolls or have cast ballots in the past.

In the email — which was sent last year, but is newly acquired by NPR — DHS personnel shared a 78-page document listing counties and states that offer election materials and ballots in non-English languages. The list of jurisdictions was attached alongside a Department of Justice criminal checklist outlining requirements for prosecution of voter-related charges.

The email was released as part of a tranche of materials after the Democratic National Committee filed suit over a public records request, and was then shared with NPR.

Sponsor Message

Democrats fear that the Trump administration's efforts to root out noncitizen voters will entangle or intimidate eligible voters and dampen turnout in this year's midterms. DHS has surged resources to investigate noncitizen voting, even as prior audits have found such fraud to be extremely rare.

Nothing in the document alludes to enforcement activity at the locations mentioned. The email is heavily redacted, so it's unclear why the list of non-English jurisdictions was attached. A court filing by DHS defending its redactions described the email as a "subordinate sharing initial thoughts and opinions with leadership."

When asked by NPR about the document, DHS said in a statement that anyone who votes illegally shouldn't be able to "use a purported lack of knowledge" of English to avoid prosecution. In recent weeks, federal authorities have charged a number of individuals with alleged illegal voting.

Fears about the Trump administration's election plans have led civil rights coalitions to sue to stop DHS from deploying federal officers to the polls, which administration officials have at times suggested could happen. The newest of those lawsuits, first reported by NPR, was just filed Friday.

Federal interference at the polls is against the law, but that concern is also what motivated the DNC to seek records from the Trump administration. Last year, it filed Freedom of Information Act requests across the federal government to learn if there were any plans to deploy federal agents or troops to polling places, drop boxes and election offices in the upcoming elections.

Sponsor Message

The document worries Dan Freeman, the DNC's litigation director and a former DOJ Voting Section attorney, especially when combined with the fact that DHS deemed the email responsive to the FOIA request about potential federal agents at the polls.

"The very simple connection that I logically drew is that they're targeting [these jurisdictions]," said Freeman. "We are hoping to learn more. But right now, the logical inference that I think anyone would make is that they are thinking about prosecution of federal election crimes in jurisdictions where elections are conducted in a language other than English."

DHS said in its statement that it "is not planning operations targeting polling locations."

But administration officials have also inflamed fears about the possibility. Earlier this month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents could serve warrants at polling places, and in May, President Trump said he would do "anything necessary" to make sure the U.S. has "honest" elections, when he was asked directly about the possibility of agents at the polls.

toggle caption Stephen Maturen/Getty Images

It's unclear who compiled the list of multilingual voting jurisdictions, but it was shared as part of an email dated Dec. 19 from a DHS border policy acting director, whose name is redacted, to Rob Law, the undersecretary for strategy, policy and plans. Other DHS officials from that office were included on the email, as well as Heather Honey, who is leading the administration's efforts to root out noncitizen voting.

In areas where more than 5% of voting-age citizens primarily speak a language other than English, the Voting Rights Act requires election officials to provide materials in that language. That information is public, and the document encompassed those jurisdictions as well as some state and local policies as well.

Much of the tranche of materials released to the DNC is redacted. The DNC is still litigating to get more records from the federal government.

Sponsor Message

But it's clear the rhetoric around possible administration plans is already impacting voters too.

Roughly 40% of voters now think it's likely ICE agents will be present at voting locations in their area, according to new polling released this week from the University of California San Diego. That includes roughly a third or more of Democrats, Republicans and independents.

The survey also found voters of color were significantly more likely than white voters to say they feared voting could put them at risk of being questioned by immigration authorities despite being U.S. citizens.

Voting officials worry that could impact turnout even if no enforcement efforts materialize.

"What they're trying to do is put it out there to discourage people from voting, to create an atmosphere of fear, and it creates a chilling effect on the democratic process," said Paul López, the top voting official in Denver and a plaintiff in a lawsuit looking to prevent federal agents from the polls.

Denver is one of many jurisdictions also mentioned in the DHS document as a place that offers multilingual election materials. Close to a third of the city's population is Hispanic or Latino, according to census data.

But when López was told by NPR about the document's existence and Denver's inclusion in it, he said he wasn't concerned, because federal law is on his side.

"It is illegal for folks to be targeted on the basis of their language," López said. "My message to voters is, 'Don't let these thugs scare you. Don't let them intimidate you. You're not going to be bullied and we're not going to be intimidated.'

"Democracy will happen."

World.title: Carney wants Canada to join Europe's Erasmus+ program. What is it?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Canada and the EU court closer ties, Prime Minister Mark Carney signalled clear interest in joining Erasmus+, a popular European exchange program.

While many details of the suggested new partnership are left to be ironed out — like what it would mean to be the EU's first "associate member" — Carney specifically pitched Canadian involvement in Erasmus+ when he delivered a speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday.

"Canadian membership of Erasmus+ would give your students and ours more opportunity to learn at some of the world's top universities, to broaden their horizons and to build those lasting ties that will sustain our alliance for the future," Carney said.

Carney has been clear that Canada is not seeking full EU membership and that the possible new partnership requires a different framework.

He also expressed interest in getting involved in the next iteration of Horizon, Europe's research and innovation funding program in which Canada already participates. The current Horizon framework for 2021-2027 has over $140 billion in funding.

WATCH | Carney's full speech in Strasbourg: FULL SPEECH | Carney calls for 'alliance for the future' in speech at European Parliament | Duration closed caption 22:52 Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered remarks about Canada-Europe ties a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen opened the door to Canada becoming an 'associate' member of the EU.

Speaking to reporters alongside Carney, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said the EU is optimistic for new opportunities with allies like Canada.

"If you ask our young people what they associate the European Union with, I would tell you Erasmus is the first thing they mention," Metsola said. "Horizon is the second thing they mention in terms of opportunities that with Canada could only get bigger."

"Just think of the opportunity young people in Europe, in Canada, to study in our two jurisdictions, to live and work in those jurisdictions, to learn from each other, build the bonds that will strengthen our ties," Carney said.

While there were no concrete details of what Canada's involvement in Erasmus+ would entail, the U.K.'s recent agreement to join the exchange program could serve as a possible roadmap, given they aren't an EU member either.

The U.K. signed a temporary deal to join Erasmus+ in April. The deal currently only lasts for one year where the U.K. is expected to contribute 570 million pounds (over $1 billion Cdn) to the program in 2027.

What is the exchange program?

First established in 1987 as Erasmus, the flagship EU program allows people to study and train at institutions across Europe for up to a year.

The initial program focused on university exchanges, but has since expanded to include exchanges for work experience, apprenticeships and sport.

Over 16 million people have taken part in the program since its inception, according to the program's 2024 report.

In 2014, the program expanded under a new name, Erasmus+, to include a number of separate initiatives and cover new areas like European competence and sport, receiving €14.7 billion (over $23 billion Cdn) in funding from the EU for 2014 to 2020.

What questions do you have about the proposed partnership between Canada and the EU? Send them to ask@cbc.ca.

The EU's budget is composed of member states' contributions, which are based on their respective gross national incomes.

The program's total funding doubled for the current period of 2021-2027 to an estimated €28.5 billion — roughly $45 billion Cdn — according to its 2024 report.

The report shows 60 per cent of its budget supports learning mobility. The remainder of the program's funding supports its other goals, namely co-operation projects and policy development activities.

Erasmus+ includes all 27 EU member states and also Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Serbia, Turkey, North Macedonia and the U.K.

World.title: 'Cocaine eyes' to cash bribes: 5 revelations from Project South wiretaps
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Newly reportable court documents in the Project South case reveal how investigators surveilled and wiretapped Toronto police officers for months, allegedly catching them selling and using cocaine.

A police officer doing drugs before his shift, a trunk of police uniforms to sell, details on drug deals and plans to open massage parlours are some of the revelations Project South investigators allegedly captured through wiretaps as part of their sweeping corruption probe, according to newly reportable details from an Information to Obtain (ITO) application in the case.

A publication ban was lifted on those allegations, and many others, from the Project South ITO this week in a ruling from Ontario Superior Court Justice Laura Bird.

“The importance of public scrutiny in this case cannot be overstated. What is, perhaps, most concerning about the allegations of widespread police corruption in this case is the fact that the York Regional Police only stumbled upon it in the course of their investigation,” wrote Bird in her decision.

The investigation began in June 2025, when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections official from Toronto South Detention Centre (TSDC). Subsequently, police discovered that Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt allegedly ran an unauthorized search on the official's licence plate less than a month before the attempted hit.

“There is no evidence that anyone was suspicious of Mr. Barnhardt or his associates until that moment," Bird wrote.

"That is something that should be of tremendous concern to the public because it demonstrates that a trusted public official can engage in widespread illegal conduct and go undetected.”

CBC News was part of a group of media organizations fighting to lift a publication ban on the ITO — which lays out months' worth of evidence police had compiled from wiretaps and other warrants.

The allegations in the ITO have not been tested in court, but many of the conversations intercepted by investigators paint a picture of the corruption investigators allege Barnhardt and other Toronto police officers and civilians engaged in over several months in 2025 and early this year before their arrests.

These are five of the most shocking conversations police intercepted.

Going to daycare with ‘cocaine eyes’

In early October 2025, investigators intercepted Barnhardt buying cocaine from Const. Saurabjit Bedi in a Brampton, Ont., plaza, according to the ITO. Barnhardt’s vehicle was bugged with audio and video recording devices and investigators say the pair are “seen and heard weighing out the drugs and can be heard negotiating a price of $230 for Barnhardt to pay.”

Afterward, Bedi called Barnhardt and the following exchange was captured, according to the portions of transcript in the ITO.

Bedi asked Barnhardt if he “looked f--ked up when you saw me? … cuz I’m going to daycare now.”

Barnhard replied: “Just put your sunglasses on that’s all, you got … what do they call them … cocaine eyes.”

Const. Timothy Barnhardt is facing a long list of charges in connection with allegedly assisting organized crime. (@10rcop/X)

From there police say the pair discussed drug dosages.

In December 2025, the ITO said police also observed Bedi “consuming what appeared to be cocaine” in the parking lot of 12 Division before starting his shift.

Both Barnhardt and Bedi are charged with trafficking cocaine. None of the charges against them have been tested in court yet. Barnhardt’s lawyer declined to comment on allegations from the ITO and Bedi’s did not respond to a request for comment.

‘All they want is protection’

Police intercepted Barnhardt and Bedi drinking and doing drugs in late November 2025 while discussing plans for a marijuana dispensary and a massage parlour, according to the ITO.

Bedi explained to Barnhardt that he has “girls,” and “all they want is protection and safety and we get their cuts.” He also allegedly told Barnhardt it would be better to use hotels.

Investigators say Barnhardt then clarified to Bedi he was not talking about escorts, but rather massage parlours.

Both men are charged with conspiracy to obstruct justice and breach of trust.

‘What about all this s--t in the f--cking trunk man?’

In late October 2025, investigators intercepted a meeting between Barnhardt and civilian Brian Da Costa in Barnhardt’s vehicle. Da Costa is the one who allegedly paid Barnhardt to “routinely” run unauthorized database searches, including the one on the senior corrections official.

But on this night, the ITO says Da Costa paid Barnhardt cash for police uniform items that Barnhardt had in his trunk.

Brian Da Costa is accused of paying Toronto cop Timothy Barnhardt to run unauthorized police database searches. (Pam Davies/CBC)

This is a transcript of the conversation included in the ITO:

Barnhardt: "What about all this s--t in the f--king trunk man…?"

Da Costa: "Oh s--t yeah my bad f--k; I forgot for a second what you were trying to hand me."

Barnhardt: "I'm like what the f--k 36, 38, 40 are the pants, and the f--king NCO pants are in here too, there is like 1, 2 ,3 jackets.... l got the other jacket I just gotta pick up with the toque and everything."

Da Costa: "I might qet a couple of bucks for this s--t and get more, okay?"

Barnhardt: "I’m gonna get you the hats and ball caps."

Da Costa: "We gotta go get the badges and s--t okay?"

Then, police said Da Costa was observed handing money to Barnhardt, while counting each bill aloud.

Da Costa: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, 10."

Barnhardt: "You are the f--king best, man."

Both men are charged with trafficking police uniforms. Da Costa remains in custody. His lawyer declined a request for comment on the ITO allegations.

Barnhardt jokes about visiting massage parlour daily

In early September 2025, Da Costa was intercepted asking Barnhardt if he wanted to partner with him opening a massage parlour, according to the ITO.

Barnhardt: "Oh f--k bro I’ve been trying to do that myself ... l just didn’t have the link for the women" [...] “I’ll put all my effort towards that, f--k it, a hundred percent.... I'm excited."

Da Costa allegedly jokes about receiving free services at the proposed massage parlour, to which the ITO says Barnhardt replied he would be there daily.

The inside of Toronto South Detention Centre is pictured here in this 2013 file photo. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

‘Inflammatory’ conversation still under pub ban

There is one conversation transcript in the ITO that Justice Bird decided to keep under a pub ban. It involves Barnhardt and Da Costa.

“The comments attributed to Mr. Barnhardt are particularly inflammatory and memorable,” wrote Bird in her decision.

“I am satisfied that they are the type of comments that could create an indelible impression of guilt in the minds of potential jurors that could not be dealt with by resort to alternative measures.”

Elsewhere in the ITO, CBC News previously reported that police say Barnhardt “explicitly stated that he did not care if individuals were harmed” as a result of information he sold to Da Costa from database searches.

York Regional Police Deputy Chief Ryan Hogan speaks about Project South, an investigation into organized crime and corruption involving police, at York Regional Police headquarters in Aurora, Ont., on Feb. 5. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

This ITO was used by police to obtain more than 50 search warrants in the Project South investigation in early February.

The search warrants were executed as investigators arrested and charged seven Toronto police officers, one retired cop and 19 civilians in Project South. The charge against one of those civilians has since been stayed, and one of the officers retired and pleaded guilty to two charges in July.

The charges against the others accused in Project South have not yet been tested in court.

World.title: As Carney's popularity soars, Conservatives weigh what to do about their own leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A number of Conservative MPs have soured on Pierre Poilievre as leader, but despite this growing angst, his position is relatively secure because there is no strong appetite to oust him and choose someone new right now, according to party and caucus sources who spoke to CBC News.

Last year, Poilievre was on the cusp of leading his party to the largest Conservative government in a generation only to fall short when the Liberals replaced an unpopular incumbent with a leader offering a new vision.

He has struggled to recover ever since, facing accusations from some critics that he's yesterday's man, and poorly placed to deal with the issue of our time: an increasingly hostile U.S. government determined to wreck Canada economically.

Poilievre earned plaudits for a series of pro-Canada interviews on U.S. television last week, but he hasn't said if he supports the government's retaliatory tariffs on American products. He says he wants to wait for an "analysis" of the expected economic costs before taking a position.

WATCH | Poilievre on the Conservatives' role as Opposition: Criticizing government's 'costly decisions' is a 'great act of patriotism': Poilievre | Duration closed caption 0:54 Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre addressed his caucus on Wednesday saying the role of the Opposition is 'holding the government accountable here at home' and that 'a country is always more than its government.'

His lines about this fight have largely focused on trying to cajole the government to bring Parliament back sooner than planned and reveal a failed trade deal that negotiators say is protected by confidentiality clauses.

Sources speaking to CBC News on the sidelines of the party's caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C., describe caucus morale as low because the U.S. dispute dominates the news cycle, putting their leader and the team at a disadvantage.

One MP said Canadians simply "don't want to hear from us right now," and their relevance is in question.

Poilievre has made a career out of fiercely opposing Liberal policies he says have ruined this country. That sort of rhetoric doesn't sell as well as it used to given the current patriotic climate, this MP said.

CBC News has agreed not to name the sources so they can speak freely about internal dynamics.

But at least one MP, Jamil Jivani, who has said Canadians have thrown "an anti-America hissy fit" and that the government is overreacting to the trade war, publicly suggested he wants his leader to take a harder line.

During Poilievre's U.S. media tour, which was largely deferential to Carney, Jivani, a close friend of Vice-President JD Vance, said: "You have people who should be offering an alternative to the Liberals instead going out there to appease people in positions of power."

In this context, the party's poll numbers have fallen further. The recent performance in federal byelections — losing one seat and considerable support in two others — has only increased the sense of doom among some Conservatives.

"I think you have to be quite honest, this is not the position that we want to be in at this juncture — there’s no question about that," Conservative deputy leader Melissa Lantsman told reporters after meeting with her caucus mates in the B.C. interior.

WATCH | Lantsman on the Conservatives' position: Conservatives not in 'position we want to be in,' says deputy leader | Duration closed caption 0:47 Conservative Party deputy leader Melissa Lantsman says her caucus is united on the issue of fighting for Canadians, and that the party's retreat in Penticton, B.C., will allow MPs to come together.

Lantsman said that given the underperformance, the party will make some "changes" to the Conservative playbook this fall.

What's unlikely to change is the leader. While some MPs say behind closed doors that they are decidedly done with Poilievre, most don't want to take the next step and trigger a Reform Act ousting, like the one parliamentarians used to remove the last leader, Erin O'Toole, sources said.

Such a move could split the party, as some of the more stridently populist members might revolt against what could be perceived as an elite-driven coup, said one MP.

Conservative MP Michael Barrett said the party base strongly supported Poilievre at his leadership review in January — Poilievre won a commanding 88 per cent of the vote — so the caucus will stick with him.

When asked if Poilievre is the best person to lead the party right now, Barrett deferred to the grassroots.

"The Conservative membership made a very strong decision this year for Mr. Poilievre to lead our party. And that's the direction that we've taken," he said in an interview.

Conservative MPs listen as Poilievre speaks at the party's caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C., on Wednesday. (Stephane Richer/CBC)

One senior Conservative staffer said replacing Poilievre now would just needlessly "burn through" another leader given the perception that the Liberals would likely win if there's another election sometime soon.

This staffer posited that it's better to let Poilievre lead the party into another election, potentially lose and then resign to trigger a new leadership process. That would be less divisive than trying to remove a leader who has a strong and vocal online following, especially one who sailed through a recent leadership review, the staffer said.

Another ex-campaign staffer close to Poilievre said even if a Reform Act ouster prompted the leadership selection process, Poilievre could always run again and win — given few people have expressed serious interest in the job.

While he came up short, Poilievre did lead his party to a respectable showing in the last campaign, taking 41 per cent of the vote and 144 seats, a figure that has since been whittled down by floor-crossings and defections.

Poilievre could reassure skeptical members that while things aren't looking good now, they can change on a dime in politics, this ex-campaign staffer said.

Plus, given the divisions in caucus over how to handle the U.S., as well as other longstanding divides on social issues, Poilievre is best placed to hold this disparate group together, the staffer said.

WATCH | Where do Conservatives go from here? Conservatives try to chart a way forward as Carney's popularity soars | Duration closed caption 2:03 Conservatives are discussing party priorities ahead of Parliament's return from summer break. The caucus retreat comes as widespread support for Prime Minister Mark Carney's trade strategy has left Conservatives grasping for political footing.

Chad Rogers, a longtime Conservative and a partner at the public affairs firm Crestview Strategy, said all is not lost for Poilievre.

Rogers said he is old enough to remember when some pundits claimed former prime minister Paul Martin would win a "super majority" in 2004, leaving the unpopular Stephen Harper on the Opposition benches for years.

That never panned out — Martin limped to a minority, and Harper eventually won and governed for nearly a decade.

Carney's aura could also wear off as it did for that Liberal leader some 20 years ago, Rogers said. Poilievre is struggling to punch through now, but that might not always be the case, he said.

He said Poilievre's plan to go all-in on affordability concerns during this fall sitting of Parliament could bear fruit, given that voters consistently tell pollsters it's a major issue for them.

"I don't know that I would want to be an incumbent premier or prime minister anywhere in Canada with the inflation numbers, the debt numbers. There are a number of bills soon coming due to pay," he said.

"I think as a Conservative, I have a medium-term optimism that Canadians are about to hire us back to clean up the economy."

MP Michelle Rempel Garner said Poilievre's understanding of what average Canadians are going through in an economy wracked by higher prices makes him a good leader for this moment.

"I'm proud to serve under his leadership this fall," she said.

World.title: New cat species identified for the 1st time in a century
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia's cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.

The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is ‌part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America.

It was found in Bolivia's lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 46 centimetres (18 inches) long and weighs around three pounds, making it smaller than the average domestic cat.

Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, ​and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.

"Its fur is ​light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body," said Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.

Little is yet known about the cat's biology and ​lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be ⁠more active at night, Nogales Ascarrunz said.

A close-up of a Leopardus tilcayo cat, the only known individual of the newly identified species living in protective captivity. (Fernando Faciole/National Geographic via Reuters)

Tiger ⁠cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, ‌said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart, of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.

Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.

Only 2 live individuals found so far

Referring to the new species, Lescroart said, "Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records."

One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives ⁠in Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.

Nogales Ascarrunz observes the cat at the Senda Verde animal refuge in Bolivia on Sept. 1. (Fernando Faciole/National Geographic via Reuters)

Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because "its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats," Nogales Ascarrunz said. "This made us wonder: What tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?"

The team analyzed DNA from 38 cats sampled across ‌several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.

"We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal — subspecies or otherwise," Lescroart said.

Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.

"The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we ​estimate those lineages to have been physically separated," Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.

The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru's Yungas, naming it Leopardus ⁠tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca Empire that included the area it inhabits.

New species may be listed as endangered

The International Union for Conservation of Nature's red list, ⁠tracking the status of species, currently treats tiger cats as two "vulnerable" species with declining populations.

The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review ⁠will assess ⁠the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could potentially be considered endangered when assessed on their own.

WATCH | See some of the new species discovered in 2025: See some of the new species discovered in 2025 | Duration 0:56 Scientists are discovering species more quickly than ever before. CBC Kids News contributor Manny Brennan shares some of the cool species discovered in 2025.

The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute ​in the Yungas, one of the region's most ⁠threatened ecosystems.

The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales Ascarrunz added.

"Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message," said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study.

"There are many undiscovered species out there ⁠in the world, and they are at risk of ‌disappearing before we even discover them."

World.title: Montreal mayor mulls legal action against Quebec after baby found at encampment
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez-Ferrada is threatening to take legal action against Quebec after a baby was found living with their mother in an encampment on Notre-Dame Street.

The baby, who is just over a year old, was found last Friday in a tent with their mother, according to the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM). Police officers recovered the child, who was then placed into the care of Quebec youth services (DPJ), while their mother was taken into the care of social services.

According to police, the baby's life, health and safety are not at risk, and they are currently in the care of a family member.

After saying on Thursday that the case is a sign that the province is not doing enough to address the homelessness crisis in Montreal, Martinez-Ferrada doubled down on her criticism in an interview with Radio-Canada on Friday.

"I believe there are concrete actions the Quebec government can and must take," Martinez-Ferrada said in French, adding that a lack of provincial funding is limiting her administration's ability to address homelessness in Montreal.

"If I have to go to court to secure that support, it is an option I am seriously considering right now," she said.

The people living in encampments along Notre Dame street are on land owned by Quebec, and superior court judges have on several occasions blocked the city's efforts to dismantle tents there.

Politicians respond

Quebec Premier and Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette said the case is heartbreaking, and that it must not happen again.

She said all levels of government need to work together to combat homelessness in Montreal and across the province, adding that she plans to meet with Martinez-Ferrada in the coming days.

Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard echoed Fréchette's sentiment, saying that elected officials at all levels shoulder responsibility for the homelessness crisis. He also said that officials should focus more on addressing the root causes of the crisis.

Ruba Ghazal, meanwhile, expressed anger at the situation. The Qu é bec Solidaire co-spokesperson said she was shocked at the news, while arguing that more investment and political will is needed to solve homelessness in the province.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon also expressed outrage at the situation, saying that it was embarassing for Quebec. He argued for better social safety nets for vulnerable people in the province.

When asked about the situation, Éric Duhaime was more blunt. The Conservative Party of Quebec leader said he was sympathetic to people living in encampments, but he argued that encampments should be dismantled as soon as possible.

All five party leaders have agreed to participate in a forum on homelessness in 2027.

World.title: ‘I feel so betrayed’: Iranian conscripts in Canada face deportation threats over terrorist designation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of Iranian families have received a letter from the federal immigration department declaring them inadmissible to Canada. Time is running out for them to prove they are not members of a terrorist organization.

“We chose Canada to live in a fair place, but now I realize there is no justice here,” Sanam Mohammadzadeh said.

“We are shocked and speechless.”

The Windsor, Ont. resident is among the affected Iranian families in Canada who are concerned about their future here. Many are planning to stage a protest on Sept. 22 on Parliament Hill.

CBC News reviewed approximately 50 such procedural fairness letters issued on Aug. 6 from the immigration department. They all used the same wording that an applicant is being considered “inadmissible” because of their prior conscription service with IRGC. (Pratyush Dayal/CBC)

A Procedural Fairness Letter (PFL) from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is issued to an applicant when the IRCC officer has concerns about the application. CBC News reviewed approximately 50 such PFL letters issued on Aug. 6. They all used the same wording that an applicant is being considered “inadmissible” because of their prior conscription service.

Experts say all men in Iran, age 18 and older, must do mandatory service with one of the arms of the military, and many are assigned to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). In July 2024, the Canadian government listed IRGC as a terrorist organization under Criminal Code. Then-Justice Minister Arif Virani had shared concerns about the impact of the designation on the conscripts.

"If an individual was conscripted at one point in time and no longer serves with the IRGC, that would affect the analysis," he said in 2024.

‘I feel so betrayed’

Mohammadzadeh is an award-winning post-doctoral fellow at the University of Windsor. Her husband, who works in auto manufacturing, received the letter for his IRGC conscription service, which happened in 2010. Mohammadzadeh said they immigrated to Canada because they were against the Iranian regime and IRGC, and they participated in many protests against the regime once here. Now, they fear their safety is at risk if they have to return.

WATCH | Former conscript to Iran's Revolutionary Guard may have to leave Canada: Iranian told he may have to leave Canada over past IRGC service | Duration closed caption 1:58 An Iranian man is one of hundreds told by the government that he may have to leave over his past mandatory service in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Canada considers a terrorist organization. Farzin Jafari says he had an administrative job in 2011, and has since protested the IRGC publicly.

The couple has been waiting for permanent residency approval since 2024, and are angry IRCC has labelled all conscripts as terrorists. Mohammadzadeh said if her husband’s past conscription was such an obstacle, why did the Canadian government allow them to come in the first place?

“I'm exactly the same person with the identical information I provided. Now suddenly, I'm a terrorist,” she said. “I feel so betrayed.”

CBC News talked with more than 30 affected people across Canada in the past month, who all received PFLs on the same date, telling them they have 30 days to prove they are not active members of the IRGC. They say there are more than 400 families in limbo, and even after staging multiple protests across major Canadian cities and contacting local MPs, their efforts have been in vain.

In an emailed statement, IRCC said the safety and security of Canadians and the fair and consistent application of Canada’s immigration laws are priorities for the department.

“IRCC has not adopted a blanket approach to individuals who completed compulsory military service. We recognize that some individuals may have served because of conscription. Each case is assessed on its individual facts and circumstances, and compulsory service alone does not necessarily result in inadmissibility,” IRCC spokesperson Anahita Beladi said.

“PFLs are not final decisions or findings of inadmissibility. They are a routine and well-established part of the immigration decision-making process, with thousands sent regularly.”

IRCC added the standardized letter templates are used for consistency and to clearly explain the concerns being raised.

IRCC did not confirm the number of letters sent to PR applicants with IRGC ties.

'We live in darkness'

Winnipeg resident Mahdi Shahmohammadi said he applied for his PR in 2022, and it took IRCC more than four years to issue him the PFL for his IRGC conscription in early 2000s.

“We live in darkness. There's no future… There's a foggy road in front of us, and it doesn't matter how powerful our headlights are. We can't see anything,” he said.

Shahmohammadi said he works in quality control in Manitoba and worries about his future as his permit expires next March. He said it’s “a nightmare” to be put in this delay.

“It's increased our distrust and anxiety. It’s like torture.”

Winnipeg resident Mahdi Shahmohammadi says he has been waiting for his PR for more than four years and is now living in "constant darkness" as he awaits a decision on his PFL letter. (Submitted by Mahdi Shahmohammadi)

Fredericton resident Hamid Alikhani has been left in limbo for his conscription in 2013. He's concerned what this will mean for his two-year-old daughter’s future. She is a Canadian citizen.

“It has really destroyed my life. It's really a difficult situation for us and I didn't expect this behaviour from Canada. That is really unfair treatment,” he said with tears.

“I paid a lot of expenses to come to Canada, and now I got this terrorist label. I wish I didn’t come to Canada.”

Having participated in anti-regime protests, Alikhani said he cannot go back to Iran, and will look at moving elsewhere in the Middle East if his journey doesn’t pan out in Canada.

“Careless and negligent” decision: activist

Kaveh Shahrooz, a lawyer and senior fellow at the MacDonald Laurier Institute, was one of the activists asking for the IRGC to be designated as a terrorist entity, but they was “consistently given assurances that conscripts would not be included.”

While national security is paramount, he said there’s a real sense of frustration in the Iranian community to see their immigration being affected by this.

“I feel let down by the Liberal government because they had consistently delayed listing the IRGC as a terrorist organization because they said they were working through issues related to conscription. That had always been the basis of the delay,” he said.

“As an activist, my assumption had always been that the government would have a solution for this. Once it was announced that the RGC was being listed, there was no exemption for conscripts.”

Kaveh Shahrooz is a lawyer and human rights activist based in Toronto (CBC)

Calling it “careless and negligent”, Kaveh said the 2024 decision is affecting countless innocent people who had “no choice” for their mandatory conscription service.

“Unfortunately, the government seems to be approaching this issue without a sense of balance.”

Groups such as International Center for Human Rights are also urging Ottawa for exemptions.

“Blanket approach” is problematic: immigration lawyer

Immigration lawyer Zeynab Ziaie Moayyed said the United Kingdom took a better approach by excluding conscripts when IRGC was designated a terrorist entity.

“In the U.K., they specifically carved out conscripts recognizing that they do not have a choice in terms of where they are assigned. By not having that carve out, we've ended up in this situation,” she said.

Ziaie Moayyed said instead IRCC has taken a “blanket approach” which is stressing many families and will also take up resources and create backlogs at CBSA.

“There is a very difficult balancing act that IRCC and CBSA have to do. The challenge is that a lot of people who are caught in this really weren't intended to be the kinds of applicants that were going to face this additional scrutiny to begin with.”

Zeynab Ziaie Moayyed is an immigration lawyer based in Toronto who has represented lients at the Federal Court. She says IRGC conscripts who have received the PFLs can be in a limbo for some time. (Zeynab Ziaie Moayyed)

Ziaie Moayyed said 30 days “is not a lot of time to respond” to PFLs and urges soliciting counsel who have experience on this to provide a very complete response to IRCC.

She said applicants can potentially be in limbo for a couple of years as IRCC goes through their responses, which can in turn cause complications for expiring permit holders.

World.title: Ottawa mayoral candidate charged for alleged death threats against Doug Ford and Mark Sutcliffe
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas was charged on Sept. 15 with two counts of criminal harassment and two counts of uttering death threats. (Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas/Facebook)

WARNING: This story contains descriptions of violent language and imagery.

A candidate for mayor of Ottawa is facing multiple charges for allegedly making death threats against Ontario Premier Doug Ford and incumbent Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe.

Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas was charged on Sept. 15 with two counts of criminal harassment, as well as two counts of uttering death threats allegedly made by social media posts between the dates of Sept. 6 and Sept. 13.

CBC News has obtained court documents that detail the charges and name the targets of the alleged offences as Ford and Sutcliffe, who is running for re-election as Ottawa mayor.

The documents say the conduct took place in Kingston, Ont., and could reasonably be expected to cause the premier and mayor to believe their safety was threatened.

Griplas previously ran for Ottawa city council in 2018 for Ward 1, which covers part of the eastern community of Orléans. He received 65 votes, coming 16th of 17 candidates.

He has had earlier run-ins with the justice system that include multiple harassment charges.

He registered to run for Ottawa mayor on Aug. 21 of this year, the last day of nominations for the Oct. 26 election.

While the name posted on the public list of candidates is Geoff Nicholas, the candidate provided a full name including Griplas elsewhere on his nomination documents, which also include an address matching that on the charge sheet.

Social media posts

CBC News has viewed social media posts that remain on a Facebook page using the name Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas.

A post dated Sept. 6 shows a flyer for the Silver Lake campsite on fire with the words "kill Da Cliff" and another message partly obscured by the flames. It is captioned with the words "shame on you Mark!"

A video showing the same flyer was posted on Sept. 10, where the words "mayor must die" are fully visible.

A video post dated Sept. 12 shows a trashed room where the bedsheets have been streaked with a red substance, while other markings spell out the words "F-k Ford" and "Kill Ford."

Another post dated Sept. 14, a day that is outside the period covered by the charges, includes text saying "the Great Debate is approaching." An attached video shows a man with a concealed face brandishing what appears to be a revolver and screaming various phrases, including the words "dead, dead, dead."

The Kingston courthouse confirmed that Griplas appeared virtually on Thursday and remains in custody. His next court appearance is scheduled for Monday, Sept. 21 for a potential bail hearing.

Police were present at a campaign launch event Sutcliffe held on Wednesday. When asked if they are providing the mayor with a security detail, the Ottawa Police Service (OPS) declined to comment on any security measures or posture it is taking, citing the need to protect operational security and reduce risk to public safety.

But it said it is taking the threats seriously.

"In response to threats against Mayor Mark Sutcliffe, OPS assessed the information available and took appropriate steps to enhance our policing response," it said in a written statement.

Sutcliffe's office declined comment, while Ford's office said it won't comment on matters before the court.

The 2018 election

According to court documents from the Ottawa Courthouse, Griplas faced criminal harassment charges following the 2018 election.

In one case, that resulted in a guilty plea for mischief and a sentence of three years probation, while in two other cases he was found not criminally responsible.

Sutcliffe moderated a Rogers TV debate that Griplas participated in for his unsuccessful 2018 city council run. In his opening statement at that debate, Griplas said he had been previously incarcerated and was "brainwashed to perform an act of terrorism."

The bar to register to run for mayor of Ottawa is low. Candidates must pay $200 and provide signatures from 25 Ottawa residents, a rule that is common to all Ontario municipalities with 4,000 or more voters.

All of the signatures on Griplas's nomination documents are dated the day of or the day before he registered.

Starting on Sept. 1, mayoral candidates are able to access a voter list that includes the name and address of eligible voters across the city.

Candidates must submit a request. Elections Ottawa staff told CBC News that would produce a record and they confirmed that there is no such record of Griplas requesting those materials during the 2026 campaign period.

When CBC News asked city media relations whether they would be able to prevent him from doing so in the future, they said city clerk Caitlin Salter MacDonald, the top official responsible for the election, was not in a position to respond or comment further on that at this time.

Asked if Griplas will remain on the ballot on Oct. 26, Salter MacDonald said that certified candidates are required to be listed on the ballot in accordance with the Municipal Elections Act.

World.title: Canada's top general is up for a senior NATO post. Will Trump get in her way?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Top military commanders from 32 Western nations will vote Saturday on whether they prefer Canada's chief of the defence staff or her German counterpart to lead a significant NATO committee.

Gen. Jennie Carignan and Gen. Carsten Breuer are vying for the top job at the NATO Military Committee, a post not held by a Canadian in almost two decades.

The Liberal government of Prime Minister Mark Carney has thrown its weight behind her candidacy. The election at a meeting of alliance chiefs of defence staff comes as Canada and Europe explore closer political, economic and defence co-operation.

If elected, Carignan will be the first woman to lead the military committee in the 77-year history of the alliance.

In an interview with CBC News, Carignan said it's "a privilege to be considered," especially at a time when the alliance faces heightened tensions with Russia, hybrid attacks and the war in Ukraine.

"Don't get me wrong. I absolutely know what I'm getting myself into, but such an important time to work with NATO as partners," Carignan said. "And I think I can make a difference in that way."

Carignan said she was encouraged to put her name forward by some of her fellow defence chiefs.

The chair of NATO's Military Committee is the alliance's senior military officer and, in practical terms, the bridge between NATO's political leadership and its military commanders.

The committee assesses threats, capabilities and operational requirements and provides military advice to the North Atlantic Council. The current chair is Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, who took office in January 2025.

WATCH | More about the new EU alliance: Is Canada becoming an ‘associate member’ of the European Union? | Duration 2:05 Associate membership? Strategic alliance? Whatever you want to call it, Prime Minister Mark Carney's push for deeper ties to Europe are well underway. The CBC’s Marina von Stackelberg breaks down some of the changes Canadians could see should Ottawa and Brussels formalize the agreement.

The position of chair is different from the more high-profile Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) which is responsible for operations and potential warfighting.

The vote comes following Carney's visit to Strasbourg, France, this week where European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed the idea of Canada becoming the EU's first "associate member." It's unclear precisely what that kind of status could mean but it has the potential to substantially deepen economic and political integration.

Carney welcomed the proposal. Donald Trump did not.

The U.S. president, on the one hand, called it "laughable" but then also described it as a potentially "hostile act" that would prompt more tariffs.

Steve Saideman, a defence expert at Carleton University who has written extensively on NATO, said Carignan "absolutely has a shot" at the committee chair's position.

"I think that Carney probably did his homework and wouldn't put the name forward if she didn't have a chance," said Saideman, who added the geopolitical timing is extraordinary.

"I also think that Canada, right now, is being highly sought after by the Europeans to be anchored in all kinds of European structures. So, I think it's a possibility."

There is, however, also the possibility the Trump administration could attempt to block consensus, said Saideman.

A Canadian last held the role of NATO's Military Committee chair two decades ago. (Alexander Quon/CBC)

"Trump is not going to let a Canadian or a woman be the head of the military committee, if anybody around him has paid attention to it," he said.

"He's very upset at Canada for daring to actually have agency. His reaction yesterday to the news about associate membership suggests that he'll find any opportunity, particularly one that is as relatively cost-free as this, to block Canada from whatever aspirations it has."

The election of chair is decided by majority vote in a secret ballot among the defence chiefs. The vote takes place during a closed, private session of the committee.

Retired general Ray Henault was the last Canadian officer to hold the NATO post between 2005 and 2008. He said it took three rounds of balloting to secure his election.

"My experience has always been a couple of rounds, at least right before you get to a final outcome," Henault said.

Like Carignan, he said he was approached by fellow European defence chiefs to run for the position.

"My gut feel though is that Jennie is very well-respected," Henault said. "She's a very capable lady. She's got operational experience in excess of most people, quite frankly, as a combat engineer. She's been in a number of the operational theaters that Canada has been in."

Henault didn't speculate on the position the U.S. might take.

The voice of the U.S. chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff has always carried a lot of weight, he said.

"I think they would probably pay attention to what the U.S. chief of defence was saying. They won't know what he's going to vote, of course, because it'll be a closed vote." Henault said.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

Integrate

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issue to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Colombia’s social organizations and labor unions announce national strike in November
World.content:
Some 1,500 representatives of social organizations and labor unions agreed to begin organizing an anti-government national strike that should take place throughout Colombia either on November 11 or on November 20.

The organizations agreed to the mass mobilization during the National Gathering for the Defense of Life, Dignity, Democracy, Peace, Sovereignty, and Social Reforms that had been organized by labor unions in the capital Bogota.

The first and fundamental decision of the Meeting is to declare the most radical opposition to the illegitimate government of Abelardo de la Espriella because of the course it has imposed on the country—one of subordination to the interests of U.S. imperialism and alignment with the agenda of the international far right—which constitutes a direct threat to national sovereignty, democracy, and the rights won by the Colombian people, and an undeniable shift toward fascism. Social organizations and labor unions

In a statement, the organizations said that the national strike will be preceded by regional protests on October 10 and 14 that will seek to generate momentum for the national strike.

Indigenous organizations will additionally organize a Day of Indigenous, Afro and Popular Resistance on October 12.

A final date for the national strike has yet to be defined.

The organizations decided to call a strike to protest the government’s security and defense policy, the ending of peace processes with illegal armed groups and in defense of social reforms that had been implemented by former President Gustavo Petro.

The protests additionally seek to express solidarity with the people of Palestine, western Sahara, Iran, Bolivia and Venezuela, and reject US imperialism in the Americas.

We must categorically reject the interference of U.S. government officials in the formulation of domestic policies under the guise of so-called friendly aid, which in reality masks the ambition to intensify overexploitation, extractivism, territorial control, and the presence of foreign troops on our soil. Social organizations and labor unions

The organizations agreed to “prepare, through the most intense and massive agitation and propaganda campaign, a national strike.”

World.title: Judge suspends Colombia’s aerial fumigation pilot
World.content:
A Putumayo from the southern Putumayo province suspended the government’s announced resumption of the aerial spraying of coca, ordering information that would allow “a sufficiently informed decision on the merits.”

Earlier this week, the National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine, “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

The National Police subsequently said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo, a province inside the Amazon forest.

These announcements triggered a local foundation to sue the administration, claiming that the plans to do a pilot were in violation of the 2015 ban on aerial fumigation and threatened both locals and the environment.

The judge agreed and ordered the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to provide information on the environmental and health risk involved in the aerial spraying with glufosinate ammonium.

The potential implementation of the pilot plan before gathering and analyzing the studies, documents, and technical evidence cited by the administration itself as the basis for the decision could render the requested constitutional protection ineffective and jeopardize the possibility of reaching a sufficiently informed decision on the merits; Indeed, the combination of the announced imminence of the measure, the current lack of essential information needed to understand its territorial, social, and environmental scope, and the particular ecological sensitivity of the department of Putumayo necessitates preventive action aimed at preserving the effectiveness of this constitutional action. Putumayo court

The suspension of the aerial spraying comes days after De la Espriella promised US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he would resume aerial fumigation, a notoriously ineffective way to get rid of coca.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”
