World.title: EU weighs windfall taxes on energy firms amid growing economic strain
World.content:
A windfall tax for firms profiting from energy price volatility is one of the ideas circulating among EU ministers meeting in Dublin on Friday and Saturday for the periodic meetings of the Eurogroup and Economic and Financial Council.

 

With the war in the Middle East continuing, Brent crude oil prices have surpassed $100 per barrel, and extreme volatility in energy prices is driving inflation higher across the bloc, which is not expected to return to the 2% target before the end of 2027.

While growth indicators are still performing well this year, the European Commission expects economic growth to slow down in 2027.

The EU is urging member states to pursue prudent fiscal policies and remain within the existing fiscal flexibility of 1.5% for defence spending, of which 0.3% can be used to contain energy prices.

Meanwhile, the European Central Bank (ECB) is gradually raising interest rates to contain inflation.

“There are several member states that put forward this initiative, it is part of our discussions," European Commissioner for Economy Valdis Dombrovskis said during a press conference on Friday, referring to the windfall tax.

"Member states can already implement windfall profit taxes at the national level if they decide to do so. From the Commission side, we are ready to support those member states by sharing best practices and finding a good way forward.”

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is pressing the European Commission to present models for a windfall tax, asking to have something on the table by the next Economic and Finance Council meeting in October.

"You know that I have been fighting for this for a long time, together with other European finance ministers," Klingbeil said on the sidelines of Friday's meeting.

The Spanish Finance Minister Carlos Cuerpo also expressed his favour for the proposal on Friday.

“We are managing to lower the bill for homes, companies, industries, transport companies, and this at the expense of the taxpayer's money. We believe there may be fairer ways to distribute this cost,” Cuerpo said.

Related European leaders rush to counter looming diesel price surge as Saudi pipeline attacked

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure has been more cautious about the proposal.

“This [energy] shock can have a different impact on different countries. We do feel that whatever discussion we have, whatever work has been done, needs to take into account the specificities of each country," he said ahead of the meeting on Friday, specifying that France has a "bigger electricity mix".

To the direct question on whether he supports the proposal or not, Lescure said that he support any work that’s being done, but that "I can’t support something before I’ve seen it".

"I’ll see what the work comes out with, and then we’ll have a discussion.”

Energy taxes: the bulk of pricing

Although the energy crisis is affecting the bloc, not all member states are affected in the same way, with prices at the pump varying greatly.

Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands, the three EU countries currently paying the most for diesel, impose some of the highest fuel taxes in the world, pushing retail diesel prices much higher.

On the other hand, countries in Eastern Europe such as Bulgaria and Poland set excise duties far lower, keeping their pump prices down.

Yet according to EU official data published on Thursday, the EU country paying the least for diesel is Malta, with €1.20 per litre charged at the pump on 14 September.

The significant discrepancy in diesel prices across the EU is driven mainly by divergent national tax policies – excise duties and VAT – which make up the largest portion of the retail price of diesel.

However, the difference between diesel prices before and after taxes is staggering. Per the data released on Thursday, Finland’s diesel price stood €1.48 per litre before taxes and €2.50 after taxes.

Related Spain wins EU backing for temporary fuel tax cuts as Middle East crisis keeps prices high

Denmark also ranked high, with diesel at €1.43 before taxes and €2.50 per litre after taxes, while Dutch citizens would pay only €1.50 per litre of diesel without taxes and €2.49 with taxes.

France, which has the third-highest government debt in the EU, has chosen targeted to offer assistance for the sectors most exposed to the price shock rather than cutting fuel taxes.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked ministers to extend support for sectors most exposed to higher energy costs until 31 December. Meanwhile, diesel prices at the French pump stood at €2.29 per litre on 14 September, against €1.30 before taxes.

Regional refining capacity also further amplifies energy pricing. All EU countries buy crude oil from the same volatile global markets, but the price motorists ultimately pay at the pump depends on whether there is sufficient refining capacity nearby, how easily fuel can be transported from other regions and how well local refineries can process the particular type of crude available.

During a supply shock like the one the EU is currently suffering, EU countries with spare refining capacity, diversified import routes and strong links to neighbouring fuel markets may be able to cushion the disruption more easily.

World.title: ‘Race-cation’ boom: Searches for 24-hour city breaks rise by 500% as runners plan marathon trips
World.content:
From marathons in Amsterdam to HYROX in Hamburg, autumn is shaping up to be the season of the “race-cation”.

 

Google searches for “marathon abroad” have soared by some 1,255% in the past year, as runners increasingly combine race day with a quick city break – and new data suggests they’re already planning what to do once they cross the finish line.

Findings from Bókun, a Tripadvisor-owned company, have revealed that searches for overseas marathons have hit an all-time high in 2026, and it’s perfect timing, as research shows that a quarter of marathons globally take place in October.

Now, searches for 24-hour itineraries in marathon cities have surged by up to 500%, leading travel experts to predict that race-cations could drive trip bookings well beyond the summer peak.

But what is a race-cation?

Another trend in the world of travel, it’s popular with people interested in health and fitness who want to combine the challenge of a major race with visiting a new and exciting destination.

Here’s everything you need to know about the trend - and how to do it yourself.

Marathons spark growing interest in whirlwind city breaks

In addition to Bókun looking at Google search data and drawing insights from the trends observed over the past five years, it also examined social media trends.

On platforms like TikTok, videos focusing on the likes of “the best locations to do a Hyrox in” and “marathon holiday itineraries” can gain thousands of views, which highlights the growing appeal of combining fitness events with travel experiences.

While marathons are typically year-round events, 42% of them take place in the autumn, with October alone playing host to 23% of all events.

Some of the top European sporting events this autumn include HYROX Rome and Berlin marathon in September, as well as the Amsterdam, Munich, Lisbon and Budapest marathons and HYROX Valencia in October. HYROX Hamburg runs from 28 October to 1 November.

The research saw a 500% surge in people searching what to do in Hamburg Moritz Kindler/Unsplash

With those dates in mind, Bókun analysed Google Trends data from the past 30 days for searches relating to 24-hour trips to cities hosting major marathons and fitness events coming this autumn.

It found that interest in 24-hour city break queries has increased across almost every destination ahead of these events.

Hamburg saw the most traction, with a 500% surge in Google searches for “what to do in Hamburg” in the last month.

Searches for “what to do in Lisbon for a day” increased by 400%, while “what to do in Munich for a day” rose by 250%.

There was also a 119% increase in people googling what to do in Berlin for a day, “24 hours in Budapest” was up by 84%, and tips for a day-long trip to Amsterdam rose by 70%, all over the course of the last month.

Race-cations also seem to be tapping into another travel trend: micro-adventures.

While sporting events do play a part in search demand for 24-hour trips to European cities this autumn, the increase also highlights the wider trend of micro-cations, or short getaways where travellers can maximise their experience of a destination within a limited time and, often, immerse themselves in a city for just 24 hours.

For marathoners and micro-cationers alike, guided tours and organised experiences are a decent way to get to know a destination and soak up the local culture.

Bókun’s research also showed that search demand for day tours and experiences across different European cities has surged in the past year.

Searches for “Budapest day tours” have increased by more than 400%, while search demand for “Amsterdam day tours" has increased by more than 100% and searches for “day tours in Lisbon” have increased by more than 70% in the past 12 months.

It’s not just seeing the sights that matters to these travellers.

Searches for “Lisbon cooking class” were up by a significant 488%, and “Rome food tour” searches increased by 94%, too.

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: A city at the crossroads of history: Unearthing Gaza's ancient heritage
World.content:
Before Gaza became synonymous with conflict, it was a place where merchants sold wine from local vineyards, pilgrims crossed continents, fishermen set out before dawn, and generations of families lived between sea and desert. RFI explores its deep history.

Advertising

Sitting on the coastal corridor linking Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean, the port city has always been a strategic crossroads.

Like many places around the Mediterranean, Gaza's identity wasn't built by a single people or culture. It was shaped by generations of arrivals, departures and exchanges.

As the Mid-East Junction podcast returns from a six-year hiatus, we'll trace the city's history from the age of the Philistines until the creation of Israel in 1948.

In this first episode of season 3, a Gazan archaeologist, a historian, and a professor of contemporary Arab people shed light on Gaza’s little-known yet fascinating ancient history.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora.

World.title: Canada and EU association: Are there other arrangements?
World.content:
While Canada may be some distance from Europe geographically, closer political ties are in the cards. With talk of an associate membership, DW takes a look at other arrangements the EU has with particular countries.

Canada and the EU "see the world with the same eyes," according to European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.

And the feeling appears mutual.

"Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," said Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

In that spirit, and with both parties grasping for an effective way to deal with Donald Trump and his tariffs, von der Leyen floated the idea of Canada becoming the EU's first associate member on Thursday.

Given the concept of associate membership does not yet exist, it's difficult to determine exactly what that would mean. Germany proposed a similar arrangement for Ukraine earlier this year, only for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to reject the idea on the grounds that the country wants full membership.

Though not officially recognized as associates, there are plenty of countries that have strong ties or agreements with the bloc. DW looks at some of them and how they work.

EFTA and single market access — Norway, Liechtenstein, Iceland

Under this model, the ‘European Free Trade Association (EFTA)' countries are part of the EU's internal market, so people, goods and services can move freely in the Schengen area. The three countries also follow many EU rules in areas like tourism, environment and education.

But there are some key distinctions. The countries have no part in the decision-making process, bar some input into policy preparation, such as participation in expert groups. They are also not in the customs union, do not use the Euro and are not bound by the EU's common trade policy or justice laws. Iceland held a referendum on whether to go for full membership last month, but the government's push to do so failed and they remain an EFTA country.

Bilateral agreements — Switzerland

While it borders four EU member states (Germany, Italy, France and Austria), Switzerland has never been a full member. Instead, more than 120 bilateral deals have been agreed upon by the EU and Switzerland over the last 50 years. These relate to areas such as trade, transport, security and education. A new package of deals was finalized last year, 20 years after they were last agreed.

As Trump menaces, some think Canada should join the EU To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

More than 1.5 million EU citizens live and work in Switzerland, while 466,200 Swiss have gone the other way. That is possible as Switzerland is also part of theSchengen area, allowing for free movement of people across borders.

Switzerland makes financial contributions to a number of EU member states that joined after expansion in 2004, mostly in the east of Europe, but it has no EU voting rights and adopts only some EU laws. Switzerland can also participate in certain EU programs and research projects, through individual negotiations.

The post Brexit agreement — UK

More than four years after the UK voted to leave the EU in a 2016 referendum, the two parties signed a trade and cooperation agreement. Negotiations were fraught and complex, and the UK now has limited access to the EU market and is aligned with the EU on some areas of policy and regulation, for now at least.

There is no longer free movement of people from the UK to the EU or vice versa, and the UK are not in the single market or the customs union. Since the center-left Labour party replaced the Conservatives in government in 2024, talk of a return to the customs union and alignment on other selected EU policy areas has been more frequent. But any return to full member status seems unlikely for now.

A decade after Brexit, youth in Britain want the EU back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Stabilization and association process – Western Balkan countries

The EU has not admitted a new member state since Croatia in 2013. Several nearby countries in the region are hoping to join the bloc, but must first fulfill a number of criteria under the EU's "stabilization and association process" designed for the "Western Balkans." These are: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia.

Under the plan, the EU has promised to "prepare Western Balkan partners for accession through economic reforms and investment and to bring some of the benefits of EU membership to citizens in the region."

States must first become official candidates for member state status by applying to the EU, with each of the member nations agreeing to them as a candidate country. Then follows a process of negotiation, such as that currently underway with Ukraine, Serbia and Montenegro. Finally, an accession treaty is prepared, which the European Commission, the European Council and the European Parliament must agree with. Only once that treaty has been signed and ratified by all member states and the candidate country will said country become an EU member.

World.title: Tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are spilling oil into the Persian Gulf
World.content:
As war disrupts one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, satellite images reveal oil spreading toward protected coral reefs and mangrove forests.

A dark, muddied patch of blue, incongruent with the rest of the ocean; a winding thread of silvery white; a reflective metallic sheen — these are some of the telltale signs on a satellite image that oil may be leaking into the water.

Experts have identified these and many other visual signatures in the Strait of Hormuz, leading them to conclude there's an environmental crisis playing out amid the US-Iran war, as tankers are struck by missiles, set on fire or sunk.

One recent example: In June, a Russian tanker carrying about 800,000 barrels of oil stranded off the coast of Oman, causing a major spill.

Earlier in the war, there were as many as 85 large oil-laden tankers stuck in the Strait — that number has since dropped to 13, according to Greenpeace. Each stranded tanker, plus every other vessel trying to move through the waterway, poses a distinct risk for attack and thus a spill. Since the start of the war, the environmental organization has used satellite imagery to track more than 100 spills.

There are likely several other spills we don't know of, amid widespread GPS spoofing in the region that causes ships to broadcast false positions. Greenpeace released a report this week calling the situation an "ecological catastrophe" and pinpointing a number of oil slicks that are extending into protected and fragile ecosystems.

"People should be concerned," Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief, told DW. The war has taken "a very, very heavy toll on the environment," she added, with the damage now reaching new scales.

Where is the oil spreading?

Greenpeace identified five major oil slicks earlier this week with a total visible area of 240 square kilometers (about 93 square miles) in the Strait of Hormuz. That's about four times the size of Manhattan.

These patches of oil floating on the ocean's surface are getting smaller — now about 80 square kilometers — according to more up-to-date satellite images, as weather conditions have likely made the slicks disperse. But that does not mean the ecological impact is any less severe, Noelle said. "Oil can also sink into the sediment and impact the ecosystems for years and years."

What's concerning is where the slicks were identified. One was found near Musandam National Park, a protected area in Oman that's home to coral reefs, sea life and important breeding grounds for sea birds. Another is close to Iran's Minab River Delta and its protected mudflats and mangrove forests. This kind of damage can take decades for ecosystems to recover from.

Tracking an unclear picture

It's hard to say exactly how far the oil has reached and how severe the damage is.

"What we have put out is the conservative estimate," Noelle said. "It might be worse. It's definitely not better."

Greenpeace and other environmental organizations are relying on satellite images provided by the Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites. They're part of the European Union's Earth observation program and are publicly available.

There are also private satellite providers like Planet Labs that tend to have higher-resolution images. But they've limited access to satellite imagery during the war to prevent their data from being used for military targeting. And there are limits to on-the-ground reports too.

"We don't have a lot of information coming from the country itself, both in Iran as well as the Gulf states," Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher using open-source methods at the Dutch peace organization Pax, told DW. "There is quite restrictive policies of people posting imagery from what's happening on the shore."

The toll on wildlife and people

Oil pooling into the Gulf poses a number of threats, both to biodiversity and to humans.

For sea birds, oil can be deadly. It coats their feathers, reducing their natural waterproofing and buoyancy, making it harder to stay afloat, fly, and hunt for food. Even small amounts of oil can damage eggs too, causing them not to hatch or to be born with deformities.

Mangrove habitats, which provide safe harbor for coastal species, are also hit hard.

"Mangroves have aerial roots and the oil is covering these roots like a film and actually hindering the mangroves in exchanging gases," Noelle said. "They're kind of suffocated by the oil. Most of the time, it leads to the trees dying."

The risks extend to people as well. Coastal communities rely on fish that die off after being exposed to oil. And oil spills contaminate water used for Gulf states' drinking supply. Desalination — or converting seawater into drinkable water — is where 90% of drinking water in Kuwait comes from, along with about 86% in Oman and 70% in Saudi Arabia.

Vessels anchor near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman Image: REUTERS

Clean-up is no easy fix either.

"It's unlikely that it will be addressed quickly, because of the war," Zwijnenburg said. "War in general makes it very difficult to respond fast to these kind of emergencies. There are a range of limitations because of the military movement, because of mines — so it's very difficult to get vessels and clean-up operations to start."

Environmental groups have pointed to the war in Iran — and the rising scale of oil spills it's causing — as further evidence that the world needs to move away from its dependence on fossil fuels.

"The most sustainable long-term damage prevention for things like that would be to reduce and ultimately end our dependency on oil and gas," Noelle said. "Because as long as our energy systems and transport routes are centered around fossil fuels, there will be a continued environmental risk."

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

World.title: Dual citizenship means Germany now in competition for talent
World.content:
Coach Jürgen Klopp has named several players to his first Germany squad who are eligible to play for other countries. Some still aren't committed to Germany long term.

When Jürgen Klopp named his oversized squad for Germany for the upcoming international break, a number of other national team coaches will have taken notice.

Among them was Mohamed Ouahbi of Morocco, who lamented that he had already had Eintracht Frankfurt striker Younes on his radar since last season.

"He had a profile that interested us. I spoke to him on the phone and explained the Morocco project to him—without making any promises," Ouahbi said.

If the 23-year-old Ebnoutalib sees any action in the UEFA Nations League over the next couple of weeks, as expected, he will be cap-tied to Germany – and ineligible to play for Morocco in the future.

Several players with multiple options

This is by no means a unique situation, as a growing number of Germany players in recent years hold other citizenships through their parents and thus have other options for their international careers.

This applies to several other members of Klopp's 44-man squad. Vitaly Janelt, whose father moved to Germany to play professional ice hockey, is also eligible to represent Czechia. Bambasé Conté's father is from Guinea, and Josha Vagnoman has an Ivorian father. Finn Dahmen has an English mother, while fellow goalkeeper Noah Atubolu has Nigerian roots. Said El Mala's father hails from Lebanon, and Brajan Gruda's father was an Albania international.

Said El Mala and Brajan Gruda have represented Germany at the under-21 level Image: Marco Steinbrenner/DeFodi Images/picture alliance

All of them were all born and raised in Germany and have represented the country a tyouth levels. Vagnoman has even made two senior international appearances for Germany, though he has yet to play a competitive match.

High number of dual nationals

There are also numerous established Germany players who could have chosen another nation. These include Felix Nmecha (England), Kevin Schade (Nigeria), Jamal Musiala (Nigeria, England), Karim Adeyemi (Nigeria, Romania), Jonathan Tah and Serge Gnabry (Ivory Coast), Malick Thiaw (Senegal, Finland), Nathaniel Brown (USA), Nadiem Amiri (Afghanistan), Aleksandar Pavlovic (Serbia), Waldemar Anton (Russia), Yann Aurel Bisseck (Cameroon), and Ridle Baku (DR Congo).

The men's national team reflects German society as a whole; according to the Federal Statistical Office, 21.8 million of Germany's approximately 83 million inhabitants have an immigrant background.

"More than 40% of children in Germany under the age of five have a migration background. This means they will later have the option to play for one country or the other," Andreas Rettig, the German FA's (DFB) outgoing managing director for sport told DW prior to last summer's World Cup.

This forces the DFB to compete with other countries for talent for its national teams, and it hasn't always been successful.

A prime example is Ibrahim Maza of Bayer Leverkusen. Born and raised in Berlin to an Algerian father and a Vietnamese mother, he holds not just German but also Algerian and Vietnamese citizenship.

Ibrahim Maza (second from right) chose to represent Algeria rather than Germany Image: Thor Wegner/DeFodi Images/IMAGO

The midfielder possesses many qualities that could help Germany, yet two years ago he opted to play for Algeria and represented the "Desert Foxes" at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and the 2026 World Cup.

Germany also missed out on Paul Wanner and Can Uzun. Wanner, a top prospect developed at Bayern Munich, chose Austria—his mother's home country. Can Uzun of Eintracht Frankfurt has been playing for Turkey since September 2024. Both took part in last summer's World Cup.

International break a cap-tying opportunity

Had Maza, Wanner, and Uzun chosen Germany instead, each of them would have stood a good chance of being named to Klopp's first squad as national team coach.

With this international break featuring four instead of the previous customary two matches – and to see as many players as possible, Klopp named two squads for this break – meaning every player selected has a strong chance of getting playing time.

The upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures—away against the Netherlands, home and away against Greece, and at home against Serbia, are all competitive matches. This means that even if it wasn't the primary factor in his selection process, over the next couple of weeks, Klopp could wind up cap-tying a few more players for Germany.

This article was adapted from German.

World.title: France: Macron orders defense against Russian hybrid attacks
World.content:
Emmanuel Macron said Russia's hybrid threat had "intensified" and called for plans to protect critical infrastructure.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday highlighted the threat of Russian hybrid attacks and called for measures to protect key infrastructure.

"The Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," Macron said, adding that he had asked "the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure."

The plan would also involve protecting the "most sensitive" defense industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks.

What else did Macron say?

Macron said that France would continue supporting Ukraine following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 and vowed to respond to Russia's shadow attacks.

"This will not go unanswered," Macron said, without elaborating.

"The intention behind it is to intimidate us and to derail the effort to support the Ukrainians. The consequence will be the opposite," he added.

"We are not intimidated, because we know that what is at stake today in Ukraine is our security."

How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU states concerned over Russian hybrid threat

The comments come amid increasing concern from European states that Russia is ramping up hybrid threats that include acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and possible drone incursions.

Poland, Germany and Denmark have in recent weeks accused Russia of being being a series of drone incursions as well as instances of sabotage, arson, and surveillance of defense facilities.

Moscow has also been accused of planning to use a drone carrying explosives to attack an airport.

Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU needed a mechanism similar to NATO that would allow for a better response to hybrid attacks blamed on Russia.

The EU chief cited incidents such as an attempted drone attack on Leipzig last month that German authorities have attributed to Russia.

Von der Leyen said the EU needed to develop "a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents ... that fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security."

World.title: Beethoven and Andy Warhol: Rebel icons on show in Bonn
World.content:
The new exhibition "Beethoven by Warhol" at the Beethoven House in Bonn presents the pop artist's late masterpiece: a picture of Ludwig van Beethoven. The exhibition shares the story of the work with the public.

Andy Warhol portrait of Ludwig van Beethoven offers an unprecedented visual take on the great composer.

Warhol's 1987 silkscreen dispenses with the stern face usually seen on historical portraits and statues of the musical genius. Instead, Warhol uses pop art's vivid colors and striking visual language to turn Beethoven into a modern icon.

Originally conceived as a commercial work for the pop art guru's New York City studio, known as The Factory, the image was produced in a limited edition of 60 and proved to be one of the most innovative artistic engagements with Ludwig van Beethoven in the 20th century.

Warhol created the famous Beethoven color silkscreen prints just a few weeks before his sudden death on February 22, 1987. The series is among his final works.

The final silkscreen print was preceded by numerous attempts in many colors Image: Beethoven-Haus Bonn

How did Warhol approach Beethoven as a subject? And in what context did the work emerge in its numerous colored variations? A special exhibition, "Beethoven by Warhol," on show until April 2027 at the Beethoven House in Bonn — the composer's birthplace — explores these questions and more.

Like-minded geniuses?

The exhibition presents rare works that visitors would otherwise never get to see. Over the course of three years, the team of curators at the Beethoven House and Archive Bonn, led by Malte Boecker, unearthed these valuable pieces from the depths of archives and private collections.

In 1986, Andy Warhol had his picture taken with a bust of Beethoven Image: 2026 The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc./Licensed by Artists Rights Society (ARS)

Alongside Warhol's iconic depiction of Beethoven, visitors can see drawings the artist did while searching for his Beethoven motif in Bonn. There are also proofs of prints that document his exploration of the series' color scheme.

The curators highlight an elaborately crafted Beethoven print on canvas, which belongs to an anonymous collector from the Rhineland.

Curator Silke Bettermann said that, with such works, "Warhol tells us: Look here! This man, Beethoven, is completely modern! He's a superstar!"

Warhol's approach to subjects

Whenever something looks effortless and easy, there's almost always a great deal of work behind it. The same is true of Warhol's Beethoven series.

In his research process, Warhol compared numerous depictions of the composer before developing his own concept. He also did drawings based on likenesses of Beethoven, including the statue of the composer at Münsterplatz in Bonn.



Boecker is director of the Beethovenhaus and the initiator of the project Image: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance

Ultimately, Warhol decided to base his work on the iconic portrait by Joseph Karl Stieler, painted in 1820 on commission from the Frankfurt couple Franz and Antonie Brentano — a merchant family and patrons of the arts who were friends with the composer. The portrait sought to capture not only Beethoven's outward appearance but also his rebellious personality.

Warhol adopts the graphic design of Stieler's work, transforming its colors and overlaying it with a handwritten Beethoven score. However, rather than using the notes of the "Credo" of the "Missa Solemnis," as Stieler did, he chose music from the "Moonlight Sonata," probably Beethoven's most famous work. "Warhol's Beethoven speaks to us quite literally through and by means of his music," curator Silke Bettermann told DW.

Sports star at Beethoven House

Bonn-based Warhol gallerist Hermann Wünsche played a key role in the creation of Warhol's Beethoven works. He not only visited the artist in New York, but also brought him to the Rhineland several times. It's thanks to Wünsche that the artist created numerous Germany-related pieces, including the portraits of Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1976 and soccer star Toni Schumacher, whom Warhol portrayed in 1983.

Warhol depicted Toni Schumacher in a print. The German soccer star also came to the exhibition's opening Image: Meike Böschemeyer/Beethovenhaus

The exhibition's organizers brought the work depicting Schumacher to Bonn — on loan from the soccer star's private collection. The former goalkeeper himself also paid a visit.

In 1983, Schumacher sat as a model for Warhol. "It really gave me goosebumps!" he said.

Schumacher recalls his meeting with the US artist: "Back then, in the mid-1980s, in all modesty, I was already a star, too. But then Andy Warhol came along. And when we were together in the same room, I felt like I was looking at a superstar, so I took a bit of a back seat."

Warhol and music

Also on display for the first time at the Beethoven House is a unique collection of record covers designed by Warhol, assembled by Belgian collector and Warhol expert Guy Minnebach.

Also displayed is a private collection from Belgium showcasing Warhol's album covers Image: Meike Böschemeyer/Beethovenhaus

Over the course of three decades, Andy Warhol designed strikingly beautiful and individual covers for more than 50 records.

The range extends from a relatively classical, yet already whimsically playful, Mendelssohn record featuring Vladimir Horowitz, whom Warhol also knew personally, to the legendary jeans cover with a real zipper for The Rolling Stones' "Sticky Fingers" (1971) and the famous banana album cover for The Velvet Underground & Nico (1967).

According to eyewitness accounts, music played continuously at Warhol's studio. His record covers offer a glimpse into the artist's musical tastes. Beethoven, notably, is not among them.

Wolfram Weimer: 'We need more Beethoven'

The Warhol exhibition is the prelude to an important event at the Beethoven House. In March 2027, people around the world will commemorate the 200th anniversary of Beethoven's death with a special edition of the Beethoven Festival.

Germany's state minister for culture and media, Wolfram Weimer, attended the opening in Bonn Image: Meike Böschemeyer/Beethovenhaus

"This exhibition is a wonderful opening to the Beethoven commemorative year," Wolfram Weimer, Germany's state minister for culture and media, told DW. As patron of the exhibition at the Beethoven House, he traveled to Bonn to see it and speak at the opening ceremony. "Today, we need more Beethoven," he said during his speech.



"Beethoven was not only a musical genius who delighted the world with the greatest musical works of art imaginable," Weimer said. The composer also embodied the idea of freedom: "He was a rebel, he broke norms, and he questioned the power structures of his time. He was a messenger of freedom, and that is a good message for us today. We need more freedom today, too!"

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Pakistan suicide bombing targets police facility in Kohat
World.content:
A police official said the explosion killed at least 16 people, injuring many more. The attacker targeted a police facility and damaged a mosque at the site. The president blamed the attack on the TTP Pakistani Taliban.

A bomb attack in Kohat, Pakistan, near the Afghan border killed at least 16 people, police said on Friday.

No group immediately claimed responsibility but Pakistan's president blamed the Tehreek-e-Taliban (TTP).

Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan's Taliban rulers are fraught, with Islamabad alleging that the TTP uses safe havens across the Afghan border to plot and train for attacks in Pakistan.

Security personnel tried to guard the site following Friday's attack Image: Basit Shah/AFP

What do we know about the attack?

Stated casualty figures varied amid ongoing rescue operations on Friday after the explosives-laden car caused a large explosion and damaged a mosque at a police compound.

But provincial police chief Zulfikar Hameed told Reuters that at least 16 people, including five police personnel, were killed in the attack. A rescue official also told AFP that five police officers, 10 civilians and the attacker had died.

Figures on the number of wounded also varied but were put above 30 or even 50.

Police said in a statement that the blast occurred near a mosque as officers, their relatives and other civilians were worshipping inside.

They referred to it as a suicide attack.

Police also said that its forces and other attackers engaged in a subsequent gun battle after at least two other militants tried to to enter the facility.

Kohat, a city of around 220,000 people south of Peshawar, is fairly close to the Afghan border Image: B.S. Gillani/AP Photo/picture alliance

Government blames TTP amid attack in Afghan border area

No group claimed responsibility for the attack in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack and expressed sorrow over the casualties. He directed authorities to accelerate rescue operations. The Interior Ministry said that the "cowardly actions" of the attackers would not weaken "the nation's resolve."

President Asif Ali Zardari appeared to assign the blame to the TTP Tehreek-e-Taliban group.

"The complete elimination of Fitna-al-Khawarij and terrorists operating with foreign backing it essential for national security," Zardari said, using another term for the TTP.

Pakistan blames the increase of attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the border province of Balochistan further south in large part on the Taliban administration in neighboring Afghanistan.

How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Taliban rejects these allegations.

The accusations have sparked a bitter rift and even incidents of armed conflict between the neighboring countries.

Pakistan has carried out airstrikes it says targets militants taking refuge on Afghan soil, including this June.

Authorities in Kabul have in turn decried these attacks and reported civilian casualties.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Germans have soured on Chancellor Merz — can they trade him?
World.content:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's record-low approval ratings have emboldened his opponents. There are three ways to remove a chancellor from office in Germany.

It is the hot topic this week in Berlin: Does German Chancellor Friedrich Merz still have the backing of his own party, the Christian Democrats (CDU), and the coalition partners, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)? Will he be ousted? How would that work? Can he just step down?

Support for the chancellor has reached a record low: In the latest Deutschlandtrend representative survey, conducted by pollsters Infratest-Dimap for German public broadcaster ARD in early September, only 13% of respondents said Merz was doing a good job.

In early September, Merz's CDU suffered a resounding loss in the state of Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentary election, seeing the party's result halved from the 2021 election.

The election result has reinforced criticism of Merz, even from within his own ranks, and his communication style, which frequently alienates his audience.

But Merz remains chancellor. What are the options to change that? Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, grants the position a strong standing. German chancellors are not so easy to unseat.

Option 1: Resignation

Merz himself can decide to resign for any reason. That would not necessarily mean the end of the coalition government he leads. An example: In May 1974, then Chancellor Willy Brandt of the SPD resigned after a spy from the communist East Germany (DDR) was discovered to have been working in his inner circle. The governing parties, the SPD and the business-oriented Free Democrats (FDP), quickly agreed to continue their alliance.

Only 10 days later, Finance Minister Helmut Schmidt, also of the SPD, was elected as the new chancellor. To do this, an absolute majority of all lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, was needed (not only those present during the vote). This majority is called the "chancellor majority". Schmidt achieved this effortlessly, eventually got reelected and remained head of the German government for 8 years.

How likely is Merz to step down? Today's chancellor seems determined not to give up.

Option 2: A constructive vote of no-confidence

If a new majority were formed through alliances in the Bundestag or if a chancellor fell so far out of favor that their own supporters no longer believed in them, the instrument of a "constructive vote of no-confidence" could come into play. That means the majority of lawmakers vote in favor of a new candidate for chancellor.

An example: Helmut Schmidt of the SPD, lost the support of his junior coalition partner, the FDP, in 1982. The FDP wanted to push through changes to economic policy, which Schmidt rejected. They joined forces with the conservatives from the CDU and CSU, and jointly put CDU leader Helmut Kohl forward as a new chancellor. He won a majority in parliament, replaced Schmidt and moved into the chancellor's office where he remained for 16 years.

The probability of this happening in Merz's case is very remote. The conservatives and Social Democrats do not want to end their coalition. There is no clear rival candidate for Merz. North Rhine-Westphalia's State Premier Hendrik Wüst of the CDU is seen as a possible successor, but has not made a step forward. Besides: The CDU is usually very loyal toward its political leaders; ousting the chancellor via a vote of no confidence on the open stage of the Bundestag is simply unthinkable for most conservative lawmakers.

Option 3: A confidence vote

Germany's parliament cannot simply dissolve itself and call new elections. Lawmakers can, however, call a confidence vote on the chancellor and his government. Several chancellors have already used this mechanism, coupling it with a vote on a contentious issue.

As chancellor in November 2001, Gerhard Schröder (SPD) put forward a confidence vote in the Bundestag and linked it with the question of whether his government should deploy the German military to Afghanistan to support the NATO mission led by the United States following the September 11 attacks. Schröder won, remained in office and continued with his military policy.

Merz has already said he sees no point in calling for a confidence vote. There are also no signs of large breakaway movements from members of his coalition in Parliament.

If a chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Bundestag can be dissolved and fresh elections called. Following the defeat in the Bundestag, the chancellor can ask the German President to dissolve parliament and call voters to the polls. The president is not obliged to do so, but usually does.

It seems that Merz has ruled out this option. Neither the SPD nor the conservative Union (of CDU/CSU) are interested in calling new elections at a time when their approval ratings are low.

So will the government remain the same? Right now, it seems so. However, things have been so dynamic in recent days and weeks in Berlin political circles that nothing should be ruled out.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Rise of the AfD: The all-or-nothing party
World.content:
Germany's far-right AfD party is riding high after its latest electoral triumph in Saxony-Anhalt. But one question remains: Does it actually want to govern?

With just under 44% of the vote, the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as by far the strongest party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. It fell only narrowly short of an absolute majority in the newly elected state parliament, and with it the opportunity to govern on its own.

From the outset, the AfD made clear that governing alone was its preferred outcome. Only by avoiding having to compromise with coalition partners, the party argued, could it fully implement its agenda, which included compulsory work schemes for asylum-seekers, citizen patrols monitoring migration-related issues, and the abolition of all public funding for democracy and civic engagement programs.

After AfD's record result: Voices from Saxony-Anhalt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While Germany was debating whether the so-called "firewall" against the AfD was an appropriate means of protecting democracy, the party itself had long since built a wall of its own. For years, it has dismissed its political rivals as "cartel parties," effectively grouping them together with criminal organizations.

Teresa Haussmann of the University of Potsdam has been studying the AfD and other populist parties for years. In her view, the AfD sees "all other parties as part of a political elite that must be opposed."

Ulrich Siegmund: 'No compromises!'

On election night, at the height of the celebrations, the AfD's emerging star and lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, adopted a notably more conciliatory tone than he had done throughout his campaign.

"As a democrat, I extend my hand to all political forces willing to pursue a fundamental change of course with us," he said in an interview with German public broadcaster ARD.

Moments later, however, he qualified the offer: "There will be no bending on my part, no compromises."

Siegmund (center, giving the thumbs-up sign) and his AfD colleagues were all smiles the day after the Saxony-Anhalt vote Image: Odd Andersen/AFP

Within the AfD, compromise is frequently portrayed as a sign of weakness or a betrayal of principle. According to Haussmann, this is typical of populist parties not only in Germany but in many other countries as well.

"The basic premise is that a clearly identifiable popular will exists. If that is the case, then there can be only one correct political course. Any compromise would call that premise into question, because it would mean acknowledging that more than one legitimate path exists," she said.

Little remains of the conciliatory tone struck on election night. As they did throughout the campaign, senior AfD politicians are once again targeting their political opponents with insults and inflammatory rhetoric.

Few power-sharing options for AfD

In fact, the parties most likely to be considered potential coalition partners are often the ones the AfD attacks most fiercely. At present, the most obvious candidates are the center-right conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and the smaller left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

Merz, Weidel clash in parliament after AfD election win To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Immediately after the election victory, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel launched a blistering attack on the chancellor's party, declaring: "The CDU/CSU will never be able to win another federal election. That's a fact."

The Christian Democrats were the big losers of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. Some conservatives believe the party has drifted too far to the left — and it's precisely those disillusioned voters that the AfD is hoping to attract.

At the same time, the AfD has adopted increasingly radical rhetoric and, in Saxony-Anhalt, is classified by the security authorities as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization. The primary reason is that the party questions the legal equality of Germans with an immigrant background.

AfD aims for opponents' destruction

Leading figures within the AfD have repeatedly described the CDU's "destruction" as a political objective. Torben Braga, a prominent lawyer, party strategist and AfD member of parliament, made the party's confrontational stance toward its political rivals clear during a panel discussion organized by the far-right publishing house Antaios.

According to Braga, the AfD's goal is to become strong enough either to govern on its own or to trigger such profound upheaval within competing parties that they are effectively transformed into entirely new political forces.

The AfD thus appears to be pinning its hopes on the CDU's gradual decline, focusing on attracting disillusioned conservative voters rather than working with the party.

Could the BSW become a coalition partner?

For the moment, that leaves only one realistic partner: the relatively new Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW). The party was founded by former Left Party star Sahra Wagenknecht, who has achieved electoral success with a left-wing economic platform and a foreign policy stance widely seen as sympathetic to Russia.

For the first time, the BSW has entered the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament and could now emerge as kingmaker for the AfD. The party has signaled its openness to talks and potential cooperation. The two parties also share significant common ground on policy.

Why MAGA supports Germany's rise of the far right To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But shortly after its election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD also turned its fire on the BSW. Appearing on the far-right online channel Compact TV, AfD parliamentary group leader Oliver Kirchner referred to BSW politician Fabio De Masi as a "half-Italian." He went on to suggest that the BSW could not be relied upon if problems were ever to arise within a governing partnership.

The influential AfD leader in Thuringia, Björn Höcke, dismissed the BSW as the "latest cartel party." The signals coming from the AfD point neither to a willingness to compromise nor to any desire for rapprochement. On the contrary, even without a majority of its own, the party appears determined to stay the course and pursue its radical agenda.

AfD's national leadership wants to govern

But what if that still doesn't lead to an AfD-led government? "Then we'll simply have to hold another election. That's just how it is," Kirchner said on Compact TV.

That prospect, however, is unlikely to be welcomed by everyone within the party. "At the federal level, there is a strong interest in seeing the AfD lead the government in Saxony-Anhalt," observed political scientist Haussmann. Above all, the party's influential co-leader Weidel hopes to use an AfD-led state government as a stepping stone toward her long-term ambition of one day becoming chancellor.

Irregular migration 'a trigger point for radical parties' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DW also asked the AfD parliamentary group in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament, as well as a member of the party's state executive board, how the AfD is currently conducting coalition negotiations. Neither responded to a request for comment.

Despite its ongoing electoral successes, the AfD continues to face considerable internal tensions between its fundamentalist and pragmatic factions. Even if the party were to enter government through a coalition, public skepticism toward it in Germany would remain substantial.

"Even if the AfD were to succeed in forming a coalition with another party, that fact alone would not make it a more democratic party," said Haussmann

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Firmé las arras de un piso en junio y ahora el vendedor me dice que hay una derrama de 13.000 euros. ¿A quién corresponde pagarla?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. A principios de junio firmé un contrato de arras con un plazo de tres meses para escriturar la compra de la vivienda. A finales de junio la junta de la comunidad aprobó una derrama de 13.000 euros por el arreglo del portal y el ascensor. Todavía no he firmado la compraventa y ahora el vendedor me indica que debo hacerme cargo de dichos gastos. ¿A quién corresponde el pago? Jesús María G.

Respuesta. El pago de una derrama corresponde a quien ostente la condición de propietario en el momento en que se exijan cada una de sus cuotas, conforme a lo dispuesto en el artículo 17.11 de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal.

En consecuencia, las cuotas vencidas antes de la firma de la escritura deberán ser abonadas por el vendedor, ya que era el propietario cuando dichas cantidades eran exigibles. Por el contrario, las cuotas cuyo vencimiento se produzca con posterioridad a la firma corresponderán al comprador, al haber adquirido la titularidad de la vivienda, aunque la derrama hubiera sido aprobada antes de la compraventa.

Por último, las derramas que se aprueben una vez formalizada la venta serán asumidas íntegramente por el comprador.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: 24 horas en Ayamonte, la ciudad de Huelva donde vivir uno de los mejores atardeceres de Europa
World.content:
Esta localidad onubense se define por su luz y por su condición fronteriza con Portugal. Hay que visitar su parte alta y la baja, a pie del río Guadiana, y aprovechar el viaje para ir al cercano paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina

Ayamonte es una localidad onubense que se define por su condición fronteriza. Su localización geográfica, en la desembocadura del Guadiana, es un punto estratégico en el que estuvieron fenicios, romanos, musulmanes y cristianos y en el que confluyen el mencionado río, el océano Atlántico, marismas, esteros, dunas y dos culturas: la local y la vecina portuguesa. En la orilla de enfrente, se encuentran los pueblos lusos de Vila Real de Santo António y Castro Marim. Las costumbres de unos y otros se filtran en ambas orillas de manera natural. Son humedades enriquecedoras, como ese fado del cantante Carlos Cano titulado María la portuguesa, que narra el trágico incidente de contrabando y amoríos que le costó la vida a un ayamontino en los años ochenta.

Esa posición geográfica aúna valor estratégico y estético. Localización que hizo que Ayamonte, desde el siglo XVI, tuviera un vínculo especial con la navegación, el comercio marítimo y la pesca del atún y de la sardina, actividades que hicieron que la localidad se desarrollara económica y socialmente. En el siglo XIX, tras el tsunami provocado por el terremoto de Lisboa de 1755 y que tanto afectó a Ayamonte, fue el turno de la industria conservera y salazonera. En 1991, se inauguró el Puente Internacional del Guadiana, lo que supuso un gran hito en la relación con Portugal, en la movilidad y en la economía.

Más información Cinco ciudades en España para comer muy bien más allá de Madrid y Barcelona

A su patrimonio histórico y arquitectónico se ha sumado el de la luz. El proyecto europeo Atlantic Sunset ha situado a Ayamonte entre los lugares del arco atlántico donde el sol se pone más tarde —los estudios científicos del proyecto lo han identificado como el lugar donde se produce el último atardecer de la España peninsular entre los meses de octubre y febrero—. Un espectáculo natural que suma otro motivo más por el que merece la pena el periplo hasta aquí. Por carretera se llega desde las ciudades de Huelva, Sevilla y Faro, en Portugal, donde se encuentra el aeropuerto más próximo a Ayamonte y principal puerta de entrada de muchos de los turistas extranjeros que se ven paseando por las calles y las plazas del Rosario, de La Laguna y de La Ribera. En estos escenarios tiene lugar en el mes de agosto Un paseo por el Arte, evento que tiene el fin de mostrar en la calle las obras pictóricas, escultóricas y fotográficas de cientos de artistas locales o con alguna vinculación con la ciudad.

La plaza de la Laguna, en Ayamonte. Vibrant Pictures (Alamy / cordon Press)

10.00 Una habitación con vistas

Si la de Virginia Woolf era una habitación propia, las del Parador Nacional de Ayamonte (1) lo son con vistas; al Guadiana, al Puente Internacional que lo cruza y a la ciudad. Aquí antes hubo un castillo de origen romano, reedificado por los musulmanes después y finalmente ocupado por los cristianos.

Desde lo alto de la colina se divisa el río, Portugal y Ayamonte, que está a sus pies. El pueblo tiene una zona plana, a orillas del Guadiana, y otra alta, donde está el parador. Aia, en árabe, significa zona elevada. Cuando llegaron los cristianos, se encontraron un pueblo que se llamaba Aia y ellos le añadieron el sufijo “monte”. La parte más baja del pueblo se encuentra a unos tres metros sobre el nivel del mar, en las zonas cercanas al estuario; la parte más elevada es la del parador, a 63 metros de altura.

11.00 Antes y después del terremoto

A mediados del siglo XIII, Ayamonte pasó de manos portuguesas a las castellanas. A partir de ese momento, creció al amparo de la familia Guzmán y se vertebró en torno a dos partes: La Villa, la parte alta, donde se concentraban los edificios administrativos y religiosos, y La Ribera, la parte baja, donde se concentraba la vida marítima y comercial.

La Villa está llena de calles estrechas, miradores, fachadas tradicionales, balcones floridos y pequeños rincones con encanto. En este barrio se encuentran templos como El Salvador (2), San Francisco (3) y San Sebastián (4), además de antiguos palacios y casas señoriales. Uno de los edificios más emblemáticos es el antiguo Palacio de los Marqueses (5), junto al “Patio de la Jabonería”.

La iglesia de El Salvador, en la localidad onubense. Felipe Rodriguez (Alamy / cordon Press)

En La Ribera están las casas blancas, el paseo fluvial y el ambiente que evoca su origen marinero. Destacan el Centro Cultural Casa Grande Manuel Rivero “El Pintado” (6), el Ayuntamiento (7), las plazas de la Laguna y de La Ribera, conventos como el de las Hermanas de Santa Clara (8) y la capilla de San Antonio (9) las iglesias de La Merced (10) y Las Angustias (11). La Casa Grande es la única casa que se conserva anterior al terremoto de Lisboa de 1775. Seísmo que derivó en un tsunami que afectó gravemente a Ayamonte y otras localidades de Huelva, como Isla Cristina. Destruyó muchos edificios y hubo que reconstruir gran parte de su casco urbano. Las fachadas que hoy se ven datan de aquella época.

La plaza de La Laguna —aquí antes había una— es el corazón histórico y social de la ciudad. En ella hay una la réplica de La pesca del atún en Ayamonte, obra de Joaquín Sorolla integrada en la colección Visión de España que la Hispanic Society de Nueva York encargó al pintor. La plaza de La Ribera la diseñó el arquitecto José Granados, inspirada en las obras de Aníbal González, arquitecto sevillano que hizo la plaza de España. En la misma hay cerámica y ladrillo mudéjar forjado en las farolas, los bancos...

14.00 Geografía en el plato

Puesto de mercado y marisco en el mercado central de Ayamonte. Marcos del Mazo (Alamy / cordon Press)

La gastronomía, como el turismo y la pesca, son algunos de los sectores que forman parte de la economía azul, esa que se nutre de los recursos marinos de manera responsable, generando un crecimiento económico y empleo al tiempo que preserva la salud de los ecosistemas acuáticos de la zona. El abanico de delicias que se pueden degustar incluye la gamba blanca de Huelva, el choco, el atún, la sardina, la caballa, el arroz marinero y la mojama, el jamón del mar.

Estas delicias se preparan desde hace 60 años en el Restaurante Casa Luciano (12). El negocio hoy lo lleva el hijo del marinero que lo abrió, Luciano Ramos. El menú depende de lo que se coja en el día. En la carta, unos días hay y otros no, morro de atún, gambas a la plancha, cazón seco con tomate, cocido de garbanzos con rape, etcétera. Mucha de esa materia prima viene de Isla Cristina, donde se encuentra la principal lonja de Andalucía y la segunda más importante de España, después de la de Vigo. Cerca de la misma se puede comer en el Bar Marinero (13) y en Doña Lola (14), a orillas de la ría Carreras.

17.00 Parajes naturales

“Un lugar con tanta riqueza ecológica, como Ayamonte y sus alrededores, tiene un gran potencial como destino de viaje responsable”, sentencia Margarita Arjona, directora de Healing Planet, consultora de turismo sostenible. Alrededor de Ayamonte hay dunas y las marismas del Guadiana y el paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina, bañado por la ría Carreras, donde se encuentran Las Salinas del Alemán (15). Es una explotación artesanal, entre esteros y caños, que tuvo como primer propietario a un espía germano que envió el gobierno nazi en 1939 a la zona, Hans Burghard (o Juanito el alemán, para los lugareños), y que en la década de los ochenta se puso al frente de las mismas Manuel Gómez, al que le siguieron su hija (Manuela) y sus nietas (Estefanía y Sabina).

El paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina. Sonia Bonet (Alamy / cordon Press)

Además de esta sal por aquí hay salicornia o espárrago de mar, una planta que nace en las marismas y que el proyecto Marshfood produce de manera pionera. Cocineros como Ángel León, Martín Berasategui y Quique Dacosta la han usado.

18.30 La luz como fuente de orgullo

Si en Ayamonte el Guadiana es frontera, la luz es un orgullo. El pasado mes de enero esta localidad acogió una jornada divulgativa en el marco del proyecto europeo Atlantic Sunset que sitúa al municipio onubense entre los enclaves del arco atlántico donde el sol se pone más tarde. Es decir, es uno de los mejores escenarios europeos para ver el atardecer. Algo que se puede ver en tierra firme o a bordo de una embarcación, ya sea la que hace una travesía por el Guadiana o la que lo cruza con destino la orilla portuguesa.

World.title: Muslims launch hotline to report attacks on Dutch mosques
World.content:
Muslim liaison organisation CMO has set up a national hotline to report attacks on Dutch mosques amid concern that many incidents are going unreported.

Police have admitted that discrimination is underreported in the Netherlands, while community leaders hope the hotline will encourage victims to come forward.

Muhsin Köktas, chair of the CMO, said he believed the online portal, which will go live on September 20, “will lower the threshold for our community to report incidents here”.

Last year 414 cases of discrimination against Muslims were reported to police, 20 of which came from mosques, but Köktas said many crimes were not reported “because often nothing happens or if someone reports an incident, they don’t know what happens with it afterwards”.

A police spokesman said the force was aware of the low reporting rate, but urged victims to come forward.

“In broad terms discrimination is rarely reported, including discrimination against Muslims or incidents at mosques,” the spokesman said.

“[The hotline] can help people who experience discrimination to give their account, but we encourage these people to come to us as well. We can only take action, get a picture of problems in society and respond to them if we know what is going on.”

New Netherlands head coach Xavi Hernández has recalled Joey Veerman to the squad for the opening Nations League match against Germany next week.

The Borussia Dortmund midfielder, who has won 17 international caps, was left out of the squad for this summer’s World Cup in North America after falling out with Xavi’s predecessor Ronald Koeman.

The Spanish coach’s first squad is a mixture of youth and experience, with some senior players retained while others have made way for the Eredivisie’s young stars. Three members of the 26-man squad play their football in the Netherlands, while half are with clubs in the English Premier League.

Captain Virgil van Dijk is expected to win his 97th cap in Amsterdam next Thursday, ending speculation that the 35-year-old was considering retiring from international football.

Tijjani Reijnders and Crysencio Summerville have also kept their places despite moving to Saudi Arabia in the summer, in a departure from Koeman’s policy of not picking players from the Saudi league.

But there is no place for the Netherlands’ all-time leading scorer, Memphis Depay, who has struggled with injuries this year.

Twente’s veteran striker Wout Weghorst has also been left out, while Feyenoord’s in-form striker Gjivai Zechiël and PSV winger Ruben van Bommel, son of World Cup finalist Mark, are also in line to win their first caps.

After playing Germany in the Amsterdam Arena, Oranje will travel to Belgrade to take on Serbia on Sunday in their second match.

World.title: Dutch housing update: money for new homes, rising interest rates
World.content:
There was some good news for home buyers in this week’s budget with the announcement of a massive financial package to boost new residential development. There are also signs that house price rises are slowing down, although interest rates are shooting up and the issue of foundations continues to be confusing. This and more in the latest housing news round-up.

Budget briefing

There was not much in the way of direct measures impacting on the Dutch housing market in this week’s budget. For example, the government did not announce any new changes to the current mortgage interest deduction set up, although there will be a slight rise in income tax rate in the first and second tax bands, which will have a minimal impact on your rebate.

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan did come up with a string of measures she hopes will boost supply in the rental sector and new construction, and is pressing ahead with plans to cut the property transfer tax for holiday homes and investment properties from 8% to 7%.

Most relevant for would-be home buyers? “Plenty of investment in large scale developments of new homes, so if you are looking for a new-build property, you could be lucky – although the changes will take time to filter through,” says Matthijs van der Heijden, a mortgage advisor with Expat Mortgages, which has been helping internationals buy a home for over 20 years.

The government is also putting a further €100 million into a special fund to help first-time buyers get a foot on the housing ladder.

Interest rate increases

Over the past 18 months interest rates have been pretty stable but have been trending upwards since the second quarter of the year, and are currently rising sharply as geopolitical uncertainties continue.

“We are not yet seeing these higher rates have an impact on house prices,” says Matthijs, “but there does seem to be a little bit of room for negotiation. And some buyers are able to have a second viewing of a property before they decide whether to put in a bid.

“So there is more opportunity for people who don’t want to rush into a purchase. And we have noticed that some estate agents are helping their clients to negotiate on or just under the asking price.”

The higher interest rates are also making it more important to have some savings if you are planning to buy, just to keep your costs as low as you can. “If you have €50,000 that you can put down towards the cost of your house, that means €50,000 you won’t have to borrow at well over 4% interest,” Matthijs points out.

Ask your mortgage-related questions

Expat Mortgages will be at the IamExpat Fair in Eindhoven on October 3, so come along and meet the team in person, or 

Seminars, whether online or in person, are a great way of getting direct answers to your questions and sharing your experiences with others. “We also try to focus on the more specific situations – people who have not even moved here yet, and entrepreneurs who may not have been active in the Netherlands for more than a year, when most banks want three years,” says Matthijs.

“We’ve also seen an increase in the number of PhD students wanting to buy, and banks are becoming a little bit more lenient. They used to say ‘no permanent contract, no mortgage,’ but that is changing as well.”

More homes on the market?

Despite there being room for negotiation in some parts of the market, the shortage of cheaper homes to buy is continuing, and single people or single-income families wanting to buy a home are still facing an uphill struggle. Demand continues to be very high for properties at the lower end of the market.

“Things have been very slow over the summer, but now more people are getting out there and looking,” says Matthijs. “And you can still expect to have to overbid if you are looking at cheaper properties. Much depends on what areas you are looking in as well.”

The fundamentals of foundations

Since April, banks have been taking more account of a property’s foundations when deciding whether or not to back a mortgage application. As yet, says Matthijs, there is no overall consensus about what to do if a property’s foundations are in need of urgent, or not-so-urgent, action. “It is primarily the bigger banks which have been the frontrunners on this,” says Matthijs. “It is very early days.”

“However, you can assume if the report shows there is €100,000 worth of repairs which need to be done before the house is properly stable, the banks are going to wonder how this is going to be paid. This could be done, for example, by increasing your mortgage loan – although many people are nowadays stretched to capacity because of the high house prices – or through having the savings in your bank account. One way or another, your bank will want to know if you can pay for the work.”

Are you thinking about buying a home in the Netherlands? Make an appointment to talk directly to a mortgage advisor and find out how much you can borrow.
