World.title: Turkmenistan proposes UN-backed code for peaceful AI use
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. Turkmenistan proposed developing an International Code for the Peaceful Use of Artificial Intelligence in international relations and diplomacy under UN auspices at a briefing in Ashgabat today.

This was reflected in a statement published by the press service of the Turkmen government.

According to the information, the proposal was presented by Rovshen Annaberdyev, Head of the Department of International Organizations at Turkmenistan's Foreign Ministry.

Annaberdyev highlighted the potential of artificial intelligence in diplomacy, crisis analysis and early warning systems, while noting risks related to data security, state sovereignty and human oversight.

“Such a document could establish agreed international standards and ethical principles for the use of artificial intelligence in preventive diplomacy, mediation and negotiation processes,” the press service reported, citing Annaberdyev.

The initiative was presented as part of Turkmenistan's priorities for the upcoming 81st session of the UN General Assembly, particularly in the areas of international peace, security and multilateral cooperation.

The briefing also highlighted Turkmenistan's proposals on sustainable transport and climate cooperation, including the continuation of work on a Global Atlas of Sustainable Transport Connectivity and the creation of an Ashgabat Climate Dialogue.

Meanwhile, the United Nations in Turkmenistan serves as a development partner, endorsing national priorities aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals through the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (2021-2025/2026-2030). The Country Team, led by the UN Resident Coordinator, collaborates with the government on health, education, economic, and social reforms. Key focuses include people-centered governance, inclusive economic growth, and quality services. Major UN agencies involved are UNDP, WHO, UNICEF, and UNODC.

Additionally, the UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia addresses regional security. Key projects encompass legal aid strengthening, violence protection for women and children, trade improvement, water resource management, and pandemic preparedness, supported by significant government financial contributions.

World.title: Canberra ends Wests' NRLW fairytale in finals shut out
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Zahara Temara's big-game experience has driven Canberra to their first NRLW finals win, helping break the heart of Wests Tigers with a low-scoring 6-0 shut out at Campbelltown Stadium.

With both sides playing their maiden finals match after four years in the competition, it was Temara who shone brightest on Friday night.

The former Queensland State of Origin star laid on a bullet cut-out pass for Isabella Waterman for Canberra's first-half try.

With the Raiders holding a slender four-point lead for much of the second half, the Canberra No.7 then broke the line wide open and drew a penalty to go 6-0 up.

Beyond that, the Canberra halfback's management of the game proved the difference, forcing two dropouts and kicking the Tigers into submission.

Temara won a premiership with the Sydney Roosters in the 2021 season and could now come up against her old club next Saturday in a grand-final qualifier.

The Raiders will play the Tricolours if the all-star Brisbane roster beats Newcastle this weekend, otherwise they will face Gold Coast if the Knights win through.

Canberra controlled the majority of Friday night's game, with prop Chloe Saunders laying an immense platform with 173 metres and 73 of them post contact.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

In truth the Tigers did well to hold on as well as they did, forced to make 85 more tackles with the Raiders camped on their line for the majority of the first half.

But they were unable to land a blow at any point in the second half, with a 10-5 penalty count against them stifling the chance for many opportunities.

And when Tigers fullback Caitlin Turnbull put on a last-minute kick and chase to try and pull off a miracle, it was again Temara who was there to clean it up.

The defeat ends what has been a fairytale season for the Tigers, who won only five games combined in their first NRLW three seasons and collected the past two wooden spoons.

The joint venture had been in contention for a top-two spot before a brutal end to the season, as they reached the first top-flight men's or women's finals series in 15 years.

But their momentum was halted when they were flogged 58-0 by the Titans a fortnight ago, before last week's 22-10 loss to Canberra.

The Raiders, meanwhile, have beaten the Broncos and pushed both Gold Coast and the Roosters, making them a genuine threat over the next fortnight.

AAP

World.title: Third man charged over shooting in Melbourne's northern suburbs
World.content:
Detectives have charged a man in relation to a fatal shooting in Melbourne's north earlier this month, arresting him as he tried to board a flight out of Australia.

Police say the 20-year-old was arrested at Melbourne International Airport shortly before 4am Friday.

The arrest is part of the investigation into a fatal shooting in Thomastown on September 10, when 22-year-old Daniel Hussein was killed in front of friends at HR Uren Reserve in Thomastown.

In video from the night, loved ones could be heard crying and screaming as paramedics tried to revive Mr Hussein, but he died at the scene.

Plumber Daniel Hussein was killed in front of friends at HR Uren Reserve in Thomastown on September 10. (Supplied)

Three men are now facing murder charges over the fatal shooting.

Homicide detectives previously charged brothers Marcus Jajou, 19, and Lucas Jajou, 20, of Donnybrook, with Mr Hussein's murder.

Shortly after the September 10 shooting, relatives said Mr Hussein, a plumber, was engaged to be married and had recently bought a house.

"He had his whole life ahead of him," his brother said at the scene of the shooting earlier this month.

Mr Hussein's uncle, Abdallah Hussein, said he had never imagined he would have to say goodbye to his nephew.

"I still cannot believe you are gone," he wrote on social media in the days after the shooting.

"I still cannot understand that I will never see your smile again, never hear your voice, never watch you walk through that door again."

World.title: North Melbourne's 32-game winning streak over after shock loss to Hawthorn
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

North Melbourne's record 32-matchwinning streak is over after Hawthorn pulled off a massive AFLW upset.

The Hawks' 4.8 (32) to 3.7 (25) win on Friday night in Cairns is their greatest win since they joined the women's league in 2022.

The Kangaroos' sequence of straight wins is the longest in AFL, VFL and AFLW history. They had not been beaten since 2023, going undefeated in their 2024 and 2025 premiership runs.

Hawthorn's Jacqueline Dupuy said the feeling was "unreal".

"In my head, I was just panicking, thinking, 'How long have we got?' I reckon I looked at the bench three or four times in the last 90 seconds, just praying for the siren," Dupuy told ABC Sport.

"It was pretty unreal when it finally went. And to be able to look around at these girls I love so much and just see the sheer joy and feel that myself was amazing."

Hawthorn's win was made even more impressive given the absence of captain Emily Bates, who went down with an ACL rupture last weekend.

The triumph came off the back of relentless pressure.

North led by 10 points at the main break in blustery and humid Cairns conditions, but Hawthorn's Mikayla Williamson kicked the only goal of the third term, pulling the match to within three points.

Four straight behinds gave Hawthorn the lead in the last term for the first time since the first quarter. Cairns native Jacqueline Dupuy then kicked a goal to give Hawthorn a seven-point buffer at nine minutes.

Jacqueline Dupuy of the Hawks said the win was unreal. (Getty: Emily Barker)

But North was not done, with Blaithin Bogue kicking a goal against the run of play.

Inside the last two minutes, Hawks ruck Lucy Wales snapped the sealing goal.

"It's just a credit to the kind of player Lucy is. She's clutch. She is one of the most consistent players for us and I just feel like it was very fitting that she was able to kick that winning goal," Dupuy said.

North's last loss was the 2023 grand final against Brisbane. The Kangaroos then started the 2024 season with a win and a draw, before starting their historic streak.

Friday night's tally was also their lowest score since 2023.

It is a great start to the weekend for the Hawks, ahead of Saturday's AFL preliminary final against Brisbane, when they will also start as underdogs against the two-time defending premiers.

The AFLW victory puts the team just outside the top four.

"It's always tough to go to sleep after a game, and certainly feeling pretty jacked right now," Dupuy said.

"But I'm sure we'll get a rest and go up again in six days, which would be exciting to head down to Geelong."

With AAP

World.title: Australian finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize 'nervous but excited'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Indigenous rangers responsible for one of the largest cultural burning programs in the world have been named finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize.

The prize, which comes with $1.9 million to support each winner's work, aims to reward environmental projects "that will drive significant progress towards repairing the planet".

The alliance celebrated its 10th anniversary with a conference at Uluru in 2024. (Supplied: IDA/ Salty Davenport)

Samantha Murray, CEO of the Indigenous Desert Alliance (IDA), said she was proud the network of 70 ranger teams across Central Australia had been given global recognition.

"To be recognised on such a massive scale is something that we work really hard at, to make sure that desert rangers are known, they're heard, they're seen."

More than 150 judges selected the IDA from among 7,000 nominations from 169 countries, with Ms Murray admitting she was "slightly nervous, but really excited" about the alliance's prospects.

In the past four years the alliance has engaged 1,300 Indigenous participants, trained 885 rangers and managed fuel loads and restored biodiversity across 145 million hectares of land — an area four times the size of Germany.

Sam Murray says desert rangers are integral to climate talks. (ABC: Nicholas Martyr)

Ms Murray, a proud Yilka, Wongutha and Nyoongar woman, said the Right Way Fire program, which combines cultural and Western ways of burning, was key to their nomination for the prize.

The rangers conduct targeted burns to create a mosaic of vegetation which reduces fuel loads, improves native habitats and lessens the risk of large, destructive bushfires.

"Those ways of reading country are when to burn, who to burn by the right people, what times, what weather, what country," Ms Murray said.

She said alliance, formed more than a decade ago, relied on land management practices developed and passed down over tens of thousands of years.

"It really just helped to elevate the way my desert people have been connecting for a very, very long time across different country," she said.

"It's really big about making sure we're continuing that caring for country from our ancestors and our elders, for ourselves and our children."

Nyikina Mangala Rangers from the Kimberley region conduct burning. (Supplied: IDA/ Ewan Noakes)

Prince impressed by 'scale' of IDA's work: CEO

Rangers across the desert carry out culturally informed fire management. (Supplied: IDA/ Ngurrara Rangers)

Prince William created the Earthshot Prize in 2020, saying he wanted to reward new ideas and technologies for tackling climate change.

Earthshot Prize CEO Jason Knauf said the prince would be among those who decided who would win in Mumbai in November.

"I think he was absolutely amazed by just the scale [of IDA's work]," he said.

"To have one initiative that is protecting 2.7 million square kilometres — we haven't seen anything like that in the previous six years."

The first Earthshot award ceremony was held in 2021 in London. (Supplied: Reuters/ Henry Nicholls)

The IDA is one of three finalists in Earthshot's "protect and restore nature" category.

It is up against the Himalayan country Bhutan, which has enshrined environmental protection in its constitution, and the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative which protects habitats along the Rocky Mountains on the Canada-US border.

Jason Knauf says there is strong competition for the 2026 prize. (ABC: Scott Preston)

Mr Knauf said investing in the knowledge of Indigenous people was key to meeting the global commitment of protecting and conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030.

"Indigenous communities right around the world who are protecting a disproportionate share of the land that we all rely on for our economy … have the deep knowledge about what is going to work in the face of climate change."

Earthshot Prize announcement The Earthshot Prize is an ambitious environmental program that aims to find new ideas and technologies around the world to tackle climate change.

If the IDA won, Ms Murray said the funds would boost the alliance's fire protection work, as well as increase the grants available for projects such as trips on country for intergenerational knowledge transfer or ranger exchanges.

She would like to see more desert communities having a "visible presence" in global conversations about climate change.

"We can't ignore the impacts of climate change and how it's impacting and shaping country a little bit differently and making it much harder for desert rangers out there," she said.

'Loudest voice in any room'

The Queensland Indigenous Womens Ranger Network protects the Great Barrier Reef. (Supplied: BBC)

Australia has been a strong contender for the prize in the past, with the Indigenous Women Rangers Network in Queensland winning the "revive our oceans" category in 2022.

Local finalists have also included the world's first fully upcycled skyscraper Quay Quarter Tower, the Sydney Institute of Marine Science's living seawalls project, and an Australian-owned cattle and sheep feed supplement which used seaweed.

The great desert skink is being protected. (Supplied: IDA/Karenza Sunfly)

Mr Knauf said he hoped the recognition would mean the work of the Indigenous Desert Alliance would be shared worldwide.

"We get our whole global network behind them to scale, replicate their work and really champion what they're doing on a global stage," he said.

"We say that we want our finalist to be the loudest voice in any room that they walk into and we help them to achieve that."

World.title: Adelaide workers expected to bear brunt of Bendigo Bank cuts
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A union says 137 workers at the Bendigo and Adelaide Bank are slated for redundancy as part of an ongoing company restructure, but the company says its plans are "yet to be finalised".

They would form part of a total of 299 job changes across the bank's Consumer Lending Operations and Customer Care divisions.

ABC News understands that the bank's Adelaide staff would be impacted more than its other city and regional workforces.

That restructure began in April, when Bendigo Bank announced partnerships with two international companies: IT service provider Infosys, and agentic AI company Genpact.

In a statement the union said about 445 Bendigo Bank positions had been "lost or reduced through restructures" since January 2025 and that forthcoming losses had "a strong documented relationship to AI, automation or broader technological change".

"The bank has told us that as a partnership with an offshore technological company, that it's making efficiencies through these redundancies," ASU SA-NT branch secretary Ella Waters said.

"We're yet to see what that means for whether or not these workers are going to be completely replaced by AI, but we're extremely concerned that, in the name of technological advancement, hundreds of jobs are being cut."

Ella Waters is concerned Bendigo Bank jobs will be sent offshore. (ABC News )

A Bendigo Bank spokesperson referred ABC News to an April statement announcing the partnerships with Infosys and Genpact, saying the bank "continues to review its business operations and processes".

The spokesperson did not confirm whether AI would replace workers.

"The detailed design for all impacted areas is yet to be finalised," the spokesperson said.

"The process and operational improvements expected to be delivered will lead to workforce changes that will impact our people.

"The bank is committed to supporting all employees through this period of change, including exploring opportunities for redeployment for those whose roles will no longer be required, where possible."

World.title: At least three dead in Philippines school shooting
World.content:
At least three students are dead and eight others injured following a shooting at a high school in the southern Philippines, authorities have confirmed.

The announcement came after the country's education department revealed the incident occurred at Banga National High School in Banga in the province of South Cotabato.

Provincial Governor Reynaldo Tamayo told Reuters that the shooter was among the three people killed.

Banga Mayor Albert Palencia later confirmed the shooter was 16 years old and that four of the eight people injured were in a critical condition. The victims were aged between 14 and 17.

"The suspect supposedly sat beside his friends and told them to go home, 'Because after lunch, I will be executing my plan,'" Mr Palencia told Reuters.

"His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker."

In a video posted to Facebook and verified by AFP, a man can be seen carrying what appears to be an injured child from the school, rushing him into the sidecar of a waiting motorbike.

In another, a teacher speaking in a local dialect could be heard saying there were two shooters and a student insisting they were outsiders.

The local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office said school classes had been suspended across the Banga municipality.

The incident follows two shootings since June at schools in the south of the country.

School shootings were previously rare in the Philippines, but the incidents led to nationwide live shooter drills being conducted this month.

The incident marks the third school shooting in the south-east Asian country since June. (AFP: Philippe Turping/PhotoNonStop)

Last month a student live-streamed himself shooting and killing another student in a classroom in Zamboanga before taking ‌his own life.

In June, at least three students were killed and about 20 others injured an attack at a public high school in Tacloban when two classmates opened fire on campus.

The latest incident came just days after three other people were killed and 15 injured in a separate shooting in Cotabato during the first parliamentary election held in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

The Philippines has relatively strict gun ownership regulations, including background checks and psychological evaluation requirements, although illegal firearms remain in circulation.

Mr Tamayo urged parents to ensure guns were kept out of reach of minors.

"We need to be responsible in storing firearms. Gun owners, in particular, must make sure that minors do not have access to them," he told Reuters.

"We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address."

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Freo flies into grand final after stunning fightback against Sydney
World.content:
Fremantle has pulled off a sensational last-quarter comeback to surge into the AFL grand final with a tense 12-point win over Sydney.

Trailing by 27 points late in the third quarter, the Dockers kicked the last six goals of their preliminary final to win 12.11 (83) to 10.11 (71) at the SCG.

Fremantle advances to the second grand final in club history, where they will meet either Hawthorn or Brisbane.

Justin Longmuir's men were staring down the barrel of an early exit before Hayden Young converted a difficult set shot after the three-quarter time siren, and were full of running in a gripping finish.

Young (28 disposals), Andrew Brayshaw (29), Caleb Serong (28) and Shai Bolton (two goals) were instrumental in the victory.

But it wasn't assured until the dying stages, when Isaiah Dudley ran into an open goal with less than two minutes on the clock.

"Words can't describe how proud I am of everyone for stepping up," Fremantle captain Alex Pearce told Channel 7.

"There were just so many moments where guys stood up under the fiercest of pressure.

" We played our best footy in the last quarter when everything was against us. "

Luke Jackson finished with two goals in an entertaining ruck battle with Brodie Grundy.

Dudley's second major was the Dockers' fifth of a dominant final quarter, in which Patrick Voss's huge fend-off and checkside goal on the run was a highlight.

"[Our forwards] were beaten early, and it was hurting us a little bit," Pearce said.

"Our ball use into the forward line was diabolical at times. We were just kicking it to the red jumper.

"But wow, our forwards stood up [in the final quarter]. They stood up like big men."

Sydney's brave effort came without injured captain Callum Mills and the five stars banned in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Errol Gulden (36 disposals) was brilliant in setting up their lead, with Logan McDonald (three goals) dangerous in attack.

"It's gut-wrenching, devastating, but I'm overwhelmed with pride in what we've been able to do over the last couple weeks," Swans stand-in captain Dane Rampe said.

"We didn't get that result tonight, but I felt over the last couple of weeks we took a couple of steps in the right direction towards [getting] back respect and trust of not only our fans and our club, but the AFL community in general."

AAP

World.title: Federal finance minister threatens to bypass NT government on funding
World.content:
Federal Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has met with the Northern Territory's acting chief minister over concerns the NT government is not spending Commonwealth money where it is needed.

With more than 70 per cent of the NT government's revenue coming from the Commonwealth, Ms Gallagher travelled to Darwin today to take issue with how some of the funding was being distributed.

Ms Gallagher said she and Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy had initially organised to meet with Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, who is now on leave, and instead met with Acting Chief Minister Gerard Maley.

"We had hoped to meet with the Chief Minister," she said.

"We made that appointment some two weeks ago and the reason behind that was we were certainly, from the Commonwealth's point of view, experiencing some concerns about how particular programs are being run."

Malarndirri McCarthy and Katy Gallagher met with Gerard Maley this week after Lia Finocchiaro went on leave. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Ms Gallagher pointed to areas such as disaster relief, domestic violence service provision and housing, where she believed the tough-on-crime NT government had dropped the ball.

The federal parliament heard last month that $330 million allocated under a Commonwealth housing agreement had not been spent, and the NT government was seeking to reduce its 10-year housing target from 2,700 to 1,800.

Ms Gallagher also said the federal government was concerned a lack of money hitting the ground was exacerbating social dysfunction, as the NT goes backwards on seven Closing the Gap targets — the worst performance of any jurisdiction.

NT goes backwards on Closing the Gap targets The NT government has released its Aboriginal Affairs framework as the territory goes backwards on several Closing the Gap targets.

A string of serious crime incidents have occurred in the territory this month, including one where two boys, aged eight and 11, allegedly held up two Darwin businesses at knifepoint while wearing balaclavas.

"The money that we are investing is to reach the outcome that we want, which is to provide better services and better supports in housing, in particular in relation to overcrowding, in domestic, family and sexual violence, to make sure the service system is able to cope with the level of violence that exists right across the country," Ms Gallagher said.

"So when we're seeing delays or reductions in the Northern Territory's own expenditure, that concerns us.

"That was why we wanted to put it on the table — we wanted to come up to the chief minister and say 'Look, these are all of our concerns, it's across a number of portfolios'."

Ms Gallagher said if the NT government did not act, the Commonwealth would bypass it and deliver more funding directly to frontline services.

"If we are going to ... not see the money getting to where it's needed ... we would look to directly fund those organisations," she said.

Katy Gallagher says the federal government isn't afraid to pull funding from the NT government and give it directly to service providers. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"The Commonwealth is serious that we are not going to see our investments sit there and not get progressed.

"In housing, we want the houses built, in domestic, family and sexual violence, we want the service system supported."

Before the meeting, Mr Maley said it was "a bit rich" for Ms Gallagher to "come up here and tell us what to do".

"They need to have a good, hard look at themselves in relation to the non-government organisations they fund and the funding that they put in to the Northern Territory and where that money is spent," he said.

Gerard Maley says the federal government should look more closely at the services it funds directly. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"We have asked for a full audit in relation to that money many times and it has fallen on deaf ears.

" They need to have a good, hard look at themselves because they are spending money in my view where it should not be spent. "

Disaster funding not applied for

The Northern Territory experienced a series of natural disasters over the most recent wet season, including Cyclone Fina and floods which caused the displacement of hundreds of people.

Ms Gallagher said the NT government still had not applied for disaster relief funding for events that occurred last year.

"Some of those disasters happened in November 2025, so it's been some 10 months, and we're still waiting for the paperwork," she said.

"What that means is those communities are still waiting for Commonwealth funds to flow under those arrangements."

NT community still without key services months after floods Months after record flooding, Nauiyu / Daly River remains significantly damaged and without key services.

But Ms Gallagher said "we made some progress in the meeting on that front".

"The Northern Territory government [is] committed to having the paperwork for various projects they want funded under that category in to the Commonwealth by Christmas, but it has taken a long time to get here," she said.

A spokesperson from the Office of the Chief Minister said the meeting was "productive" but "it was clear the federal ministers had come with closed minds and pre-prepared press lines".

"The CLP government will continue to focus on reducing crime, rebuilding the economy and restoring lifestyle and leave the carping and hand-wringing to Canberra," they said.

World.title: Purple pain: Swans left heartbroken in front of 45,000 at the SCG as Dockers storm home; Pearce says dreams won’t help Dockers win flag

Hayden Young celebrates his goal. AFL Photos

World.title: Sydney v Fremantle player ratings: Brightest stars and stunning moments on a night of agony and ecstasy
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Sydney v Fremantle player ratings: Brightest stars and stunning moments on a night of agony and ecstasy

Loading

Some fairytales just don’t come true. After the events of past month in Melbourne, the second-on-the-ladder Swans couldn’t have seemed further away from another grand final berth. But what happened since – despite missing a host of their best players after they were handed season-ending suspensions by the Swans for failing to meet the club’s standards after their round 23 win over Essendon – has been nothing short of remarkable. On Friday night, they finished just 13 points shy of the decider as the Dockers roared home. Marc McGowan (Sydney) and Steve Barrett (Fremantle) run their eye over every player in from the preliminary final at the SCG.



Shai Bolton and Isaiah Dudley celebrate a crucial goal in their thrilling win over Sydney. Getty Images Sydney (2) Hayden McLean: Relieved Brodie Grundy in the ruck and comfortably won those stints against Mason Cox. His intercept marking was also a feature. 6/10 (4) Brodie Grundy: Grundy took the first-half honours against Luke Jackson and was a key reason the Swans started so well, but the star Docker rose to the occasion after half-time. It was a great ruck battle. 6.5/10



(6) Logan McDonald: McDonald was excellent again, after kicking six goals in the Swans’ qualifying final drubbing of the Lions. He was often Sydney’s deepest forward and constantly presented, and was rewarded with a game-high three goals. 8/10 Logan McDonald loomed as a potential match winner for the Swans. AFL Photos (8) James Rowbottom: Had a series of defensive efforts that led to Angus Sheldrick’s third-quarter goal and there is never any question on his effort. 6.5/10 (9) Jesse Dattoli: A quiet night for the second-year Swan, who otherwise grabbed his opportunity late in the season. 1/10 (11) Tom Papley: Papley was sensational in the opening half, whether kicking or setting up goals, executing diving smothers or stealing handballs. But he would have loved a better return than 1.3. 8/10



(12) Angus Sheldrick: Sheldrick is as tough as nails and kicked a goal in the third quarter, but won only 12 disposals. 6/10 Related Article AFL 2026 Only one of the Serong boys will reach the grand final this year. Their mum is already taking sides (13) Jai Serong: Who would have picked the ex-Hawk at the start of the year to be a centre-bounce midfielder in a preliminary final? Serong’s been a bargain recruit and was a strong performer on the night. 7/10 (15) Sam Wicks: Wicks won enough of the ball, but was a bit sloppy with his disposals, and wasn’t quite as good defensively as usual. 5/10 (16) Braeden Campbell: Started the game strongly, including a terrific snap for a goal, and seemed headed for a big night, but faded dramatically before getting a few touches late. 4/10



(21) Errol Gulden: Had an early turnover that gifted Fremantle a goal, but quickly returned to his dominant self that extended his purple patch. Gulden’s 36 disposals were seven more than any other player, but probably wasn’t quite as damaging as usual. 8.5/10 (24) Dane Rampe: Returned to the captaincy after Callum Mills’ ACL rupture, and typically gave his all in what may have been his last game. Copped a huge fend-off from Patrick Voss in the last quarter before the Docker’s key goal. 6/10 Joel Hamling and Mason Cox to toe-to-toe. Getty Images (25) Billy Cootee: Had a second-quarter handball blunder that almost cost the Swans a goal, but was part of the Swans’ ground-wide defensive effort. 3/10 (27) Justin McInerney: One of many Swans who faded badly in the final term, picking up just one of his 14 disposals. Sydney rolled the dice in selecting him for his first match since June, and he was OK without doing a great deal. 5/10



(29) Joel Hamling: The premiership-winning Bulldog and ex-Docker grabbed a few intercept marks and spent time on Jye Amiss and Voss. Can hold his head up high. 7/10 Tom McCartin keeps a close eye on Patrick Voss. AFL Photos (30) Tom McCartin: Big moment early with a goal-saving tackle on Voss and finished with a game-high 11 intercept possessions, which sums up how strong he was aerially. Conceded a goal to Jackson with a no-look hack kick in his defensive 50. 7.5/10 (32) Harry Kyle: Kyle did not look out of place down back and looks a promising prospect who will play further afield in the future. 6/10 (33) Caiden Cleary: Cleary’s turnover off a risky corridor kick when the game was in the balance late could have been incredibly costly. His tackling pressure was good, but didn’t win a heap of the Sherrin. 5/10



(34) Matt Roberts: Roberts was a solid performer without having a major impact. He has played much better games than this. 6/10 James Rowbottom and Charlie Curnow were left heartbroken with the result. AFL Photos (35) Charlie Curnow: It was not Charlie’s night. Outside of a brilliant hanger over Oscar McDonald, which preceded his sole goal, Curnow failed to have his usual impact when the Swans needed him most. 2/10 (40) Tom Hanily: Did his best work in the first quarter, when his repeated strong efforts were rewarded with an opportunistic goal. But he had only four touches after quarter-time. 3/10 (43) Lewis Melican: Lost contact with Mason Cox in the final term when the ex-Pie marked and kicked Fremantle ahead, then dropped a mark before Isaiah Dudley’s sealing goal. Was solid in the first three quarters. 4/10



(44) Jake Lloyd: Lloyd did as he has throughout his career, providing strong rebound out of defence and generally using the ball well. 7/10 View post on X Fremantle (3) Caleb Serong: After seeing off Oisin Mullin’s tag a week ago, Serong got away from Rowbottom, before Sydney dispensed with the run-with role at half-time. The lion-hearted midfielder misfired with 0.3 but set others up with his 28 disposals and 10 clearances. 7.5/10



(5) Heath Chapman: His aerial game was sturdy, and he used the footy neatly off half-back, aside from one obviously costly moment, which resulted in a third quarter goal which sparked Sydney’s resurgence. 6/10 (6) Jordan Clark: Had 497 metres gained, with his customary dash out of defence, but that was offset by some imprecise use of the footy and below-par decision-making. 5/10 (8) Andrew Brayshaw: A typically industrious display in the centre-square. Brayshaw’s disposal was a tad off in the preliminary final heat, but his heart and head – covered in blood approaching three-quarter-time – could never be questioned, amassing a team-high 29 touches. 7/10 View post on X (9) Luke Jackson: A week after destroying Geelong, Jackson was always going to be in for a more challenging night against Grundy. Still, “the Unicorn” narrowly took the individual honours, booting two important goals and letting Grundy know about it. 7/10



(10) Shai Bolton: Constantly hurried in the first half and unsighted in the third term, Bolton came alive in the fourth. He booted two fourth-quarter goals, his shift from midfield to deep forward proving a masterstroke. He also laid eight tackles. A cameo by his standards, but what a cameo. 7.5/10 (13) Luke Ryan: Generated rebound out of defensive 50 and rarely wasted the footy. He was important down the stretch and went at 94 per cent disposal efficiency. 7/10 (16) Murphy Reid: That trademark craftiness, creativity and poise – all of it was absent in the first half. Reid was under the pump against Sydney’s hounding pressure, before bouncing back to his best with some key, deft touches after the break. 7/10 They’ve done it: Murphy Reid, Caleb Serong and Hayden Young are through to a grand final. Getty Images (17) Judd McVee: Had the challenging task of minding Papley and, after a more than rough start, held his own. 6/10



(18) Mason Cox: Won his share of hitouts but was unimpactful around the ground ... until his moment came. The big fella’s strong mark and goal put the Dockers in front in the final term. 5/10 (20) Patrick Voss: Talk about a mixed bag. Outstanding. 8.5/10 View post on X (28) Neil Erasmus: Kicked the first goal of the night with a smart snap and was solid on his wing, aside from a few shaky moments. 6/10

World.title: Swans’ rollercoaster month ends with heartbreak after Fremantle fightback
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Swans’ rollercoaster month ends with heartbreak after Fremantle fightback Vince Rugari September 18, 2026 — 10:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The Sydney Swans have put their supporters through a vast range of emotions within the past month. On Friday night, they served up a new one: heartbreak. Classic, traditional sporting trauma. It turns out you don’t need to be at Optus Stadium to experience Wharfie Time. It doesn’t have to be a Fremantle home game for the purple haze to suddenly descend and dull the senses. It can happen anywhere, to anyone. Loading Fears that the Swans had “played their grand final” a fortnight ago were totally unfounded. From the outset of this classic preliminary final on Friday night, the Swans were rabid, aggressive, relentless, playing like their lives depended on it. Again. If their first effort didn’t stick, there was a second, third, fourth, fifth to follow. They knew where they wanted to go and wanted to get there in a hurry. Whatever concoction sustained them in that qualifying final against the Brisbane Lions, there was more of it left … until, at some point in the final quarter, the punch bowl was empty. They were out of juice. The Dockers noticed, and they went to work.



“It looked a little bit like that,” said Swans coach Dean Cox. “This time of the year, you can’t give a team any momentum, and they took it.” For three quarters, the Dockers were nowhere near it. Everyone knew they were the better side considering Sydney’s long list of absentees, but the Swans played like the better side, and the scoreboard reflected it. Yet they had left the door ever so slightly ajar for Freo, hitting the post four times and letting a number of other key opportunities slip, particularly in the first quarter. Swans players Tom Papley, Errol Gulden and James Rowbottom after Friday’s loss to Fremantle. via Getty Images Hayden Young’s goal for Fremantle on the three-quarter-time siren reduced Sydney’s margin to a manageable 21 points and restored in themselves a modicum of belief. So who pushed the “Wharfie Time” button? You can take your pick, but it may well have been Patrick Voss, aka “the Prancing Pony”, who had hitherto been playing like a donkey. His only possession for the entire first half was a set shot after the half-time siren which did not even make the distance.





The Swans tried to hold on throughout the 10-minute arm wrestle that followed Voss’ goal, but they were cooked, and they knew it. Goals from Shai Bolton, Mason Cox and Isaiah Dudley finished them off, and the pain was etched all over the faces and bodies of Sydney’s players when the final siren eventually sounded and put them all out of their misery. “I’m just extremely proud of everyone uniting, galvanising and coming together to try and get our season to the last game, and we fell short,” Cox said. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 Purple pain: Swans left heartbroken in front of 45,000 at the SCG as Dockers storm home; Pearce says dreams won’t help Dockers win flag “It’s hard to say it’s a missed opportunity when you play a really good footy team. Prelims are big games and there’s a lot at stake because there’s a grand final next week. We missed the opportunity to take those moments to put ourselves in a grand final. The older players, they certainly understand that they don’t just come around every year. Some of the young ones, they just [think], ‘How good is it to be a part of it, and I’m learning everything, and I’ll grow from playing in them,’ but they’re hard to get to.” So the ride ends here. After a month defined by the scandal at the Pullman Hotel and the on- and off-field fallout, the Swans can be immensely proud of the way their remaining players have gallantly defended the club’s colours and culture, as well as disappointed that it couldn’t take them all the way. They will never know how far they could have gone if “the Pullman Five” had simply behaved themselves that night, and that hurts, too.



What happens next for those players remains to be seen, and in any case will be largely determined by Victoria Police. But during their absence, the Swans found something else: Proof that whatever this club is supposed to stand for is bigger than any individuals, and sturdy enough to survive the damage they caused. Now they can try and build again. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Significant persons of interest’: Victorians linked to gun used in killing of Sydney student
World.content:
Four Melburnians have been charged after being extradited to NSW over alleged links to the gun used in the fatal shooting of an innocent university student in Sydney’s south-west as part of the city’s gangland war. Police alleged in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Thursday that Vaifaalie Tuafuti, Omar Mohamed, Amenah Abusud and a child worked for the notorious Alameddine crime family in a recent spate of violence against the so-called Coconut Cartel. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Sydney home. The group were driven across the border on Friday, where they were handed over to NSW Police and arrested at Albury police station. They were all charged with special aggravated break and enter committing a serious and indictable offence, two counts of firing a gun at a home, and organising and partaking in criminal activity.



The adults were refused bail to appear in bail court on Saturday. The 16-year-old will appear at a children’s court on Saturday. A police summary read out in Abusud’s extradition hearing revealed investigators have linked the four to a gun found at the family home in the suburb of Glen Alpine, where Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed early on September 1. Loading NSW Police have said the wrong address was targeted in what is believed to have been a botched organised-crime killing. Two teenagers were charged with murder over the incident early on Thursday. The pair did not apply for bail and were remanded in custody to face court again on November 13. The four Victorians mentioned in court have not been charged over Tapia’s death but are accused of a home invasion in the Sydney suburb of Hurstville, and shooting cars in Turrella the night before.



Ballistic analysis found discharged cartridge cases at the two scenes matched and were then “positively matched” to the Glen Alpine homicide scene, where a firearm was found, a NSW Police investigator testified on Thursday. A 23-year-old man arrested at Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north are being extradited to NSW. NSW Police “Subsequent ballistic examination confirmed that the firearm was used to discharge rounds recovered from all three crime scenes,” he said. “Investigations relating to the homicide at Mount Sugarloaf Drive, Glen Alpine, remain ongoing.” NSW Police Raptor Squad commander Brad Abdy said the gun allegedly used at Hurstville and Turrella was found at the Glen Alpine crime scene but the investigation of Tapia’s death is “extremely complex”, and homicide detectives are still working to determine if the Melburnians can be charged with his murder.



A 26-year-old woman arrested at Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north are being extradited to NSW. NSW Police “It’s very important that all the evidence is examined before people are charged obviously with a very serious offence of murder,” Abdy said on Friday. “These people are obviously significant persons of interest.” Police say Tuafuti, Mohamed, Abusud and a child left Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north late on August 29 and drove to Campbelltown in Sydney’s south-west, arriving at an Airbnb property about 5am on August 30. A senior constable from NSW Police’s anti-gang Raptor Squad said the group were “contracted by a faction of the Alameddine organised-crime network … for the purposes of committing extremely violent crimes targeting several Sydney-based close associates of the Coconut Cartel”.



Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Trail of evidence’: Teens charged over mistaken identity murder of innocent student Court documents reveal Mohamed, Tuafuti, the 16-year-old child and an unknown fourth person are accused of breaking into a home in Hurstville about 2am on August 31. No one was at home. “Offenders utilised a sledgehammer to gain entry to the premises and discharged a round of ammunition into a wall inside,” a statement of alleged facts says. The court heard the break-in was filmed, and the occupant later received a WhatsApp message that said: “We were in your house to kill you if you were there, but God gave you life today. I promise you, we are going to make sure your kids grow up with no father.”



The four allegedly then drove to a home in Turrella that police said was “well-known to law enforcement” for links with the Coconut Cartel. Police allege four shots were fired into parked vehicles outside the house before the quartet drove back to Campbelltown. The Raptor Squad officer said the four Victorians left their Airbnb about 1.50am on September 1 and returned about 4am, “where they appear to be in a rush to collect their belongings before all leaving”. Loading Tuafuti, Mohamed and Abusud were remanded in custody after NSW Police expressed fears they could flee the country if granted bail.



Abdy said the interstate, interagency co-operation that secured the arrests should act as a deterrent to those who think they can get away with crimes in one state by fleeing to another. “Criminals can’t come interstate, commit offences, run away and hide back in their states and think they’re going to avoid detection and prosecution for their crimes,” he said. “People who are overseas tasking criminals in Australia to commit these types of offences can’t use our borders as a means of protection from prosecution and identification.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: New ‘world’s best airline’ crowned as Qantas fails to crack top 10
World.content:
Qatar Airways has lost the title of world’s best airline at the 2026 World Airline Awards, in a year when the highly regarded Middle East carrier has been disrupted by conflict in its region.

Qatar was pipped by Singapore Airlines for the Airline of the Year, which took out the No.1 spot after the Gulf carrier won the previous two years.

Singapore Airlines has been crowned the world’s best airline for 2026. Getty Images

Qatar Airways took second place – the position held by Singapore Airlines last year. It’s the sixth time Singapore Airlines has taken out the top award, a feat surpassed only by Qatar, which has won nine times.

Qantas, meanwhile, climbed two places from 14th to 12th this year, still far below its historical results where it consistently ranked in the top five, including as recently as 2022. However, the airline has continued to climb back from its nadir in 2024, where it fell to 24th amid a series of scandals including illegally sacking staff, selling fares for flights that had already been cancelled and criticisms over the availability of rewards seats for Frequent Flyer members.

World.title: Artist’s uniquely Queensland ode to her 101-year-old dad wins top portrait prize
World.content:
NationalQueenslandVisual art Artist’s uniquely Queensland ode to her 101-year-old dad wins top portrait prize Catherine Strohfeldt September 18, 2026 — 9:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a year Brisbane Portrait Prize organisers felt was dominated by a theme of belonging, a family-oriented self-portrait has taken top prize. Renowned Brisbane-based artist Pat Hoffie’s oil painting, titled Family Birthday (QLD), depicted her father’s 101st birthday at her parents’ Queensland home. Brisbane Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner and artist Pat Hoffie with her winning artwork. Brisbane Portrait Prize “The fact that they still live independently together has far more to do with how they work as a team than any mysterious gene pool … people at that age are fragile,” Hoffie said. In the piece, Hoffie sits with her father and mother, aged 101 and 98 respectively, in front of a celebratory spread of food.



Each member of the party dons a themed paper hat Hoffie made by hand. The chief judge of this year’s Prize, Queen Victoria Museum and Art Gallery director Jonathon McBurnie, said Hoffie’s piece showed “great tenderness”. “The colour is dialled up several notches to evoke a sense of verdance and humidity and

reflect Queensland’s bright natural light, ultimately giving great vibrancy to an intimate

moment of family celebration,” McBurnie said. Pat Hoffie won the Brisbane Portrait Prize with her self-portrait, Family Birthday (QLD). Brisbane Portrait Prize Brisbane Portrait Prize chair Anna Reynolds said many of the 2026 finalists were thematically linked.



“One of the main themes is home and belonging … there are a lot of really beautiful artworks that talk about family, home, friends, in quite a gentle, and tender way,” Reynolds said. “You see that with everything from people painting their grandchildren to Pat Hoffie painting her parents who are 101.” Reynolds said other themes included a “celebration of quiet achievers” and authenticity. Brisbane Portrait Prize chair Anna Reynolds said one of the key themes of the 2026 finalists was family and belonging, while another was a “celebration of quiet achievers”. Catherine Strohfeldt Among the finalists displayed in the State Library of Queensland exhibition, two members of the same family sit on the one wall – Conor Knight and his father William.



While long-time Brisbane local Knight chose to highlight his fathers’ role shaping his own art, he was also captured by fellow Brisbane artist Martina Clarke, his partner. Brisbane-based artist Martina Clarke’s piece, Soft Light. Brisbane Portrait Prize “Two years ago, we met here [at the Brisbane Portrait Prize],” Knight said. “We were having a look at, probably, my painting that was in the show, and then afterwards a big group of artists continued going out and celebrating.” Knight said he was flattered to have sat for Clarke’s entry, although the pair often used one another as their subjects.



“I think, most artists would say that having another artist be your suitor is usually quite a positive and good experience,” he said. In his own work, titled Ruddy Man, Knight said he had several motivating factors. “I was painting this portrait a lot for myself really – he’ll be 80 next year and I just wanted to have all the funny details of the room, like the power points,” he said. Conor Knight with his 2026 Brisbane Portrait Prize entry, Ruddy Man. Catherine Strohfeldt He said his father had applied to art school as a young man, and fed Knight’s interest in art from a young age.



This year’s finalists will remain on display at the State Library for the next seven weeks. From November 8, pieces that just missed the finalist cut will be displayed at the Powerhouse. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Some fairytales just don’t come true. After the events of past month in Melbourne, the second-on-the-ladder Swans couldn’t have seemed further away from another grand final berth. (6) Logan McDonald: McDonald was excellent again, after kicking six goals in the Swans’ qualifying final drubbing of the Lions. So who pushed the “Wharfie Time” button? You can take your pick, but it may well have been Patrick Voss, aka “the Prancing Pony”, who had hitherto been playing like a donkey. His only possession for the entire first half was a set shot after the half-time siren which did not even make the distance.





The Swans tried to hold on throughout the 10-minute arm wrestle that followed Voss’ goal, but they were cooked, and they knew it. Goals from Shai Bolton, Mason Cox and Isaiah Dudley finished them off, and the pain was etched all over the faces and bodies of Sydney’s players when the final siren eventually sounded and put them all out of their misery. “I’m just extremely proud of everyone uniting, galvanising and coming together to try and get our season to the last game, and we fell short,” Cox said. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 Purple pain: Swans left heartbroken in front of 45,000 at the SCG as Dockers storm home; Pearce says dreams won’t help Dockers win flag “It’s hard to say it’s a missed opportunity when you play a really good footy team. Prelims are big games and there’s a lot at stake because there’s a grand final next week. We missed the opportunity to take those moments to put ourselves in a grand final. The older players, they certainly understand that they don’t just come around every year. Some of the young ones, they just [think], ‘How good is it to be a part of it, and I’m learning everything, and I’ll grow from playing in them,’ but they’re hard to get to.” So the ride ends here. After a month defined by the scandal at the Pullman Hotel and the on- and off-field fallout, the Swans can be immensely proud of the way their remaining players have gallantly defended the club’s colours and culture, as well as disappointed that it couldn’t take them all the way. They will never know how far they could have gone if “the Pullman Five” had simply behaved themselves that night, and that hurts, too.



What happens next for those players remains to be seen, and in any case will be largely determined by Victoria Police. But during their absence, the Swans found something else: Proof that whatever this club is supposed to stand for is bigger than any individuals, and sturdy enough to survive the damage they caused. Now they can try and build again. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Significant persons of interest’: Victorians linked to gun used in killing of Sydney student
World.content:
Four Melburnians have been charged after being extradited to NSW over alleged links to the gun used in the fatal shooting of an innocent university student in Sydney’s south-west as part of the city’s gangland war. Police alleged in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Thursday that Vaifaalie Tuafuti, Omar Mohamed, Amenah Abusud and a child worked for the notorious Alameddine crime family in a recent spate of violence against the so-called Coconut Cartel. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Sydney home. The group were driven across the border on Friday, where they were handed over to NSW Police and arrested at Albury police station. They were all charged with special aggravated break and enter committing a serious and indictable offence, two counts of firing a gun at a home, and organising and partaking in criminal activity.



The adults were refused bail to appear in bail court on Saturday. The 16-year-old will appear at a children’s court on Saturday. A police summary read out in Abusud’s extradition hearing revealed investigators have linked the four to a gun found at the family home in the suburb of Glen Alpine, where Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed early on September 1. Loading NSW Police have said the wrong address was targeted in what is believed to have been a botched organised-crime killing. Two teenagers were charged with murder over the incident early on Thursday. The pair did not apply for bail and were remanded in custody to face court again on November 13. The four Victorians mentioned in court have not been charged over Tapia’s death but are accused of a home invasion in the Sydney suburb of Hurstville, and shooting cars in Turrella the night before.



Ballistic analysis found discharged cartridge cases at the two scenes matched and were then “positively matched” to the Glen Alpine homicide scene, where a firearm was found, a NSW Police investigator testified on Thursday. A 23-year-old man arrested at Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north are being extradited to NSW. NSW Police “Subsequent ballistic examination confirmed that the firearm was used to discharge rounds recovered from all three crime scenes,” he said. “Investigations relating to the homicide at Mount Sugarloaf Drive, Glen Alpine, remain ongoing.” NSW Police Raptor Squad commander Brad Abdy said the gun allegedly used at Hurstville and Turrella was found at the Glen Alpine crime scene but the investigation of Tapia’s death is “extremely complex”, and homicide detectives are still working to determine if the Melburnians can be charged with his murder.



A 26-year-old woman arrested at Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north are being extradited to NSW. NSW Police “It’s very important that all the evidence is examined before people are charged obviously with a very serious offence of murder,” Abdy said on Friday. “These people are obviously significant persons of interest.” Police say Tuafuti, Mohamed, Abusud and a child left Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north late on August 29 and drove to Campbelltown in Sydney’s south-west, arriving at an Airbnb property about 5am on August 30. A senior constable from NSW Police’s anti-gang Raptor Squad said the group were “contracted by a faction of the Alameddine organised-crime network … for the purposes of committing extremely violent crimes targeting several Sydney-based close associates of the Coconut Cartel”.



Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Trail of evidence’: Teens charged over mistaken identity murder of innocent student Court documents reveal Mohamed, Tuafuti, the 16-year-old child and an unknown fourth person are accused of breaking into a home in Hurstville about 2am on August 31. No one was at home. “Offenders utilised a sledgehammer to gain entry to the premises and discharged a round of ammunition into a wall inside,” a statement of alleged facts says. The court heard the break-in was filmed, and the occupant later received a WhatsApp message that said: “We were in your house to kill you if you were there, but God gave you life today. I promise you, we are going to make sure your kids grow up with no father.”



The four allegedly then drove to a home in Turrella that police said was “well-known to law enforcement” for links with the Coconut Cartel. Police allege four shots were fired into parked vehicles outside the house before the quartet drove back to Campbelltown. The Raptor Squad officer said the four Victorians left their Airbnb about 1.50am on September 1 and returned about 4am, “where they appear to be in a rush to collect their belongings before all leaving”. Loading Tuafuti, Mohamed and Abusud were remanded in custody after NSW Police expressed fears they could flee the country if granted bail.



Abdy said the interstate, interagency co-operation that secured the arrests should act as a deterrent to those who think they can get away with crimes in one state by fleeing to another. “Criminals can’t come interstate, commit offences, run away and hide back in their states and think they’re going to avoid detection and prosecution for their crimes,” he said. “People who are overseas tasking criminals in Australia to commit these types of offences can’t use our borders as a means of protection from prosecution and identification.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
