World.title: New ‘world’s best airline’ crowned as Qantas fails to crack top 10
World.content:
Qatar Airways has lost the title of world’s best airline at the 2026 World Airline Awards, in a year when the highly regarded Middle East carrier has been disrupted by conflict in its region.

Qatar was pipped by Singapore Airlines for the Airline of the Year, which took out the No.1 spot after the Gulf carrier won the previous two years.

Singapore Airlines has been crowned the world’s best airline for 2026. Getty Images

Qatar Airways took second place – the position held by Singapore Airlines last year. It’s the sixth time Singapore Airlines has taken out the top award, a feat surpassed only by Qatar, which has won nine times.

Qantas, meanwhile, climbed two places from 14th to 12th this year, still far below its historical results where it consistently ranked in the top five, including as recently as 2022. However, the airline has continued to climb back from its nadir in 2024, where it fell to 24th amid a series of scandals including illegally sacking staff, selling fares for flights that had already been cancelled and criticisms over the availability of rewards seats for Frequent Flyer members.

World.title: Artist’s uniquely Queensland ode to her 101-year-old dad wins top portrait prize
World.content:
NationalQueenslandVisual art Artist’s uniquely Queensland ode to her 101-year-old dad wins top portrait prize Catherine Strohfeldt September 18, 2026 — 9:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a year Brisbane Portrait Prize organisers felt was dominated by a theme of belonging, a family-oriented self-portrait has taken top prize. Renowned Brisbane-based artist Pat Hoffie’s oil painting, titled Family Birthday (QLD), depicted her father’s 101st birthday at her parents’ Queensland home. Brisbane Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner and artist Pat Hoffie with her winning artwork. Brisbane Portrait Prize “The fact that they still live independently together has far more to do with how they work as a team than any mysterious gene pool … people at that age are fragile,” Hoffie said. In the piece, Hoffie sits with her father and mother, aged 101 and 98 respectively, in front of a celebratory spread of food.



Each member of the party dons a themed paper hat Hoffie made by hand. The chief judge of this year’s Prize, Queen Victoria Museum and Art Gallery director Jonathon McBurnie, said Hoffie’s piece showed “great tenderness”. “The colour is dialled up several notches to evoke a sense of verdance and humidity and

reflect Queensland’s bright natural light, ultimately giving great vibrancy to an intimate

moment of family celebration,” McBurnie said. Pat Hoffie won the Brisbane Portrait Prize with her self-portrait, Family Birthday (QLD). Brisbane Portrait Prize Brisbane Portrait Prize chair Anna Reynolds said many of the 2026 finalists were thematically linked.



“One of the main themes is home and belonging … there are a lot of really beautiful artworks that talk about family, home, friends, in quite a gentle, and tender way,” Reynolds said. “You see that with everything from people painting their grandchildren to Pat Hoffie painting her parents who are 101.” Reynolds said other themes included a “celebration of quiet achievers” and authenticity. Brisbane Portrait Prize chair Anna Reynolds said one of the key themes of the 2026 finalists was family and belonging, while another was a “celebration of quiet achievers”. Catherine Strohfeldt Among the finalists displayed in the State Library of Queensland exhibition, two members of the same family sit on the one wall – Conor Knight and his father William.



While long-time Brisbane local Knight chose to highlight his fathers’ role shaping his own art, he was also captured by fellow Brisbane artist Martina Clarke, his partner. Brisbane-based artist Martina Clarke’s piece, Soft Light. Brisbane Portrait Prize “Two years ago, we met here [at the Brisbane Portrait Prize],” Knight said. “We were having a look at, probably, my painting that was in the show, and then afterwards a big group of artists continued going out and celebrating.” Knight said he was flattered to have sat for Clarke’s entry, although the pair often used one another as their subjects.



“I think, most artists would say that having another artist be your suitor is usually quite a positive and good experience,” he said. In his own work, titled Ruddy Man, Knight said he had several motivating factors. “I was painting this portrait a lot for myself really – he’ll be 80 next year and I just wanted to have all the funny details of the room, like the power points,” he said. Conor Knight with his 2026 Brisbane Portrait Prize entry, Ruddy Man. Catherine Strohfeldt He said his father had applied to art school as a young man, and fed Knight’s interest in art from a young age.



This year’s finalists will remain on display at the State Library for the next seven weeks. From November 8, pieces that just missed the finalist cut will be displayed at the Powerhouse. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Psychiatric patient was considered high risk of violence two weeks before murder, inquest hears
World.content:
A patient was considered a high risk of violence two weeks before he murdered a Christchurch woman after absconding from a psychiatric hospital, an inquest has heard.

Laisa Waka Tunidau was stabbed to death by Zakariye Mohamed Hussein outside her Sockburn home on 25 June 2022.

Hussein was jailed for life with a non-parole period of 13 years in November that year.

He had previously been jailed for more than six years for kidnapping, stabbing and intimidating people across Christchurch in March 2012.

At the time of Waka Tunidau's death, Hussein was allowed to leave Hillmorton on unescorted community leave, but failed to return when required.

More than 20 doctors, psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses who were part of Hussein's care were due to give evidence during the inquest.

A clinical psychologist who had six sessions with Hussein over May and June was asked about Hussein's level of assessed risk during the inquest's fifth day on Friday.

Counsel assisting the coroner Stephanie Grieve KC asked the witness - whose identity remains suppressed - about an adjustment of Hussein's profile at a multi-disciplinary team meeting on 13 June.

At the meeting, both Hussein's risk of violence and risk of unauthorised leave were recorded as high, although notes indicated that he was still deemed a low risk to the community.

"Now when would you have become aware of that?" Grieve asked.

The clinician said they would usually be told about a change at the next meeting, although they did not attend this.

"It should have been recorded in the MDT document for the day and the rationale as to why it was marked low, usually if we change we would record it.

"It would be recorded in the [document] to reflect the change, like why risk has gone from moderate to high or high to moderate, what's contributed to that change."

The risk was lowered back to medium seven days later, the court heard.

Details about Hussein's interactions with fellow patients and employees were also outlined during proceedings, including unwanted romantic advances towards staff.

In notes dated 10 June, the clinician had described Hussein as having "irritability and anger" under the surface of a relaxed demeanor.

Hussein was also described as irritable on the day he murdered Waka Tunidau.

The clinician said a patient who was presenting as irritable did not necessarily present a risk to the community.

"So you may see irritability, but you would start to become more concerned, for example, if they weren't following directions, or asserting negative attitudes and threats."

Another clinician, whose identity was also suppressed, was asked about the approach to Hussein's therapeutic risk given a string of incidents, including when he poured cordial on a fellow patient, along with recurring thoughts of violence.

The court heard that Hussein developed violent thoughts in response to a man coughing on a bus.

"Wasn't there [cases] where he was presumably unable to control himself because there are a number of these issues with peers and staff," Grieve said.

"Those things didn't give you pause to consider whether or not this therapeutic risk approach should continue?"

The clinician said the incidents were not serious enough to warrant further restrictions on his leave arrangements at Hillmorton.

Earlier this week the inquest heard Hussein had left the hospital on 35 occasions and returned without incident between being granted leave in late April 2022 and the day of Waka Tunidau's murder.

Her family has questioned how he was ever assessed as safe enough to leave the hospital on his own.

World.title: Major property developer doubts Auckland CBD height removal will prompt short-term building
World.content:
Removing Auckland CBD height limits won't work - Residential CEO Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

A major Auckland property developer says a government proposal to remove building height restrictions in the CBD is just politics and he doesn't believe there will be a single new apartment built in the short term because of the change.

Under current rules, parts of the Auckland CBD have building height limits of 72.5 metres - in other areas the limit is 35 metres.

The proposal would remove these caps for the majority of the central city and scrap other rules about how big and far apart buildings have to be.

RMA Minister Chris Bishop said that current CBD planning rules are holding back growth.

"The modelling suggests that these changes are potentially very significant. At full uptake, annual GDP is expected to increase by $1.87 billion.

"Tens of thousands of new homes in the city centre, tens of thousands of new jobs in the city centre."

Bishop commissioned a report on the planning rules, which was released today.

Its recommendations include removing height and dimension limits on high-rise buildings, and removing the heritage status of what the report refers to as "non-contributing sites" within the historic Karangahape Rd precinct.

The report estimated the changes will provide about 17,000 more dwellings in the city, and 20.3 million square metres more floor space.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the changes will help to capitalise on the newly opened $5.5 billion City Rail Link.

"I think now is the opportunity to ensure that Auckland is shaped by that investment, prioritising more growth in our city where our new CRL stations are just a stone's throw away."

Ockham residential co-founder Mark Todd www.ockham.co.nz

Developer Mark Todd, of Ockham Residential, said getting rid of height restrictions and pesky regulations downtown is all well and good, but it's not what's holding back vertical housing in the city.

"There is just this myth that if I just tweak the regulations, Auckland CBD will just suddenly start sprouting apartments," he said.

"It's not going to go vertical until there's some incentives. Enablement is good, but it's not enough. That's the key issue here.

"These are political announcements. Auckland's got enough vertically-zoned land for the rest of the century - easily."

The problem, Todd said, is the lack of people living there.

"Auckland has got less than half the residents than it should have in its CBD if you benchmark it with comparable international cities. This won't result in a single new apartment being built down there."

Todd said there won't be large-scale mixed-used developments around the CRL without local and national government support.

"You've just had 20 years proving the private sector isn't going to build you apartments in the CBD to leverage the billions of dollars we've invested.

"It's one of the most beautiful CBDs in the world - The Victoria St green belt has just been completed, amazing. CRL, amazing. Quay St, amazing, beautiful. Wynyard Quarter, Britomart, amazing.

"We've been waiting for 20 years for the people to come. It's not happening and why is that? Because policy settings are wrong."

Todd said he's never constructed a building in the CBD and is just speaking as an Aucklander.

The government's proposal is being welcomed by others in the sector.

Property Council chief executive Leonie Freeman. supplied

Property Council chief executive Leonie Freeman said it's a positive step for the city, and timely given the opening of the CRL.

"So this isn't something that's going to change the Auckland skyline in the next five years, but in the next 30 to 50 years we will see greater growth, and I think that's a positive thing."

Thom Gill, from Cohausing Projects Limited, doubts there will be anything like the building activity that the policy says will be enabled, but he welcomes the government proposal.

"I think the ability to maximise the good opportunities of a particular site without having to worry about the building height [and] all the more subjective things, in principle I think that is a good idea in a modern city."

However, Gill opposed allowing high rises around Karangahape Rd, which he said is already a coherent urban environment.

World.title: Woman describes father's death after nine hours in waiting room
World.content:
Kiwis who have experienced the disastrous effects of an overloaded healthcare system are challenging politicians to explain how they will right the ship.

Tayla Horsburgh, whose father Brent Horsburgh died at Waikato Hospital after nine hours in the waiting room, was among those gathered in Auckland's Three Kings for a community meeting on Thursday night to mark World Patient Safety Day.

"In addition to the hospital being over 100 percent capacity, they were also four doctors down and two nurses down during the afternoon shift," she recalled about the day her father died.

"Mum received a call from the hospital at one in the morning, saying he had collapsed and they were doing CPR and to get to the hospital as quickly as we could."

Tayla, alongside her sister Jordyn and mother Tracey, were told to wait in the family room.

"In the meantime, there was a nurse standing at the door and mum said to her 'can you just tell me if he's okay', and she said 'yep'," Tayla said.

"The doctor then came in moments later, and told us they could not resuscitate him and he had passed away. This was such a horrible experience and that nurse gave us a false sense of hope."

Fellow panelist Bernie Braithwaite had survived with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, for fifteen years.

"After the Christchurch earthquakes I went to donate blood and quickly moved to donating plasma," he said.

"About two months into that I got a note from the blood service saying they had seen an irregularity."

One of the drugs he needed to survive wasn't funded by Pharmac.

Tayla Horsburgh's father died at Waikato Hospital after waiting for hours in the ED. Supplied/ Waikato Hospital

"That drug, which is now funded by Pharmac, at the time it was not, it's a drug called lenalidomide. It cost me $22,000 for a three-month supply," he said.

"Every time I picked up a little capsule, it was $458, you don't want to drop it down the sink, I can tell you. Your hand shakes a bit when you stick it in your mouth, at $458."

He urged the politicians in the audience - representatives from each major party, except for Te Pāti Māori - to view medicine as an investment rather than a cost.

"As long as we continue with a cost approach rather than an investment approach, we'll never build a valid case for not just making step-change but making leap-change in how we fund not just medicines but the health system in general," he said.

"If you can fund and continue to keep people as vital and contributing members of society, they'll return a hell of a lot more than they'll cost you."

He later asked the politicians what they would do to address gaps in Pharmac's coverage, and whether they would commit to a long-term bipartisan approach.

From left to right: New Zealand First's Alfred Ngaro, Opportunity's Cody Marsh_and ACT's Antonia Modkova. FELIX WALTON / RNZ

"We're very proud of our policy to close the medicines gap with Australia," ACT's Auckland Central candidate Antonia Modkova said.

"The ACT Party is proposing to increase the portion of the health budget spent on medicines by one percent each year until 2033 to close the medicines gap."

Opportunity's Northcote candidate Cody Marsh, a former paramedic, said bipartisanship was central to the party's healthcare policy.

"We want cross-party agreement. It's the only way this is going to survive consecutive governments," he said.

Plunket nurses facing unprecedented workload in 'healthcare crisis' Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

"Policies like ACT's, we're willing to work with them on that, but I think we also need to understand where you're taking that funding from. Where is that money being taken from?"

National's Carlos Cheung, the MP for Mt Roskill, echoed the call for bipartisanship.

"We are from different parties, and we have different approaches to the healthcare system, but at the end of the day we all want a better health system for every single person here," he said.

Labour's Phil Twyford, the MP for Te Atatū, didn't commit to a specific policy.

From left to right: Green's Ricardo Menéndez March, National's Carlos Cheung and Labour's Phil Twyford. FELIX WALTON / RNZ

"We do need to spend more on medicines, and we'll have something to say closer to the election when the government has opened its financial books," he said

"Labour is a big supporter and always has been of Pharmac because of the potential for it to deliver, and the record of it delivering value for money."

Gareth Hall, who lost his 16-year-old daughter Maddy to suicide, asked the panel what they would do to keep mentally ill children safe.

Bernie Braithwaite (left) and Gareth Hall (right), holding a picture of his daughter Maddy. FELIX WALTON / RNZ

"We need a better community response to support parents, to support children, and people who actually know more than just empathy but how to wrap around the support that's needed," NZ First's Glendene candidate Alfred Ngaro said.

Green Mt Albert candidate Ricardo Menéndez March said his party would expand youth services throughout the country.

"These are critical services that help actually support young people, especially those who may have a complicated relationship with their parents," he said.

World.title: Potentially lethal drug used for animal euthanasia stolen from car in Auckland
World.content:
Police are searching for a potentially lethal medication that was stolen from a handbag inside a car in Auckland.

The medication - known as Pentobarbital - is often used to euthanise animals and could have a lethal effect if ingested by a human.

Police asked for the bagged item to be returned immediately given the risk.

The medication had been provided by a vet, Detective Senior Sergeant Mark Greaves said, and was inside a handbag which was stolen from a car parked on Athlone Rd, Glendowie overnight on Wednesday.

"The medication is in liquid form and was inside a pink handbag.

"It's likely the person has mistakenly taken the medication without knowing it was inside the bag, and we are asking for it to be handed in as soon as possible.

"Police are actively investigating this matter and treating it as a priority."

Greaves said the main concern was the person who took the item or potentially gave it to someone else did not know what they were in possession of.

"If you have information on where the bag, or the medication is, we need to hear from you to ensure it is safely retrieved."

World.title: Primary Health Organisation makes changes at Pahiatua Medical Centre
World.content:
Pahiatua medical staff calling for quick change as safety concerns mount Checkpoint Download MP3 10m

The Primary Health Organisation will install an independent manager at the Pahiatua Medical Centre, where staff are threatening to resign en masse next week, due to under-resourcing.

On Thursday, nurse practitioner Victoria Perry told RNZ Checkpoint that failure to replace departing staff had put preventative screenings for bowel, breast and prostate cancer a year behind schedule, while regular patients were waiting three months for appointments.

She feared people would die, if the clinic could not provide even its most basic of services and follow-up tests for its 5000 patients.

Staff have called for the PHO - which contacts the clinic for its services - to intervene and chief executive Tony Wai has told Checkpoint that intervention will begin with new management.

"The situation has clearly escalated, which we're treating very seriously," he said.

The Primary Health Organisation will install an independent manager at the Pahiatua Medical Centre, where staff are threatening to resign en masse next week, due to under-resourcing.

On Thursday, nurse practitioner Victoria Perry told RNZ Checkpoint that failure to replace departing staff had put preventative screenings for bowel, breast and prostate cancer a year behind schedule, while regular patients were waiting three months for appointments.

She feared people would die, if the clinic could not provide even its most basic of services and follow-up tests for its 5000 patients.

Staff have called for the PHO - which contacts the clinic for its services - to intervene and chief executive Tony Wai has told Checkpoint that intervention will begin with new management.

"The situation has clearly escalated, which we're treating very seriously," he said.

"Our immediate priority is ensuring the people of Pahiatua continue to have access to safe primary care, but equally, we need to understand and address the concerns that have brought the staff to this point.

"It's the providers' job to keep staff safe - it is our role to ensure they continue to maintain minimum services, and continuity of care for patients and the community.

"First and foremost, we need to address a number of those concerns that the staff have raised. We do plan to have an independent manager go in - we've instructed the current manager that we would be putting our own manager in there to rectify some of the issues that have been raised in staff complaints.

"These are qualified managers coming in alongside our team."

While this was the first step, Wai acknowledged staffing levels at the clinic also needed to be addressed, but could give no solid timeline around that.

"We will be getting more clinical staff - that is an important thing to do," he said. "Workforce is challenging and there are a range of different options that the existing management are looking to bring in clinical resources.

"We see that co-inciding with our plan, as we address some of the issues. We do know there are vacancies being sought at the moment and being actively recruited for, which the existing manager has let us know.

"We're expecting them to flow through when they flow through."

Wai said permanent staffing needed to be recruited for.

"That is happening, but I can't give you any exact definitive times until we work through that process."

Wai said other clinics around New Zealand faced similar challenges, but had adopted "virtual support or virtual therapy" to help fill the gaps.

"We see we need to get it to a minimum standard and, in this situation, because we've been brought in at the time we were brought in, we're having to act now to remediate this.

"Those operational pressures need to be looked after and that is why we're going in there immediately with immediate action up front.

World.title: Timaru woman finds rare moa bones during daily beach walk
World.content:
Family stumbles upon Moa bones on daily beach walk Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

A family is buzzing after a woman stumbled upon moa bones during her daily beach walk south of Timaru.

Pippa Yates found what she suspected to be the bones of the now-extinct New Zealand bird at St Andrews Beach, which the South Canterbury Museum confirmed after closer inspection.

Yates told Checkpoint the discovery was all the family could talk about.

Supplied

"Anytime we get a spare moment, we clean the bones that we've got. We've got probably a good half a bucket full of moa bones now, so they're seemingly coming up a lot better than we expected they would," she said.

"The museum said they'd crumble apart, so far we've got some really big pieces that have actually made it through being cleaned very carefully."

Yates said the family were just using plain water to clean the bones to try and emulate natural washing on the beach.

Supplied

She said she's had to sacrifice her daughter's plastic basin previously used for cleaning baby bottles.

"We put a bit of cold water over the bones, which are sort of still within clay in big chunks, and swish the water over them from side to side, let them sit for an hour or more, and then drain the water out and start again, being careful not to lose any of the tiny bits of bone as well, so it's a slow process," Yates said.

Yates said the family had been scaling the beach for about four years after hearing about a man finding a moa footprint and bones.

"I walk looking at my feet basically the entire time where we walk, specifically in all the clay banks, we always look in those areas thinking we might see a footprint, and that's something I can bring my daughter back to see," she said.

"We as a family have quite a collection of bones and oddities in our little bone cabinet at home, so we're quite familiar with the look of bone.

"The porosity of the bone, I could tell looking down on it that it looks sort of like a cross section of a bone as opposed to a piece of driftwood or something else stuck in the mud."

Four-year-old Lucy. Supplied

Yates' four-year-old daughter, Lucy, is part of an explorer club at the museum.

She said she's been going ever since she could walk.

"She's obsessed with the museum, and she knows where everything is and likes to show anybody that comes to visit us where everything is in the museum," Yates said.

"So yes, she's got a keen interest on all those kinds of things. Her dad has got her quite interested in it as well, if we find skeletal remains of any kind, dead bird, on the beach, we bag it up and bring it home for dad to make it into a display for our bone cabinet.

"We have quite a lot of seagulls and all sorts of things in the bone cabinet."

Yates said the family planned on keeping a few of the larger bones to possibly piece them together.

She hoped to put it on display in their home for visitors.

"But any of the really obviously bone-looking bones, we're going to try and give back the museum, which will be nice to have on display," she said.

"Molly's my daughter who was on my front while we were walking on the beach. So, when she has children one day, she can go and say, 'this is the bones that mum and I found when I was just a baby on her front' and her children and her great grandchildren and those kinds of things.

World.title: Waiheke Island's only respite care house for children with disabilities to be sold
World.content:
Waiheke's care house for kids with disabilities to be sold Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Waiheke Island's only respite care house for kids with disabilities will be sold on the open market, ending a crucial 30-year service.

It's been closed and vacant for a year, after Spectrum Care said the service at Melanna House was running at a loss and they made the difficult decision to pull out.

Kainga Ora owns the house and has confirmed it will sell the property because another provider could not be found to run the disability respite care service.

Different services have provided overnight and day-stay respite care there for over 30 years - including Spectrum Care for the past six years.

After it closed, Waiheke local Christobel Tomlinson gave up a full-time job to look after her daughter Gen, who needs constant care, over the school holidays.

The imminent sale of the house leaves them wondering what next?

"It really does signal an end to the government being involved in supporting services for the disabled community on Waiheke," she said.

"By selling the property they're really forcing our hand to come up with a community led solution."

Tomlinson is part of the Waiheke Special Needs Group and says there are local philanthropists keen to help, with talk of possibly buying Melanna House or another property for disability respite care.

"They see a community group in need and really want to help," she said.

"We really need the services to be available so we can spend that funding and get the respite that the families require."

Kāinga Ora intends selling the house after failing to find another provider to run the disability respite care service. Supplied

Kāinga Ora director of supported housing Lucy Ashby said they expect to put the house on the open market in the coming months.

"We know the support services previously provided from Melanna House were important to families on Waiheke Island," she said.

"We have worked extensively to find another eligible provider to operate from the property. Despite engaging with stakeholders, partner agencies, and potential providers, we have not been able to identify a suitable organisation to lease the property."

The property is in Kainga Ora's Community Group Housing portfolio, meaning it can only be leased to service providers who hold an eligible government funding contract.

"As a result, we have made the decision to sell the property on the open market. The sale process is expected to begin in the coming months," Ashby said.

Waiheke local board chair Kylee Matthews said the decision to sell the house was a blow for the community which had 15 state-owned homes - one block of 14 one-bedroom units and Melanna House.

"It's extremely disappointing. For one, KO has not invested on Waiheke for over 30 years so to lose a KO property is really devastating to our community because it means we've got less provision."

Matthews said people with disabled loved ones needed access to respite care on the island.

"With the closure of this property there's no backstop and it's really frightening and concerning."

The local board commissioned a review of what disability service the community needs.

"The findings were that there is no respite care on the island, that over half of these families have had to leave the island," Matthews said.

"What that does for them is takes away the sense of community and belonging."

Matthews said there were 36 families with disabled children when Spectrum took over the respite house six years ago but since then half have moved off the island to better access support.

Auckland Central MP Chlöe Swarbrick is helping to advocate for the community.

"It does feel rather off colour or not the appropriate thing to be doing here. We are going to continue seeing if there is any way to, at the moment, pause that sale."

She said it was a public asset that may not be replaced.

"We [could] lose this public asset which was always intended to be in public ownership for the benefit of respite care on the island which feels so deeply disappointing," Swarbrick said.

"When we sell off things like this we don't tend to get them back and it's the community who pays the price."

With the next school holidays one week away, and summer break looming, Tomlinson said families like hers were feeling stretched.

"The impact of having no services is large and it's demanding on an already stretched and time pressured family environment," she said.

"A lot of families will be in the same position as me. We're really looking for a solution to exist sooner rather than later.

World.title: 'A real degree of nastiness' and the need for respect: Andrew Bayly on politics
World.content:
Outgoing National Party MP Andrew Bayly (Port Waikato) knows better than most the highs and lows of public office. In his valedictory speech on Wednesday he described his resignation from cabinet as one of the most brutal experiences of his life.

Parliament exit interview: Andrew Bayly The House Download MP3 6m

After his farewell speech, he joined us to reflect on the good, the bad, and the ugly of being an MP, and how social media has changed the dynamic, bringing with it a "real degree of nastiness".

He recalled an incident from early in his parliamentary career, when The Post published a story about an accident involving his brother when Bayly was just 15 or 16. The incident was decades old, but the story was published under the headline "MP Shoots Brother".

Bayly said members of the public questioned why the incident was being revisited, and the newspaper eventually took the story down, but believes the media environment has gotten worse since.

"Today, I'd be beset not only by the media here in Parliament, but also on social media. I would just be brutalised."

He thinks increasing personal attacks and even threats are a deterrent to attracting talented people into politics.

"If we want good people [to leave] nice, secure jobs and an easier life and come into this demanding life in politics, it's increasingly becoming a much harder sell, because why would you do it?"

Asked what pastoral support was available to MPs, his response was fairly blunt: "Very little."

Bayly said politicians had to find their own ways of dealing with the pressure, and that in those moments, support from colleagues was particularly important.

He said the cohort of National MPs who also entered Parliament in 2014 used to meet regularly and decompress together, providing a relaxed environment to share their experiences and laugh things off. Only five of the initial ten remain and two more retire this election (Bayly and Shane Reti).

Particularly difficult periods, like his resignation from Cabinet, were managed by keeping busy. Alongside other passion projects, he began writing a book, which he hopes to publish soon.

He says it pays to have hobbies as an MP. For some, this could be knitting or playing the piano. Bayly's own hobbies aren't exactly restful - he's known to be keen on mountaineering, tramping and endurance racing.

It is fitting, then, that one passion project bridges his political and intrepid foci. In 2019 he dedicated significant time to establishing the Antarctic Parliamentarians Assembly in London.

"I look back and think, …that's a piece of history that I've created. Those are the type of things you've just got to get on and do."

I asked Bayly what he'll miss most about being an MP. He tells me it's being in the midst of the action.

"This is where it happens," he muses. "I came from a business background [where] you do a big deal, and it's reported in the paper, but it's nothing like Parliament."

Beyond the buzz, Bayly will also miss the people. He has developed friendships across the House, mostly through time spent together on select committees.

"You get to see who's really good, who's diligent, who reads the papers, who's got intellectual heft and is actually across the select committee. You get very close relationships with people."

Given the belligerence of events like Question Time, especially close to an election, the perception is that Parliament is intrinsically antagonistic, but Bayly says that's not accurate.

He believes however that MPs need to be more tolerant of different perspectives.

"Every MP here is here for the right reason. They want to do good. It's just that people have different perspectives, and actually sometimes we should just respect their perspective. Not everyone's wrong and not everyone's right. Sometimes we just need to say - what you've said there, there's a kernel of something that's really helpful and useful, and as a country, it would be better if we actually started talking about that."

For Bayly, the ability to work across differences is an important part of a functioning Parliament.

"Outside of the election period [which] is confrontational, having that [respectful] approach, makes a good parliament, it makes good democracy, and that's how we're going to move New Zealand forward."

World.title: LA Rams coach hopes his NFL team never plays in Australia again
World.content:
Los Angeles Rams coach Sean McVay hopes his NFL team never has to play in Australia again after a dismal loss to bitter rivals in Melbourne.

The coach had stuck to the script during his team's whirlwind tour Down Under, which culminated in a 27-7 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, insisting the team was "excited" and "looking forward" to last Friday's clash.

But a week on, McVay revealed his true stance on the NFL deciding to host a game about 12,700 kilometres away from his hometown, saying he wants to wipe the game from his memory and move forward with the season.

"We're not playing in Australia ever again, I hope," he said.

"Not because it wasn't a great atmosphere. That will get taken out of context."

McVay's comments come after San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan implied he also would not like to play in Australia again.

Rams coach not blaming late arrival for MCG loss LA Rams coach Sean McVay says his team's decision to arrive in Melbourne the day before the NFL's historic first match in Australia was not the reason his side was comprehensively beaten 27-7 by the San Francisco 49ers in front of 100,021 fans at the MCG.

But the country will host more games in the future as the NFL has struck a multi-year deal with Victoria to play two matches with an option for a third.

It remains unclear whether the Rams will feature in the next edition, although the Seattle Seahawks, Las Vegas Raiders and Philadelphia Eagles are likely to take the field, as they share marketing rights with the Los Angeles team in Australia.

McVay's side also made a last-ditch journey, touching down in Melbourne about 24 hours before the game, unlike the 49ers who had been there all week interacting with fans and taking in the local atmosphere.

By game time, Los Angeles did not live up to their Super Bowl contender status at all, looking sluggish as they only scored one touchdown.

San Francisco were also the more popular team in front of the 100,021 spectators at the MCG, as the Rams were met with a mixed chorus of cheers and boos when they ran out.

Sydneysider Jordan Mailata, who plays for Philadelphia and was part of the 2025 Super Bowl-winning team, had some advice for the next club that plays Down Under.

"I would have recommended going out early," the offensive lineman said earlier in the week.

"The flight is so long that I don't think 24 hours is enough to wash out that flight itself."

World.title: How the NRL's most underrated player explains the Knights
World.content:
In the modern rugby league landscape it's hard for any NRL player to be truly underrated.

Coverage of the game is more granular and intense than ever before and the rise of fantasy sports means every statistical contribution comes into focus, which makes it difficult for anyone to slide under the radar.

But Mat Croker, the man who explains how Newcastle have managed to find themselves in a sudden-death final against the Warriors on Sunday, has managed it after putting together a season of low-key excellence that makes him worthy of the title.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

The lock forward is the only Knight to have played every game this year and his ball-playing in the middle of the field is the straw that stirs the drink for their dynamic attack.

"I'm the link man to our halves and making sure our weapons out wide, guys like KP [Kalyn Ponga] and Braddy [Bradman Best] and Gags [Dane Gagai] get the ball if the cues are there in the defender," Croker said.

"If they're not, just go through the middle."

The 27-year-old makes his job sound simple, and maybe it is, but that's not the same as easy. If it was, someone else would be doing it.

Croker is a microcosm of Newcastle's turnaround from wooden spooners to the brink of the club's first preliminary final since 2013 because, like his team, he knows his strengths and has been empowered to play to them.

There are more explosive and dazzling players at the Knights but Croker's passing, communication and structure helps give them the opportunity to explode and dazzle. He is the rock on which you can build a church that worships attacking football.

Mat Croker has been a fixture at the back of the scrum for Newcastle. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

Newcastle lead the league in tries from their own half with 31. More than a quarter of those begin with Croker at first receiver, setting shape and creating time for the men outside him.

Like the other things Croker does well — chasing kicks, leading line speed in defence, slowing down the ruck — his impact in attack is a hard thing to quantify with numbers. But if you know what you're looking for, it becomes impossible to miss.

Sidelined halfback Dylan Brown believes it's invaluable and that Croker is part of the reason the Knights have been able to stay on their feet and make it to the second week of the finals despite a heavy injury toll.

Mat Croker has enjoyed the best season of his NRL career. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"He understands the game really well. His footy smarts, when to play it out the back and when to run — he knows he's not the biggest player on the field but he knows how to find a gap and he knows when the spine needs the ball," said Brown.

"We've had all these new players come in but we still have the core. We still have Mat Croker and Phoenix Crossland, they haven't changed all year, and the more the ball goes through their hands the easier it's going to be for the rest of the team.

"You need that. Every team needs those guys."

It's been a season of great improvement for Croker, who notched his 100th NRL game earlier this year.

Since his debut in 2021 he has been a solid contributor for the Knights and a good clubman who mainly came off the bench, starting just 13 of his 82 appearances prior to this year.

Mat Croker spent much of his early years coming off the bench. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

But after working closely with new coach Justin Holbrook and attack coach Steven Hales over the summer, Croker was given a chance to start in the club's trip to Las Vegas in Round 1.

He has since transformed from honest toiler to a genuine ball-playing lock, a coalfields remix of the sophisticated passing middle that every decent team needs.

"Ever since day one they've put a lot of responsibility on my shoulders and I'm really grateful they've done that because I think it's brought out the best football of my career," Croker said.

"Back in Vegas they backed a hunch and took a bit of a punt of me to start and I've had the luxury of starting every game since. That's a lot of faith and I try to repay it."

The greatest compliment you can pay a middle forward is to say "he's got a bit of footy in him" and Croker has proven he's got more than most.

Newcastle can progress to their first preliminary final since 2013 with a win on Sunday. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

The skills were always there, he just needed the chance to unlock them.

"Without being arrogant, I always felt like I had some skills with passing and I'm not a barnstorming forward, so I had to work around that and find other ways to improve," said Croker.

"The ability to pass and show and go was part of that — the cues, I've worked really hard with Halesy and Justo to see those.

"He's said the same thing to me for 28 games — if they're tight, move it, and if they're not go through it."

In sticking to that mantra, Croker has become to Newcastle what his opposite number on Sunday, reigning Dally M Lock of the Year Erin Clark, is to the Warriors or what Cameron Murray is to last week's vanquished foes, South Sydney.

Croker had a strong game in that one, leading the way for Newcastle's depleted pack by holding the middle together and making 42 tackles without a miss, and says he was inspired by the prospect of taking on Murray.

"I was coming up against a good 13 in Cameron Murray, who's one of the best players in the whole competition," Croker said.

How Knights finals rookie shut down Souths Newcastle was not short of heroes in its sudden-death finals win over South Sydney, but no player stood taller than 21-year-old backrower and play-off debutant Jermaine McEwen.

"I'm not saying I played over him but I knew I had a big challenge because we play similar roles and I tried to embrace that challenge without the two front-rowers I've beside me all year.

"I had to use my leadership a bit more and I'm proud of how I did it."

Repeating the dose against Clark and the Warriors in front of 50,000 fans at Eden Park is a tall order but few dare write the Knights off.

They're dangerous because they've had a whole season of learning how to play to their strengths, like they did against South Sydney and like Croker has all year to become the NRL's hidden gem.

If they pull off the upset, look for Croker at the heart of it and if he is he sure won't stay underrated for long.

World.title: Door not closed for Socceroos veteran despite another snub
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Mat Ryan's Socceroos days are not over, coach Tony Popovic insists, despite the decorated captain being left out of his first squad since the World Cup.

Ryan is the most eyebrow-raising omission from Popovic's squad, which includes seven uncapped players, for games against Brazil in Brisbane on September 25 and Townsville on September 28.

The 34-year-old lost his starting spot to young goalkeeper Patrick Beach at the World Cup, then was bizarrely substituted on for the round-of-32 penalty shootout against Egypt.

The Socceroos skipper, capped 105 times, said after that loss he was only told he might replace Beach as extra time kicked off, though Popovic has since insisted Ryan knew that was a possibility pre-match.

Tony Popovic's Socceroos are set to face Brazil in Brisbane and Townsville. (Stefan Koops/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Levante goalkeeper Ryan has been omitted despite a strong start to the La Liga season.

"We know what Maty Ryan is to Australian football," Popovic said.

"A player that has a distinguished career, continues to have one, over 100 caps.

"But we'd like to have a look at another keeper."

Pressed on how Ryan, who the Socceroos boss also dropped in his first games in charge in 2024, had taken the omission, Popovic said: "He's good.

"He's the ultimate professional that he is, and that's why he's had such a distinguished career.

"He's still available for us, and he's certainly not out of the picture moving forward."

Uncapped St Mirren goalkeeper Jacob Chapman replaces Ryan, joining Beach and Paul Izzo in the squad.

Untried left-back Kasey Bos, younger brother of injured star Jordan Bos, has been called up along with fellow untested defender Dylan Leonard, 19.

Former A-League sensations Marcus Younis (Brondby IF) and Eli Adams (Gamba Osaka) earn maiden call-ups alongside Kealey Adamson (QPR), Chapman and Yaya Dukuly (NK Celje) after impressive stints overseas.

"They've been rewarded for the hard work they've put in to get an opportunity overseas," Popovic said.

"They've had to go through the struggles when you go outside of your comfort zone.

"You go through the ups and downs; not playing, playing, injuries, and that helps you grow.

"And these players get mentally tougher; they know how to handle the difficult situations in games, and I believe they all deserve an opportunity."

Sixteen players from the 26-man World Cup squad return.

Star left-back Jordan Bos (knee) and central defender Cam Burgess (Achilles) are unavailable.

Court battle looms for Socceroos star Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle as the Socceroos star's lawyer confirms he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

Cristian Volpato (hamstring) is sidelined with injury.

The Sassuolo attacker was last week fined $722 for driving with cocaine in his system in July. Volpato has maintained his innocence and will challenge the charges in court.

Riley McGree and Patrick Yazbek return after missing the World Cup through injury while Alex Robertson has been recalled.

Cameron Devlin, Nishan Velupillay, Mathew Leckie, Ajdin Hrustic, Kai Trewin and Awer Mabil have been omitted.

Aziz Behich is the only A-League Men player in the squad.

The Socceroos could have played up to four games this window but have settled for two, which Popovic said allowed players to get back to their clubs.

"We feel that with the games in November, we'll be ready for the Asian Cup," he said.
