Tech.title: Khosla-backed Mazama Energy just raised $135M to drill deeper into superhot-rock geothermal
Tech.content:
Geothermal startup Mazama Energy raised $135 million in an oversubscribed Series B, the startup said Thursday.

The fresh funding will help the company develop horizontal wells in superhot rocks capable of generating 15 megawatts of electricity per well.

Mazama plans to start generating electricity sometime next year and said its first site in Oregon is capable of producing 10 gigawatts of electricity. That’s a sharp upward revision from the company’s estimate last year, when investor Vinod Khosla said the site had the potential to produce 5 gigawatts.

Enhanced geothermal startups are shaping up to be the dark horse in the battle to power AI data centers and other large loads on the grid. While tech companies and data center developers have been throwing their weight behind natural gas, geothermal startups have been quickly advancing their technology.

Unlike previous geothermal projects, enhanced geothermal startups are targeting deeper and hotter rock. Mazama, for example, has drilled past 10,000 feet in 15 days on its way to about 15,000 feet deep. At those depths, the company can access 750˚ F (400˚ C) heat, which at high pressures turns water into a “supercritical” fluid that’s neither fully liquid nor fully gas — a state that lets it absorb far more energy than ordinary steam. Mazama said that will allow each well to produce up to 10 times more power than traditional geothermal technologies.

Given the depths Mazama is targeting, the potential payoff is significant. Tapping just 1% of superhot rock worldwide could generate more than 63 terawatts of electricity, according to the University of Twente and the Clean Air Task Force.

While work at its Oregon site is still in the early stages, the startup has already secured land for a second development. Mazama aims to complete development of the first site by 2030, at which point it says it should generate 200 megawatts of electricity.

The new round was led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital, with participation from ConocoPhillips and Shell Ventures. Existing investors including Khosla Ventures and Gates Frontier returned, and new investors SiteGround Capital, H. Barton Asset Management, and the Jeffrey and Marieke Rothschild Foundation also joined the round.

Mazama was incubated at Khosla Ventures.

Tech.title: Crusoe raises $3.9B to build massive data centers and small modular ‘AI factories’
Tech.content:
Data center developer Crusoe said Thursday it raised $3.9 billion in a Series F round that pushes its valuation to $30.9 billion. The massive round was co-led by Atreides Management, Mubadala Capital, and Valor Equity Partners. Founders Fund, GIC, Nvidia, Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), Radical Ventures, and TPG also participated, according to Crusoe.

Crusoe also announced three new board members, including Cloudflare CFO Thomas Seifert; Bill Stein, partner and CIO at Primary Digital Infrastructure; and Redwood Materials founder and CEO JB Straubel, who also sits on Tesla’s board. Straubel already has ties to Crusoe; he personally invested in the company in 2021, and Crusoe later became the first customer of Redwood’s energy storage business.

The eight-year-old company’s fresh capital infusion will help finance existing data center projects, including a large site in Abilene, Texas, used by OpenAI, as well as smaller, modular AI factories that can be transported by truck and connected to large power sources almost anywhere.

By manufacturing these modular data centers, called Spark, at its own facilities, Crusoe can deploy compute capacity quickly and without the need for large construction workforces. The smaller centers could also help Crusoe sidestep, at least in part, another major obstacle facing data center developers: backlash from local communities protesting massive complexes near their neighborhoods.

Crusoe co-founder and CEO Chase Lochmiller, who is pictured above, said in a statement he believes AI will usher in an era of abundance, but to get there will mean “controlling the infrastructure from electrons to tokens, and we’re grateful to have investors who share that conviction.”

The company makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.

This three-pronged business model has helped make Crusoe one of the most valuable AI infrastructure companies. Crusoe recently signed a massive $13 billion, five-year cloud contract to supply quantitative trading firm Jane Street with GPUs and AI infrastructure, Bloomberg reported.

The company recently met with investment bankers, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, to discuss a potential IPO in the near future, Axios reported last month.

The fresh fundraise comes 10 months after Crusoe raised $1.38 billion at a $10 billion valuation last October.

The company was founded in 2018 as a crypto mining operation powered by flared natural gas, but pivoted to AI infrastructure as demand for computing power skyrocketed. Crusoe’s customers include Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle.

Tech.title: Google DeepMind launches institute to widen the AGI debate
Tech.content:
Google and Google DeepMind researchers launched the DeepMind Institute on Wednesday to advance the conversation around artificial general intelligence (AGI). The institute lists DeepMind co-founder Shane Legg, Google executive James Manyika, and Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis as directors, with Legg serving as managing editor.

The new institute aims to surface differing views between Google, Google DeepMind, and the broader global research community around AGI. “They will not always agree, and they will likely change their minds, as more data and information comes to light at the fast-moving frontier,” the announcement read.

The inaugural collection of four essays covers a range of topics: economic policies for managing potential AGI disruption, preserving human-readable model reasoning, principles for human flourishing, and a framework for evaluating frontier AI models.

One essay, by DeepMind safety researchers Rohin Shah and Anca Dragan, argues that AI’s shrinking window of transparency — the ability to see and check a model’s step-by-step reasoning — is not inevitable. As new architectures make the most powerful models harder to monitor, the authors say developers and regulators should confront the safety trade-offs directly. That could mean limiting “opaque serial depth”— the amount of sequential computation a model can perform without producing a readable reasoning trace — or requiring developers to demonstrate that less transparent systems remain just as monitorable.

In another essay, Hassabis proposes a U.S.-led frontier AI standards body to evaluate the most advanced AI models. Under his framework, developers would initially submit models voluntarily for review up to 30 days before release. Once the evaluation system has proved effective, passing its tests could become a requirement for deploying frontier models in the United States.

The body would at first design assessments in consultation with AI companies but would eventually develop independent, undisclosed evaluations — what the essay calls “held-out” tests — to prevent labs from tailoring their models to known evaluations. Hassabis said the framework could be “ratcheted up if the seriousness of the situation demands,” potentially including a coordinated slowdown among frontier AI developers.

The essays arrive as the industry’s safety debate shifts from broad statements of concern toward concrete proposals for disclosure, outside scrutiny, and, if safeguards fall behind, coordinated slowdowns. That shift accelerated this week as industry leaders endorsed elements of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “pace” frontier AI development.

Tech.title: Amazon-owned Zoox’s 100-robotaxi limit in Nevada is about to disappear
Tech.content:
A regulatory cap limiting Zoox to 100 robotaxis in Nevada is set to expire this month, clearing the way for the Amazon-owned company to expand its commercial fleet of custom-built robotaxis in Las Vegas just as competition heats up.

The Nevada Transportation Authority (NTA) permit that imposed the 100-vehicle cap is set to expire September 25, TechCrunch has learned. An NTA official and a Zoox spokesperson confirmed the change, which is also outlined in an updated permit.

This doesn’t mean Las Vegas is about to be inundated with hundreds of Zoox robotaxis. But it does give Zoox more freedom to grow — and at a critical moment. Waymo recently launched a commercial service in Las Vegas, while Tesla and Uber have secured their own driverless ride-hailing permits.

Today, Zoox has about 100 custom-built robotaxis — cube-like vehicles that lack steering wheels and pedals — spread across four U.S. cities, including Austin and Miami. The bulk of the fleet is in Las Vegas and San Francisco. And for now, Las Vegas remains the only city where Zoox is charging for rides. Zoox must still obtain another permit from California regulators before it can charge for passengers there.

Zoox began charging for robotaxi rides in Las Vegas last month after receiving a temporary exemption from certain federal motor vehicle safety standards from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

That exemption was crucial for Zoox because unlike Waymo, its robotaxis were designed without a steering wheel, pedals, or other traditional and federally mandated controls. The commercial exemption allows Zoox to deploy up to 2,500 vehicles per year for the next two years.

It’s unclear how quickly Zoox will take advantage of its newfound freedom in Nevada. A Zoox spokesperson declined to say how many robotaxis the company plans to add to its Las Vegas fleet or even how many are in operation there today. Robotaxi Tracker, which collects data on autonomous vehicles, estimates Zoox has more than 30 vehicles operating in the city.

The spokesperson told TechCrunch that Zoox plans to steadily increase the size of its robotaxi fleet over the next several months “to meet the high demand in Las Vegas and other markets.”

Zoox will have lots of company, no matter how fast it expands. In August, the NTA approved three permits that will allow Tesla, Uber, and Waymo to operate commercial robotaxi services in Clark County, home to Las Vegas. Together, the permits could bring up to 7,000 robotaxis to the area over the next 12 months.

Waymo has wasted little time acting on that permit. The company opened its robotaxi service to customers in Las Vegas earlier this month. Waymo told TechCrunch at the time that it would start with “dozens” of its new Ojai minivan robotaxis in a 23-square-mile area that includes the Strip south of Highway 589 and into Boulder Junction.

Tech.title: PrismML hopes its tiny LLM will change how we all use AI
Tech.content:
If AI lab PrismML isn’t on your radar yet, it should be — not because it’s raised gobs of money (it hasn’t yet, just a $22.25 million seed round), but because of the technical minds involved and the potentially industry-changing tech it’s developing.

PrismML is betting that capable, high-performing, reasoning large language models don’t, in fact, have to be large.

It is making reasoning models so small they can fit on PCs and smartphones. (It’s even rumored to be in talks with Apple, though CEO Babak Hassibi declined to comment on that to TechCrunch.)

On Thursday, PrismML released Bonsai 2 27B, its latest in a family of models, which compresses Qwen3.8 27B, a widely used open source model from Alibaba, down to 5.9 GB. That’s small enough to fit on a PC and, possibly, a high-end smartphone. It’s a 9x to 10x reduction in memory versus the original.

PrismML was founded by a group of Caltech researchers and is led by Hassibi, a Caltech professor and an expert in compression technologies. The startup also counts Ion Stoica as an adviser. Stoica is a co-founder of Databricks (and other companies) and the director of Berkeley’s famed Sky Computing Lab, which has birthed many technologies and startups, from Letta to SGLang.

PrismML is also backed by investors Khosla Ventures, Cerberus Capital, and Caltech.

This startup is certainly not the only company working on LLM compression tech. Multiverse Computing, founded by a well-known professor from Spain’s Donostia International Physics Center, is another. (And Multiverse Computing has raised gobs of cash.)

But Hassibi says that PrismML’s compression tech is unique because its LLMs have lost virtually no performance compared with the originals. Bonsai 2 matches 98% of Qwen’s aggregate benchmark scores. That’s up from the first Bonsai, released a couple of months ago in March, that matched 95%. That original model has already been downloaded over 11 million times, and PrismML’s even smaller models have been downloaded another 2.6 million times, the company says.

So this shows that PrismML’s compression results have improved from one release to the next. Whether it could ever get to 100% benchmark performance parity is a question that remains to be seen. Compression will likely always have some impact, Hassibi says.

Still, perfect benchmark parity is fairly academic anyway. LLMs are not so accurate in their uncompressed form, and benchmarks not so perfectly reflective of actual tasks, that a 2% degradation would likely meaningfully affect how a model performs in actual use. (Plus, the surrounding software — the harness a model runs inside of — matters a lot when it comes to accuracy, too.)

PrismML says it achieves this by shrinking the “weights” that make up a model — weights are, essentially, the information a model learns and stores during training. Normally, each weight requires 16 bits. PrismML’s approach, called “ternary” weights, simplifies that down to three: +1, −1, or 0. With far smaller values to store for each weight, the model takes up dramatically less space. (For a deeper dive on the compression technique, here’s the project’s Hugging Face page.)

The startup’s next goal is to apply this compression technique to even bigger models. “The next models that we will release, hopefully in the next couple of months, will be in the several-hundred-billion-parameter range, and I expect it will be easier to retain the intelligence there,” Hassibi told TechCrunch.

As model size grows, he added, “There is more room to be able to compress them without losing the intelligence. So I would just say, as a general trend, for larger models, it’s easier to get to 100%.”

Stoica tells us that he’s excited for this tech because it’s making it possible for advanced models to run on users’ devices. “You are going to have intelligence at your fingertips, and it’s going to be free because it’s going to run on the device you already bought. It’s also going to be private, because you’re not going to send it to the cloud.”

Tech.title: The FAA’s plan to fix air traffic? $875M worth of AI
Tech.content:
In Brief

The Federal Aviation Administration has been struggling to manage an air traffic control shortage throughout the country. The reasons for the shortage are diverse, but the government has made it known that it’s on the lookout for innovative solutions to the problem.

One of those solutions appears to be an $875 million AI software program that is expected to help air traffic controllers manage their workflows and more safely navigate flight routes.

The Wall Street Journal reports that the FAA will soon launch SMART, which stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories — an automated software program designed to help streamline air traffic operations.

A one-page readout on the program describes SMART as “a cloud-based platform system that enhances existing FAA air traffic management systems.” It adds that the program uses AI to assess “airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.”

SMART, the product of a firm called Air Space Intelligence, will cost the government that amount over a 12-year period, the outlet writes. The software will roll out in the Washington, D.C., metropolitan area first before expanding to other regions, it says.

Earlier this year, the FAA also announced a “bold, new” hiring plan that the agency said would “erase the longstanding staffing shortage,” and the government is separately engaged in a broad effort to modernize the nation’s aging air traffic systems.

Tech.title: Adopt This Data Center Plushie and Hear Its Piercing Scream
Tech.content:
Uh oh, we got a cute alert! It’s Bezzy, your adorable, cuddly, anthropomorphized server-rack and stuffed-animal friend! Give this soft lil’ doll a squeeze, and it shall sing you its telltale song: the piercing, grinding ambient squeals emitted from a real US data center.

The Bezzy doll is a stuffed plushie made in a satirical collaboration between the New York–based creative studio Basura and Big Data, the musical project of producer Alan Wilkis, best known for the song “Dangerous,” a 2013 collaboration with the band Joywave. The joint project, which is coming out the same day as a new Big Data single, is called Adopt a Data Center. The goal is to present people with a “cuddly introduction to life with a real data center.”

Data Centers are very un-vogue right now. Built out by all the big AI companies to power their increasingly power-hungry AI tools, data centers have spread across thousands of acres of land in the US. They have been heavily criticized for their energy consumption and expansion of gas power. They have also proven to be audibly annoying, stirring up complaints about noise pollution from those nearby.

The Adopt a Data Center stunt aims to make people think differently about how services produced by data centers fit into their lives. That manifests as a plush stuffie that looks like a server rack in a data center, albeit with long arms and legs and googly eyes. It’s cute in the way Don’t Hug Me I’m Scared is cute. Squeeze Bezzy’s torso and the sound bursts out. It’s a screeching few seconds of a recording taken by a neighbor of a data center in Virginia. The tag on the Bezzy plushie reads, “Hug me for ear-piercing forever hum.”

Tech.title: Meta’s Copyright System Is Being Weaponized Against Albanian Protesters
Tech.content:
European lawmakers are calling for an investigation into Meta after the mass suspension of accounts posting about anti-government protests in Albania, in what observers believe is a coordinated brigading attack.

“What happened in Albania is tantamount to censorship,” said MEP Alexandra Geese in a statement. She is one of more than 30 Members of the European Parliament who signed a letter asking the European Commission to investigate whether Meta's actions complied with the EU's Digital Services Act.

“Mark Zuckerberg’s understanding of ‘freedom of speech’ only seems to cover opinions that align with the political agenda of the Trump administration. This is precisely why we have European rules,” she added.

The “Flamingo Revolution” protests, initially sparked by the development of a luxury resort linked to Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, have been taking place daily in the Albanian capital for over three months, demanding changes in the law that allows development on protected land as well as the resignation of the country’s prime minister. The Meta account suspensions almost all appear to be the result of copyright complaints and appear to have begun in late August.

An NGO group investigating the Meta suspensions alleges to WIRED it has evidence that “strongly indicates coordinated activity” led to the complaints.

“What quickly distinguished this from ordinary content moderation was the concentration of cases around the same political and civic movement,” said Martha Dimitratou, founder of Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organization that tracks digital censorship. In at least one case, the complaint was traced to someone who claimed they had been paid to make the complaint.

Tech.title: Best Gifts for Mom (2026): E-Readers, Digital Wall Calendar, Smart Bird Feeders
Tech.content:
If you're not looking to upgrade her console just yet but need a Switch-friendly cozy game for her, Stardew Valley has another big update in the works and only costs $15. I'm also hoping we see Fields of Mistria ($14) come to the Switch eventually, but the full launch came out in August for Steam users and has major quality-of-life improvements if she has played Stardew one time too many. My husband also upgraded his gaming setup this summer with a Steam Machine (from $1,049), and I have big plans to start using it often for Fields of Mistria. If your mom loves games, she'll love any one of these new devices or new games if she already got herself the new gadget like I did.

Photo Spotlight

As a mom, I take a lot of photos of my family. A lot. And sometimes it feels like all those great photos of my son's milestones go to my camera roll and photo storage to die. There are two solutions I love for this that are incredibly giftable: a digital photo frame she can instantly upload images to, and a printed photo book where you can take the best of the best and put them at her fingertips. I have and love both for different reasons. I love the digital photo frame to add all the photos from a fun weekend at the San Diego Zoo or Los Angeles Renaissance Pleasure Faire for me to relive again and again, but I also love being able to pull a photo book from the bookshelf and relive a specific moment I know is waiting there for me. Aura makes my favorite digital photo frames (followed by Skylight and the Calendar 2 if you want a multipurpose device, but Aura has no subscription fee if you only want photos), while Mixbook has been a favorite of mine for a while when it comes to printing photos, and has great starting prices for its photo books.

A Bird’s-Eye View

If you know a mom who loves to bird-watch (I know one!), you can upgrade her bird feeder to a smart one. Smart bird feeders add a camera to the feeder so she can see a close-up feed of the birds that come to hang out in her yard, and they're adorable to boot, for a little smart curb appeal. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck recommends the original Birdfy Lite as a great gift; it's her favorite smart bird feeder and comes in adorable colors to brighten your mom's yard and catch the eye of neighborhood birds. But the one she and I both have our eye on (her for her mother, me for myself) is the Birdfy Nest Duo, which is actually a birdhouse with two cameras so you can see the birds entering the nest outside and raising a family inside.

An Adorable Pan

I didn’t know I needed a tiny cast iron pan until it arrived. Field Co’s hand-finished, preseasoned cast iron pans are already known for being both lightweight and handsome. But with a mere 5-inch cook surface, this one might even cross the line from handsome into “cute.” But that’s what makes it a good gift: Your mother almost certainly does not have a cast-iron pan this small, and yet it also has real utility. At just 2 pounds, this pan is easy to pull out and stash, easy to maneuver or flip a pancake, easy to serve from, and the perfect size to fit the perimeter of a two-egg omelet. In addition to an egg pan, it’s a great, low-effort, single-serving pan in general—whether for grilled cheese, a little bit of bacon or sausage, or a couple of chicken thighs. The egg pan can be bought all by itself. But for $60 more, the gift set is nice. It comes with a cleaning kit (with maybe my favorite chain mail scrubber in existence), some seasoning oil, and a leather handle cover in cognac, black, brown, or cherry. —Matthew Korfhage

Compression Care

There's a wellness gadget for everything now. Rings that track your sleep and blood oxygen levels, masks to make you look younger, massagers to relax your muscles, and now boots to improve circulation. WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane says her mom loves these compression boots from Therabody to improve circulation, which is a common problem for many of our aging parents. These boots combine compression, vibration, and LED therapy into a single wearable device that comes with eight preset routines to focus on legs, knees, and joints. It's a unique option if she wants better recovery for her legs or better circulation for her health.

Better Espresso

The DeLonghi Rivelia is the best and easiest and most user-friendly superautomatic espresso machine I have tested. What’s superautomatic mean? It means you pour whole beans into the hopper, put milk in the milk carafe, and select the drink you want to make on the touchscreen menu. Then you let the machine do most of the rest. The style of espresso made by a superautomatic machine like this Rivelia is generally a bit smoother and less intense than the sort you get in a café. But the process is also less finicky; you won’t be dealing with coffee grounds and portafilters. What’s especially nice with this Rivelia is the ability to make multiple “profiles” for different coffee drinkers in the house, each with their own favorite drinks—and the ability to swap out bean hoppers to make decaf coffee in the afternoon. The Rivelia is also the machine my own mother, a drinker of lattes and dark-roast beans, loves unreservedly. Like others on the WIRED Reviews team, I often ask colleagues and those close to me to test my top-rated machines over long periods to see how they hold up over months or years of regular use. My mother thanks me nearly every month for letting her test the Rivelia. —Matthew Korfhage

For Ultimate Everything Showers

Photograph: Matthew Korfhage Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Weddell Duo Shower Filter $90 Amazon $90 Weddell

For most moms, showers are sacred—especially for moms of babies or younger kids. However, heavy metals, sediments, chlorine, and PFAS can cause health problems not just in drinking water, but in water that touches the skin, as well. They can also cause buildup on hair and shower surfaces, making them harder to clean. Many municipalities—including mine—treat water with chlorine, and when I asked him which filter he'd recommend for my own shower, WIRED water filter reviewer Matthew Korfhage suggested the Weddell Duo. It's the only US filter he's found that has certification for chlorine and lead removal from NSF International, and it also cites third-party testing by IAPMO R&T showing it can remove PFAS, though there's no corresponding certification. Still, the Duo has a 2.5-gallon-per-minute flow rate and can remove most chlorine from over 8,000 gallons' worth of showers. It's an in-line filter, so it's easy to install in minutes—just screw it in between your pipe and showerhead. It even comes with a little roll of waterproof tape to ensure a leak-free fit, and because of the horizontal orientation, installation won't affect the showerhead height. The filter needs to be replaced every three months, but refills only run about $25, compared with competitors like Filterbaby or Rorra, which can cost $40 to $45. —Kat Merck

Tech.title: He Won the Nobel Prize for Protein Design. Now He Uses AI to Create Molecules Not Found in Nature
Tech.content:
The natural world as we know it represents only a fraction of what might exist. Based on this idea, AI BioDesign was born: a scientific project that combines artificial intelligence and large-scale laboratory experiments to design and test new molecules and biological functions that are not found in nature but are physically and chemically possible.

In doing so, the researchers are aiming to create databases, models, and tools that could serve as “seeds” for developing the medicines and technologies of the future. The authors envision, for example, new drugs to treat cancer and neurodegenerative diseases or enzymes capable of breaking down plastics in the ocean.

Proteins that do not exist in nature but are technically possible can be designed and constructed using AI. ILLUSTRATION: Ian C. Haydon / UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design

The initiative is led by the Allen Institute, a biomedical research nonprofit in Seattle, along with the University of Washington and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center. Among the scientists leading the charge is David Baker, who shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work in computational protein design.

For much of the history of biology, scientists have studied the solutions forged by billions of years of evolution. Exploring possibilities that nature never produced is a fundamentally new approach. And as technology makes this now possible, one that a leaders of the field even compares the potential of these methods to historic transformations such as industrialization, electrification, and the digital revolution.

However, delving into completely novel regions of biology also inevitably leads to difficult questions. WIRED en Español spoke with David Baker, chief scientific officer at AI BioDesign, to address this and other topics.

Tech.title: The Leftist Split Over AI Doom
Tech.content:
On September 10, two days after researcher Jacob Coxon, who had recently quit his job at Anthropic, sounded the alarm about the industry potentially bringing about the end of humanity, the New York City Democratic Socialists of America posted a carousel of images on Instagram. The first slide was a drawing of an ouroboros—a dragon eating its own tail—set against a hot pink background. “AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story: both keep your attention on a science-fiction future to distract you from the real harms experienced in the present,” the image reads.

The post was authored by the NYC DSA’s Tech Action Working Group, which focuses on tech regulation issues for the chapter, the largest in the country. It garnered more than 25,000 likes on Instagram. But not everyone agreed with the post: “Horrible and dangerous take,” one comment reads. “Sometimes sounding the alarm is justified.”

As politicians scramble to understand AI safety, an ideological split is opening on the American left. Among the questions it’s centered on is whether to believe tech companies’ claims that their products are so powerful that they could end the world.

Some on the left question the value in elevating theoretical concerns about AI over actual harms. They believe repeating claims promoted by the frontier labs about the dangers of AI empowers the AI companies, turning attention away from regulating the current harms of the technology and toward an impossible future.

“AI has become the latest tool of capitalist exploitation. The damage that unregulated and misused AI is already causing is clear across the country,” Alan Dang, a member of Tech Action, tells WIRED. “As socialists, we don’t trust these corporations to craft their own regulations.”

But others are following the direction of Senator Bernie Sanders, the unofficial leader of the American left, who has enthusiastically taken up the AI safety issue, asserting that AI has the potential to eliminate humanity. They say that it’s possible to address all harms from AI—both those happening now and those that could happen in the future—at once.

Tech.title: It Still Feels Like Summer in Parts of the US. Blame El Niño
Tech.content:
A summer that started early across the US has no intention of quitting, even as the calendar turns to autumn.

The culprits? El Niño and climate change, which contributed to this summer’s record-breaking warmth and are delaying pumpkin spice season.

Forecasters with the US Climate Prediction Center continue to see increased odds for hotter-than-normal temperatures across much of the country through at least the end of September.

Computer models show a pronounced ridge pattern, an atmospheric arrangement that can lock in sustained spells of warmer-than-normal conditions. This setup will feature widespread unseasonable warmth throughout the country, a pattern consistent with a strong El Niño. The greatest odds of above-normal temperatures exist around the Upper Midwest and the Deep South. Some models suggest temperatures could run 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above normal for the latter half of September.

The blast of unseasonably warm air comes after the hottest summer in US history in a year in which tens of thousands of heat records have fallen across the US. That includes nearly 44,000 record daytime highs and more than 53,000 record-high overnight minimum temperatures recorded at weather stations across the country. Thousands more monthly and all-time heat records have fallen since the start of 2026. Over the same period of time, only about 21,500 low-temperature records fell, or around one cold record for every four heat records.

Many of the busted records date back more than a century. Salt Lake City hit 109 degrees Fahrenheit on July 12, for example, marking its hottest-ever temperature since records began in 1874. Washington, DC, tied its all-time warmest overnight low of 84 degrees Fahrenheit on July 3, where daily observations date back to 1871.

Tech.title: Projector Screen: Do You Need One for Your Home Theater?
Tech.content:
GettyImages/mgstudyo

Do you need a screen for a projector? Short answer: Technically, no. Longer answer: It depends, but probably yes. Even longer answer: A screen will dramatically improve the image quality, and often the brightness, of any projector. Even a cheap screen can improve the performance of the best projectors. More expensive screens can reduce ambient light, greatly improving image quality if there’s any light in the room. Also, while your painted wall may seem smooth, there’s still a texture, and every tiny imperfection will be visible as part of your movie, TV show or game.

Look at it this way, movie theaters have screens for a reason. Spending even a little money on a screen will improve how the projector you spent a lot of money on looks in any room. It is an added cost, though, plus the added complexity of setup and mounting. So if you’re not sure, here are all the reasons why you should get a screen, especially if you have an ultra-short-throw projector, plus a few situations where you don’t need one.

To screen or not to screen

There are three main reasons to get a screen:

Brighter image: Even simple screens are better than walls of any color.

Even simple screens are better than walls of any color. Smoother image: Walls have texture that will be visible in the projected image.

Walls have texture that will be visible in the projected image. Potentially better contrast and overall image quality: Some screens can “focus” more light toward your eyes, making the image seem brighter. Others can reject ambient light, so the image is better with any lights on.

Now, in fairness, if you have a tiny, budget projector that puts out only a handful of lumens, you won’t gain much by adding a screen. There’s very little performance to begin with, so there’s not much to improve. Full-size budget projectors and anything more expensive can definitely benefit. Many screens can “add” brightness by focusing more of the light back to where you’re sitting, instead of scattering it all over the room.

That scattering is especially problematic if you have an ultra-short-throw projector. Enough so that I’ve got a whole section below about them specifically.

You don’t need a dedicated home theater to get more from your projector — just the space for a screen. GettyImages/vostok

Regardless of the type of projector, any ambient light in the room will bounce off your wall (or screen) and negatively impact the image. It will wash it out, making it harder to see. There are ambient light-rejecting and ceiling light-rejecting screens that can help considerably if you want to use a projector but also don’t want to live in a cave. More on these below, but keep in mind no screen can magically make your projector look like a TV in the daytime.

Ultra-short-throw projectors need screens

Ultra-short-throw projectors have gotten quite popular, or at least their marketing has. These projectors sit just a few inches from the wall/screen, compared to short-throw projectors (a few feet away) and traditional projectors (many feet away). That placement ends up being a significant issue due to how light bounces off flat surfaces. Without diving too far into the physics of it, what happens is that a large amount of light ends up bouncing off the projection surface into your ceiling. This lightshow is distracting, at best, and depending on your ceiling, can reflect enough light back onto the screen to reduce image quality.

The solution is a special type of screen that helps direct light in specific ways to minimize this unwanted scattering. To test UST projectors, I bought a ceiling light-rejecting screen from Elite. The difference is huge. As you can see:

These side-by-side images were taken with the same shutter speed, aperture and UST projector. The only change is the screen. On the left, a traditional white screen. On the right, a CLR screen. Note the extreme light bounce pollution on the ceiling when using the traditional screen and how much darker the entire room is when using the CLR screen. All projectors look better with lower ambient light. The ceiling reflections would be even more pronounced without the screen’s case blocking some of the light. Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

A number of companies make CLR screens, both in fixed, motorized and manually retracting versions. Due to their more complex optical properties, CLR screens are harder to manufacture than traditional models, making them more expensive. This is something often unmentioned or waved away in the marketing for UST projectors. This is especially concerning since UST projectors are more expensive than similarly performing non-UST projectors. As a package, they’re just really expensive, so if you can fit a traditional projector, or even a regular short throw, they’ll be far cheaper, even with a screen.

ALR vs. CLR

CLR screens are a subset of ALR, or ambient light-rejecting screens. Both can minimize the impact of ambient light. As their names suggest, CLR screens work best when the light is coming from above, which is the main issue with UST projectors, but also if you have recessed lighting above the screen. ALR screens are designed for mixed lighting, aka a standard assortment of lamps, windows, etc.

The manufacturers of UST projectors specifically recommend CLR screens, so it’s best to go with that type if you’re getting one of those projectors. For other projectors, an ALR screen is better for most rooms. That said, the best option for non-UST projectors is room light control. Curtains and turning off the lights will work far better than any screen. No screen is magic, but they can help if you have the budget.

Other important factors to consider (digging deeper)

So that’s all the basics, but if we dig deeper, there’s a surprising amount of physics involved in getting an image from a tiny chip inside a projector, through the air and into your eyeballs. The same projector in two different rooms could have radically different performance. Two of the biggest reasons for this are the placement of the projector and the screen.

As mentioned above, a decent screen is crucial to any projector’s performance. This is because all projectors need to reflect off a surface to be seen at all. That surface does a combination of reflection and absorption, both of which are key in how the image appears to you.

Movie theaters use real screens for lots of reasons. GettyImages/dimitri-otis

To understand how screens work, it helps to imagine three different surfaces: a thick black curtain, a mirror and a piece of white paper. Shining onto these surfaces is the light from a projector or, if it’s easier to envision, the light from a flashlight.

Firstly, a curtain will absorb most of the light coming from the projector, and the image will appear dim. The same is true, to a lesser extent, if you’re using a wall instead of a screen. Even brighter shades of paint will absorb more light than a dedicated screen.

A mirror, on the other hand, reflects nearly all the light and in such a way that it’s impossible to see the image. The light bouncing off it travels at a specific angle in relation to how it hits the mirror. This analogy is important for screens because most projectors have an upwards throw, so they’re either mounted above the top of a screen or placed on a stand/table below the screen. If the projection surface was a mirror, most of the light would bounce toward the floor (in the case of a ceiling mount) or the ceiling (in the case of a stand/table). This is the issue I mentioned above regarding ultra-short-throw projectors, since the severe angle they are in relation to the screen means that without a special screen, a lot of light gets wasted on the ceiling.

Sony

Now imagine a piece of white paper that could, theoretically, reflect light evenly. This surface could combine the best properties of the previous two types by enabling you to: 1) see the image, and 2) get most of the light reflected back to you. However, in reality the paper would scatter the light too much, or at least more than what many screens do, so the image wouldn’t be as bright as it could be.

These extremes should give you an idea of what’s necessary with a screen. At its simplest, a screen has to reflect the light evenly so you can see the image. Beyond that, many screens have additional special coatings that can direct or focus the light. Screens with a positive “gain” can make the image appear brighter where you’re sitting, similar to how a lighthouse beacon’s lens focuses the light so boats can see it farther away.

As mentioned above, CLR and ALR screens take this one step further, not only directing light coming from a sharp angle more toward your eyes, but absorbing or redirecting light coming from different angles so the image isn’t as washed out.

A few companies make reflective paint that you can apply directly to your wall instead of using a screen. Even the smoothest of these can have visible texture, which will show up in the image. They also won’t be able to focus the light as much as a higher-gain screen.

Improving brightness

If a screen isn’t in your budget but you want to improve how your projector looks, there are a few things you can do to improve the image’s brightness. They’re not going to transform a dim projector into a bright one, but they’ll help.

Size : The first, and perhaps most obvious, is to just make the image smaller. If you don’t have a screen, either at all or yet, experiment with zoom or placement to make the image smaller. A small decrease in size can greatly increase how bright the image is.

: The first, and perhaps most obvious, is to just make the image smaller. If you don’t have a screen, either at all or yet, experiment with zoom or placement to make the image smaller. A small decrease in size can greatly increase how bright the image is. Lamp and laser/LED settings : Most projectors have a setting to increase lamp power to increase brightness. This, unfortunately, has some side effects. A brighter lamp won’t last as long (not an issue with LED and laser-based projectors), so you’ll be replacing it more often. This usually means the projector’s fans will run more and at higher speeds, increasing noise in your room. Some projectors have a Dynamic lamp mode (or another feature with a similar name), which increases the lamp power for bright scenes and decreases it for dark scenes. Typically these extremes are the same as the projector in its brightest and darkest modes.

Picture settings : We recommend settings to make your projector look its best, but usually that comes at a cost of overall light output. A less accurate mode, either a cooler “bluer” color temperature, or less accurate color mode, will either make the image actually brighter, or at least appear brighter. The cost here is a worse looking image, however.

New lamp?: If you bought the projector used, or you’ve had it for a while, it’s possible replacing the lamp (if applicable) will make the image much brighter. Many projectors will have a lamp hour counter in the menu that tells you roughly how old the lamp is. You can check online to see how close this is to the recommended replacement life. If you bought it used, it’s possible the seller reset this counter, so be skeptical if it’s a few years old with no hours on the lamp. If you’ve replaced a still-working lamp, save it in case something happens with the new lamp. That way you’ll still have something while you wait for a new replacement. Avoid third-party or knock-off replacement lamps though, as they might be dim compared to their “real” counterparts. However, modern LED and laser projectors don’t have lamps, and so aren’t susceptible to this issue.

Beyond that, it’s just about getting a brighter projector. Fortunately, we’ve got a few picks along those lines.

Tech.title: The Clicks Communicator Ships in December With More RAM and New Mobile Service
Tech.content:
At a time when nearly every phone-maker is raising prices and cutting memory, one company is bucking the trend by adding more RAM.

The $649 Blackberry-inspired Clicks Communicator phone will launch in December, but the company behind it just announced that the unreleased handset will have a larger battery and more RAM than originally expected. Clicks Technology, better known for its keyboard cases and Power Keyboard accessory, released a video on Friday sharing a number of upgrades, feature details and news about the launch.

The Clicks Communicator will ship with 12GB of RAM (up from the promised 8GB) and a 4,350-mAh battery (up from 4,000 mAh). Given this year’s trends, it is absolutely wild that the company is adding more RAM while keeping the previously announced preorder price of $499. Google, Motorola, Samsung and, most recently, Apple, have raised prices on most of their phones, including the new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, citing higher RAM and component costs driven by the increased demand for memory by AI data centers.

Clicks Technology announced the keyboard phone at CES in January. The marquee feature is a built-in physical keyboard that is similar to the one found on the company’s keyboard cases. The design was inspired in part by using a Motorola Razr’s cover screen inside a Clicks keyboard case for the phone. After receiving an unexpectedly high number of preorders, Clicks was able to upgrade the design and features, including the processor.

I took this photo in March. On the left is a dummy prototype of the Clicks Communicator, and next to it is a Motorola Razr (closed) inside a Clicks Keyboard case. Notice the Razr has the Niagara launcher on its cover screen. Patrick Holland/CNET

Turns out, plenty of people want a thoughtfully designed handset that combines old-school features — including a keyboard, dedicated notification light and headphone jack — with a modern smartphone focused on messaging, calls and efficiency. The Communicator, designed by a former BlackBerry designer, is the phone I’ve been looking forward to most this year.

People who preordered the Clicks Communicator can now configure their phone’s color, keyboard layout, charging covers and accessories on the company’s website. If you’re considering buying one, you can preorder it for $499 ($150 off) until Sept. 30.

The Communicator is sold unlocked, meaning that you can use your current carrier’s nano SIM card or eSIM with it. But you also have the option to use the company’s new voice and data service for phone called Clicks Mobile. It’ll run on AT&T in the US and Vodafone in the UK.

The video also showcases a number of Communicator features in depth. Here are a handful that stood out.

The Communicator will ship with the game Brick Breaker. Patrick Holland/CNET

Clicks Care

You can extend the warranty beyond a year and add accidental damage protection. “If something happens, even from day one, we’ll ship you a replacement,” says Jeff Gadway, Clicks Technology co-founder, in the video. Clicks Care will be available in the US and Canada for $129 for two years.

Prompt Key

While the physical keyboard is the main attraction, you can press the Prompt Key for speech-to-text input. The feature is powered by an on-device model, but Clicks Technology is exploring ways for Communicator owners to use other apps and services for voice input. The Prompt Key can also be used to bring up Gemini when you’re not in a text field.

Signal Light

An LED loop around the Prompt Key glows in different colors for calendar reminders, tasks and to indicate incoming calls and messages. You can customize the Signal Light with different colors for different contacts and priorities. The light will flash in different patterns to distinguish between a call and a message. This is what Pixel HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro Max should have been; instead, that sits mostly dormant on the back of the phone and only glows during calls or when Gemini is “listening” to a prompt.

Quick replies

You can read and respond to message previews straight from the home screen, without opening the app. Gadway explains that the company is working to make it possible to reply and dismiss message previews using just keyboard shortcuts: No need to touch the screen.

Message Hub is a quick way to reply to messages without having to open apps. Patrick Holland/CNET

Message Hub

A curated pop-up on the home screen, the hub prioritizes incoming message notifications according to your Signal Light preferences. You can hop into the Message Hub at any time by pressing the Prompt Key or the Clicks Key on the keyboard.

Customizable hardware keyboard

The physical keyboard has a red Clicks Key that can be used to trigger shortcuts, similar to Click’s keyboard cases and the Power Keyboard. You can also reassign the bottom-row keys to take screenshots, switch between apps and perform other tasks.

Locking your phone

You can lock the Click Communicator by double-tapping the app list on the home screen. The phone uses a special version of Niagara Launcher, which displays apps in a list that you can navigate by sliding your finger along the right side of the screen.

The Saffiano leather charging covers will cost $79. Patrick Holland/CNET

MagSafe charging covers

The phone supports 15W Qi2 wireless charging and has a swappable backplate available in a variety of colors. There will be two Saffiano leather charging covers.

Case, bumper and screen protector

Accessory maker Dbrand is creating a $39 case for the new phone called MNML (pronounced “minimal”) and a $35 screen protector. Clicks is selling its own bumper case for $49 — it gives off a strong iPhone 4 bumper vibe.

Tech.title: What ‘Optimizing Search and Siri’ Means in iOS 27 and How to Speed It Up
Tech.content:
If you’ve updated your iPhone to iOS 27, don’t be alarmed if you see a message that reads “Optimizing Search and Siri” in Settings. The message means iOS is rebuilding its search index, a necessary process after this major iOS update because the update implements a brand-new search infrastructure, and the system cannot simply update your existing index. It must crawl through your entire storage drive from scratch.

You can download iOS 27 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

At June’s Worldwide Developers Conference, Apple announced that it was rebuilding its Search interface for iOS 27. The company said the restructure would make searching across your device faster, more reliable and more accurate. In order to do that, iOS 27 has to reindex items across your iPhone. So after you update, you’ll see a banner in Settings that reads “Optimizing Search and Siri.” This is a normal part of the update, and it could take a while to finish, but the good news is you can still use your iPhone during this process.

Here’s what you need to know about the indexing and optimization process once you download iOS 27.

What is indexing?

Data indexing is the process of scanning and organizing metadata from data assets into an index so it can be easily searched.



“Think of it like the index of a book,” data management company Komprise wrote online. “[The index] doesn’t hold the content, but it tells you where to find it, and what’s inside.”

Apple’s support page about Spotlight indexing says that Spotlight search indexes your iPhone when you first set up your device, as data changes on your device and after you update your iPhone. So your device has reindexed before and you likely never noticed – I know I didn’t.

Apple also notes that your iPhone’s index “stays on your device and isn’t shared with Apple or your other devices.”

Indexing can take hours or days

You can still use your iPhone, even when it’s indexing. LuckyDuck via Getty Images

Apple’s support page notes that indexing could take anywhere from a couple hours to a few days. When I updated my iPhone to a beta version of iOS 27, my iPhone took a couple hours to index, but the more stuff you have stored on your phone, the longer it will take.

The process takes longer this time around because Apple rebuilt its Search interface in iOS 27. So the update isn’t just adding a few more things to the index, it’s implementing a new search system.

That means the system isn’t just crawling through the new stuff — it needs to go back through all the data in your phone. Think of it like cataloging new items you’ve bought versus creating an inventory of everything in your home.

Apple does offer a few suggestions on how to speed up the process:

Plug your device into a power source.

Connect your device to Wi-Fi.

Don’t use your iPhone.

OK, can I still use my iPhone?

You can! Indexing doesn’t prevent you from using your iPhone, but it goes faster if you set the phone aside.

If you do use your iPhone during the process, your Spotlight search results might be incomplete because it hasn’t finished indexing. Otherwise, your device should operate as usual. Which is good because I couldn’t imagine going without my phone for a few days at this point – don’t judge me.

Spotlight search still not working?

If your iPhone is finished indexing – the banner in Settings will go away – and you’re still running into issues, you should review your Search settings and make sure Spotlight has access to your apps. Here’s how to check.

Tap Settings. Tap Search.

From here, you can adjust what shows up in Spotlight, and near the bottom of the menu, you can review which apps Spotlight has access to. You can tap into each app to grant or revoke Spotlight permission.

However, there doesn’t seem to be a way to grant or revoke Spotlight access across all apps at once, so you have to go into each individual app to do this.

For more on Apple, here’s what to know about iOS 27, the iPhone Duo and everything Apple announced at its “Surprise and shine” event.

Tech.title: Today’s NYT Strands Hints, Answers and Help for Sept. 18, #929
Tech.content:
Looking for the most recent NYT Strands puzzle answers? CNET publishes daily answers and hints for The New York Times Mini Crossword, Connections, Connections: Sports Edition and Strands puzzles.

Strands is like a word find game, but without the list of words to find. Sometimes I see the theme and begin recognizing the answers right away. But for those times when I can’t seem to manage this, there’s a loophole: Strands lets you make as many words of four or more letters as you want. For every three of those words you find, the puzzle will highlight one of the answers. You’re still going to have to unscramble that answer, though, which can be very tough.

I go into depth about the rules for Strands in this story.

Today’s puzzle isn’t too tough, though some of the answers are tricky to unscramble. Read on for hints and all the answers.



Hint for today’s Strands puzzle

Today’s Strands theme is: Shake on it.

If that doesn’t help you, here’s a clue: Shared understanding.

Clue words to unlock in-game hints

Your goal is to find hidden words that fit the puzzle’s theme. If you’re stuck, find any words you can. Every time you find three words of four letters or more, Strands will reveal one of the theme words. These are the words I used to get those hints, but any words of four or more letters that you find will work:

MALE, LAME, STAY, RAGE, MEAL, COAT, STEAM, TRACT, TEAL, STEAL

Answers for today’s Strands puzzle

These are the answers that tie into the theme. The goal of the puzzle is to find them all, including the “spangram,” a theme word that reaches from one side of the puzzle to the other. When you have all of them (I originally thought there were always eight, but learned that the number can vary), every letter on the board will be used. Here are the nonspangram answers:

PACT, TREATY, CONTRACT, COVENANT, AGREEMENT

Today’s Strands spangram

The completed NYT Strands puzzle for Sept. 18, 2026. NYT/Screenshot by CNET

Today’s Strands spangram is LETSMAKEADEAL. To find it, start with the L that’s two letters over on the top row, and wind down.

Tech.title: Congratulations, World: A New Supercute Cat Species Has Been Found
Tech.content:
In the midst of RAMageddon price hikes and AI doomsday claims, I bring soothing news: A tiny new feline species has been discovered, the first in over 100 years, and it’s amazingly adorable.

According to a study published in the Current Biology Journal on Thursday, the spry little feline, who looks ready for a drink out of a nice, heated cat water fountain, is called Leopardus tilcayo and hails from the cloud forests of the Bolivian Yungas in South America. You may know Leopardus from other American cat species, like the ocelot and colocolo.

The discovery was made from a collaboration between scientist Jonas Lescroart and Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, head of the Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia conservation program (among other researchers). They not only spotted this dashing little fellow, but they also made all-new discoveries about tiger cats, including a new subspecies.

The researchers didn’t need an AI pet camera to spot the new cat species, although Leopardus tilcayo is even smaller than the common house cat. Nogales-Ascarrunz, whose work is funded by National Geographic, first spotted the cat at a wildlife rehabilitation center in the area. At first, she thought it was just a kitten, but then she realized it could be a new find entirely. The cat’s spots and long tail didn’t match any recognized species in the area, so Nogales-Ascarrunz began genetic testing on cats brought in by locals.

Who named this fuzzy charmer?

Paola Nogles-Ascarrunz kept the cat’s original name from the natives who’ve known it the longest. Fernando Faciole/National Geographic

The story of Leopardus tilcayo has its roots in native communities.

“This cat, they call it tilcayo. And when you ask, ‘Does it have some meaning in Quechua or [Aymara] and other Indigenous languages?’ they say, ‘No, my grandpa told me that’s the tilcayo,’” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This is a traditional knowledge that they have in the community. We want to preserve that knowledge, and we didn’t want to give it another name.”

The tilcayo is special because, while scientists redefine mammals into new species all the time, it’s usually because a single species has split into two and become different enough for reclassification. This cat, however, was entirely new and not the offshoot of a previously recognized species, something very rare and probably deserving of its own high-tech litter box.

“We really don’t know how many cats are still in the wild,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “We need science, we need more studies to answer this question, which is actually critical for its conservation.”

I want one!

Leopardus tilcayo may be new to us, but its habitat has long been under threat. Fernando Faciole/National Geographic

Instead of pining after exotic and protected species, I highly suggest you focus on local cats that need a home and provide them with toys, smart feeding stations or helpful collars that can help keep them safe and healthy.

If you do want to get involved, look into supporting conversation efforts for the Bolivian Yungas, such as the Andes Amazon Fund. Tilcayo’s habitat is under serious threat from surrounding development and could use all the help it can get.

The authors of the research did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: A NASA Scientist Found a Huge New Crater on the Moon by Accident
Tech.content:
The moon has more than 2 million craters on its surface, but the overwhelming majority of the big ones happened long before humans ever started looking at it. That means when someone notices a new big crater, it’s a pretty big deal, and that’s exactly what happened when NASA’s Lunar Orbiter found a brand-new crater it had never seen before that was large enough to get someone’s attention.

The crater was spotted by NASA scientist Robert Wagner on a routine data-quality check and published in an article in Science Advances. Wagner says the object that crashed into the moon and created the crater likely hit sometime between April 11, 2024, and May 22, 2024, and was likely about the size of a six-story building. It left a rather sizable dent, which now has the distinction of being the biggest new crater ever spotted by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

“I just stopped, dropped everything, and started looking into what that spot was,” Wagner said in a statement.

The LRO scans the entire moon’s surface once every 14 days, meaning humans have a constant stream of new data about the surface, and since the moon has no atmosphere, its pockmarked surface remains largely intact until another asteroid or meteor barrels into it.

NASA says that the LRO has found approximately 1,000 new impact craters and over 100,000 other changes to the moon’s surface during its 17 years in service. Since the satellite can see craters only about 30 feet wide or larger, that also means many small impacts go virtually unnoticed, leaving the total number of changes to the moon’s surface a mystery.

One big hole

The new crater, circled in the left image, may not look like much, but it’s unlikely to happen again until the next century. NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner

What makes this particular crater special is that it’s huge. At 728 feet wide, it’s more than twice the size of a football field, and at 141 feet deep is about the length of three yellow school buses stacked end to end. Impact craters that big don’t show up every day, every year or even every decade.

“Crater production models indicate that an impact of this magnitude is expected to occur only once every 132 years on the moon,” Wagner wrote in the article. “As such, this event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively one-in-a-lifetime observation.”

It’s the latest in a pretty busy year for the moon, which had human visitors for the first time in 50 years with the Artemis II mission before an abandoned SpaceX rocket crash-landed into it, which left a crater substantially smaller than the one Wagner found.

NASA named the crater McGetchin, after Tom McGetchin, a scientist who became the director of the Lunar Science Institute in 1977, shortly before his death in 1979.

Tech.title: iPhone 18 Pro vs. Pixel 11 Pro: The New Apple and Google Pro Phones Are Quite Different
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo might have stolen the spotlight at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event last week, but the latest high-end iPhone 18 Pro remains the go-to option for creatives. With the inclusion of variable aperture that can control light exposure for photography and long battery life, Apple’s new Pro phone is well equipped for media capture. But the new model is more expensive than ever. At its $1,199 starting price, the phone is $100 more than the base iPhone 17 Pro and Google’s new $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro.

While Google’s Pixel 11 Pro received its own $100 price hike over last year’s 10 Pro — likely influenced by the ongoing memory shortage that’s making electronics more expensive — the phone also received camera upgrades like a larger sensor on its 48-megapixel telephoto camera that promises a 30% increase in light capture (versus the 10 Pro). That telephoto camera supports the 11 Pro’s 30x digital zoom as well as its 120x Pro Zoom — the latter using generative AI to clean up photos taken at that distance.

Both phones have a big focus on photography, but after that, Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Google’s Pixel 11 Pro differ dramatically. They have designs that will suit different crowds and functions, and spotlight the best of iOS 27 and Android 17, respectively. I’ve taken a closer look at each phone’s biggest features, so you can figure out whether the iPhone 18 Pro or the Pixel 11 Pro is the better fit for you.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro vs. Google Pixel 11 Pro: Design and display

The Google Pixel 11 Pro brought some fun colors. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While the iPhone 18 Pro and the Pixel 11 Pro have similar designs to the phones they’ve replaced — the iPhone 17 Pro and the Pixel 10 Pro, respectively — each phone has an entirely different style.

The iPhone 18 Pro sports an aluminum unibody design and, this year, a cleaner monotone look rather than the dual-tone finish of the 17 Pro. The 18 Pro comes in four colors: burgundy red, glacier blue, silver and black.

The back of the Pixel 11 Pro highlights its full-width camera bar with an added edge-to-edge glass for a more uniform look. It comes in canyon (an orange-pinkish shade), fog white, olive green and obsidian black. Both the Pixel and the iPhone have color-matching frames, giving them a seamless look. In the hand, the Pixel 11 Pro will feel lighter than the iPhone 18 Pro, with the phones weighing in at 204 grams and 211 grams, respectively — in both cases roughly the same as a medium apple.

Both phones have a 6.3-inch OLED display with support for a dynamic 120Hz refresh rate, and are IP68-rated for water and dust resistance — making them safe to take to environments like the beach where sand and water won’t get inside.

The Dynamic Island is smaller on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max (right) than last year’s 17 Pro Max (left). Patrick Holland/CNET

On the iPhone, there’s a new, smaller Dynamic Island that serves as the cutout for the selfie camera and Apple’s Face ID sensor. That space can now show up to three Live Activities at once, letting you glance at active timers or the status of a rideshare vehicle that’s en route to pick you up. The display is protected with Ceramic Shield 2, which is the same as the 17 Pro, and it has held up quite well after a year of use, so I expect similar durability here.

The Pixel 11 Pro has a traditional selfie camera cutout on the front, but its display should shine brighter in sunny environments with its 3,600-nit peak brightness. The iPhone 18 Pro, by comparison, has an also-bright 3,000-nit peak brightness. Google’s display sports Corning’s Gorilla Glass Victus 2 protection, and includes an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor underneath the screen. The Pixel 11 Pro also supports facial identification that is assisted by its front-facing camera and machine learning.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro vs. Google Pixel 11 Pro cameras

The iPhone 18 Pro supports variable aperture on its main camera. Patrick Holland/CNET

Apple and Google have worked on camera advancements in both hardware and software on their latest phones.

The iPhone 18 Pro has a variable aperture on its 48-megapixel main camera. It can manually adjust the aperture between four options (ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, and ƒ/4.0 f-stops) to control the amount of light hitting the sensor. It is accompanied by a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 48-megapixel telephoto sensor with support for 4x optical zoom and 8x hybrid zoom.

CNET’s Patrick Holland confirmed in his review that the aperture automatically adjusts itself when shooting between 1x and 3.9x magnification. It is great for shutterbugs and can shoot some amazing shots in the dark.

In comparison, the Google Pixel 11 Pro has a 50-megapixel main camera, a bigger 48-megapixel telephoto sensor with 5x optical zoom, and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. It’s got a new Camera Looks feature for built-in color profiles. CNET’s Andrew Lanxon tested and enjoyed using it: “I don’t think Google takes full advantage of this tool yet, but it’s a step in the right direction and a welcome addition for casual shutterbugs who love to simply snap away without worrying about editing later.”

For selfies, you get an 18-megapixel front camera on the new iPhone and a 42-megapixel front camera on the Google phone. Apple’s smarts include automatic framing based on the number of people in the selfie — letting you switch between horizontal and vertical without rotating your phone — and Pro controls to quickly adjust settings like aperture and shutter speed, among other things. On the other hand, the Pixel has a new Magic Capture mode (on the rear cameras), which records a short video clip and then uses AI to select the best still frames from it — and you can manually pick your favorite stills as well.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro vs. Google Pixel 11 Pro: processor and battery

The Pixel 11 Pro’s display is impressive, but its gaming performance isn’t exceptional. David Lumb/CNET

Apple’s new iPhone runs on the in-house A20 Pro chip, which is based on the 2nm process. That means the processor is denser and may have helped make room for the 18 Pro to get a larger vapor chamber to help keep the phone running cool under intensive use. In his review, Patrick said that “gaming on the iPhone 18 Pro Max has been a blast.”

He notes that the iPhone 18 Pro got warm only when downloading apps and game files (some as large as 28GB) or when charging — but not to the extent that it would be a concern. This is one of the best improvements since my iPhone 17 Pro Max used to get warm in regular use, depending on the ambient temperature.

For comparison, the Pixel 11 Pro has the new Tensor G6 processor, which powers new software and camera tricks. In my usage, it has been smooth in daily life. However, it gets warm to the touch in 10 minutes or more of gaming. While the Pixel 11 Pro’s screen makes games look good, CNET Managing Editor David Lumb finds the phone underpowered for gaming, noticing it struggles with higher graphics settings. The iPhone remains a better choice if you’re a mobile gamer, and Apple’s App Store includes several console-quality games for the iPhone that, when purchased, also work for Mac and Apple TV.

Another Apple upgrade comes in the form of battery life. The iPhone 18 Pro is claimed to last longer and charge faster than its predecessor. In CNET’s review, Patrick pointed out that the battery life “matches that of the 17 Pro and Pro Max.” It can last an entire day, but when you push it to the limits and drain the battery, it can charge faster than before.

In our 30-minute wired charging test, the 18 Pro went from empty to 82% charge. In the same test, the Pixel 11 Pro went from 55% to 88% with its 30-watt charging speed. If you opt for the Pro XL model, you get faster 45-watt charging, which can deliver more charge in the same amount of time.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro vs. Google Pixel 11 Pro: Extra features

The iPhone 18 Pro runs iOS 27, which squashes bugs and comes with a new set of features. It has improved voice-to-text capabilities and a smoother user interface. The new Apple iPhone also offers Focus Tracking and Reference Image features in the Camera app. The former can help you track a subject more efficiently, while Reference Image is like a digital version of a film negative. It grabs the pixel data at the time the image was taken before it goes through Apple’s image pipeline, so you can check the authenticity of the photo. That can be especially helpful since many Apple Intelligence features let you alter photos substantially, such as how Spatial Reframing lets you adjust the angle of a subject using generative AI.

On the other hand, the Pixel 11 Pro has many new Gemini Intelligence features, such as voice-to-text capabilities (Rambler) that filter out filler words when sending a message, or the ability to communicate in ASL via the Pixel camera. I’ve also enjoyed the new Camera Looks, while HiLight (a notification light on the camera bar that’s initially just for phone calls and Gemini) has been disappointing. Overall, both phones offer unique smart features to enhance your experience.

Tech.title: I Used AI to Animate Old Family Photos. One Was Creepy, but the Other Was Heartwarming
Tech.content:
I miss the time when things were more tangible. Photo albums, CDs, cameras and books. Nowadays, everything is centralized on one device or stored in the cloud, sometimes accidentally erased, not always owned by you and forever out of sight. But it’s this very technology that can also bring these memories and milestones back into focus, with a little help from AI.

The hug your younger self photo was a fun example, but I wanted to take it further and animate some old photos to turn them into a gift. It can make a good gift if you’ve got a big family birthday or a wedding anniversary coming up, and it can also be a beautiful way to keep a loved one who has passed close, if the AI is accurate enough in regenerating your moments. It could also be a special exercise to connect family members who have never met, like grandparents and their grandkids.

I came across AliveMoment, a moving-memory tool, which is essentially image-to-video technology. I chose this product for its no-prompt process, as well as its photo restoration features, because that grainy old photo look won’t fly here. AliveMoment was released in August 2025 and runs on a credit-based subscription model (more on that later).

Time for a walk down memory lane.

Getting set up

The biggest issue I had was hunting down my old photos, as many are in boxes and hard drives back in Australia, where I grew up. Most of my photos live on my Facebook profile or in the cloud, so I needed to spend some time going through what I had.

I wanted to find a photo of my grandparents, who I think about often. I always felt as though they were my parents, as they were big travelers and migrated from England to Australia. I’ve traveled to more than 50 countries and moved to America, while my parents never even had a passport.

So, my first task was to do some digging. I found a couple of cute baby photos with my siblings, as well as one with my nanna, but the quality of all three was bad.

I uploaded one of them to AliveMoment to see what options I had to improve it. I could choose between a few animation types, including adding a wave or a hug. Given this first photo was of my siblings and me, I selected “playful motion.”

AliveMoment/Screenshot by CNET

To proceed, I was prompted to sign up, and it processed the photo for a few seconds before my “live moment” was ready. But before I could view it, I had to purchase a subscription. Check the fine print because although it’s presented as per-credit pricing, you’re charged the first week, month or two months upfront. I chose the cheapest plan ($2.47 per “moment” credit) just to test it out.

Make sure you delete it before it renews, as that weekly plan is $60 per month, and this isn’t the kind of AI tool you need a recurring subscription for. I’ve noticed a lot of AI tools have sneaky pricing structures like this, most likely to capture as many one-time customers as possible.

Creepy or heart-warming?

Next, I got into the dashboard and could see the full range of features. I could restore, retake or relive a photo. I reuploaded the photo of my siblings to turn it into a motion photo. I had to use an extra credit for it to be in color.

Here was the original photo:

Amanda Smith/CNET

And this was the short video AI animated:

Amanda Smith/AliveMoment

Creepy. It doesn’t look like us.

Next, I wanted to see if it could do better with adults. I uploaded a photo of my nanna and me, and picked the “warm hug” animation.

This was the original still:

Amanda Smith/CNET

And this was the video:

Amanda Smith/AliveMoment

And oh my gosh, this pulled at my heart when I watched it. It captured our connection and even got my dimple. I’ll be saving this video on my phone. Worth $9.90.

At this point, I ran out of coins. If you were going to use Alivemoment for a bigger animation project, not just bringing to life single photos, you’d need to buy the top plan, but it doesn’t come cheap.

The verdict on using AI to animate old photos

I don’t think it’s worth doing for baby photos, as AI can only predict future features, especially when using old, low-quality photos. Use it for adult stills, as it’s much more accurate.

I can see many different fun use cases for animated memories. I’ll keep repeating this exercise as the technology improves over time. I’m especially interested in watching what AI can do for the bereaved.
